paragraphs.text: "Hey, Henry! Come out here!"
Henry looked out the window and saw his cousin waving at him from the sidewalk in front of his house. Maggie was nine years old and lived next door. Her mom and Henry's mom were sisters.
"What do you want?" Henry called down to Maggie. "I'm busy."
He glanced at his computer. He'd just finished lunch, and now he was playing his favorite game, Puzzle Pirates. All he had to do was solve one more puzzle, and he would reach Level Ten.
"Just come down here!" Maggie yelled again.

Henry sighed. He was two years older than Maggie, but that didn't stop her from bossing him around. His best friend, Cole, always told him that he should just ignore her. But Maggie was usually so loud and dramatic, she was hard to ignore!
Henry turned off his computer and headed outside.
Maggie was waiting for him and holding a handmade cardboard sign.
"Look at this," she said. "Isn't it awesome?"
The sign read:
MAGGIE'S LEMONADE STAND
ONE CUP: 25 cents
TWO CUPS: 45 cents
BELLTOWN'S BEST BEVERAGE!
Maggie was very artistic. She'd drawn a glass of lemonade below the words. It looked so realistic that it made Henry thirsty.
"Great sign," Henry said. "Maybe I'll buy a cup."
"You won't have to," Maggie said. "You'll get your lemonade for free."
Henry was instantly suspicious. If Maggie was running a lemonade stand to make money, why would she give away the lemonade for free?
"What do you mean?" he asked.
She grinned. "You'll get it for free because you're an employee," she said. "I hereby hire you to help me with my lemonade stand."
Henry rolled his eyes. "Are you kidding me?" he said. "Lemonade stands are for babies."
Maggie scowled. "No, they're not!"
"Yes, they are," Henry said. "Why do you want to do something like that anyway?"

"Mom and Dad said I can take horseback-riding lessons if I pay half of the cost myself," Maggie explained. "I figured I could make lots of money selling lemonade while it's hot out. I'll switch to hot chocolate when the weather turns cold."
"Sounds like a good plan," Henry said.
"So you'll help?" Maggie looked excited.
"Nope," Henry said.
Maggie tried to change his mind. She promised him all the free lemonade he could drink. Then she told him he could have 10 percent of the profits.
Henry just shook his head. "No, thanks," he said. "Good luck with your new business. I'm going to Cole's."

He walked over to Cole's house on the next block. The two of them played soccer for a while in Cole's yard. Then they headed back to Henry's house to play Puzzle Pirates. On the way they passed Maggie's lemonade stand.

The stand was a table set up on the sidewalk in front of Maggie's house. Two teenage girls were standing nearby sipping lemonade from paper cups. A boy with a skateboard was chugging his lemonade. A little boy clung to his mother's hand while she leaned against the table and talked on her cell phone.
Maggie was nearby chatting with a kid named Nathan and his little sister, Nora. It looked as if Nathan and Nora had just returned from the local swimming pool. Their bathing suits were still wet.
When Maggie spotted Henry and Cole coming, she hurried to meet them. "Want some lemonade?" she asked. "It's a dollar per cup."
"A dollar?" Henry said. "I thought you were charging 25 cents."
"Yeah!" Cole pointed to the sign. "It's written right there. See?"
Maggie tossed her head. "That's the price for normal people. Rotten cousins and their friends get charged extra."
"Fine. I wasn't thirsty anyway," Henry said, rolling his eyes. "Come on, Cole. We have plenty of soda at my house."
They started to walk away. But Maggie ran after them.

"Stop. I was just kidding," she said. "I'll sell you lemonade for fifty cents per cup." When the boys kept walking, she tried again. "Okay, okay! Twenty cents. That's my special price for cousins and friends of cousins."
"You have a deal," Cole said, turning around.
Henry and Cole headed back to the lemonade stand. Maggie poured them each a cup of lemonade. Henry fished some change out of his pocket to pay for it.
Cole took a sip. "Hey, this lemonade is really good!"
Maggie smiled. "It's the best in town," she bragged. "Everyone says so. I've made a ton of money already!"
She opened the cashbox on her table to put the boys' money away. When she looked inside the box, she gasped.
"Oh no!" she cried. "My money is gone!"
"Who stole my money?" Maggie yelled loudly.
"Maggie," Henry warned, "you have to have proof before you start accusing people of stealing." He looked into the cashbox that Maggie was holding. It was completely empty.
"Are you sure you didn't take the money out and put it in your pocket or something?" he asked her.
"Yeah," Cole said. "You probably put the money somewhere."
"No way!" Maggie looked really upset now. "There was a lot of cash in here five minutes ago when Mrs. Martin paid for little Marty's lemonade."

She pointed to the woman standing nearby, who was still talking on her cell phone. The little boy, Marty Martin, had dropped his mother's hand. He was staring at Maggie and banging a toy suitcase against his knees.
"Okay," Henry said. "Then maybe the money blew away when you opened the box."
"It's not even windy today," Maggie said. She shook her head. "I think someone stole my horseback-riding money. And I want to know who it was!"
By now everyone except Mrs. Martin was staring at her. The two teenage girls giggled and whispered to each other. Maggie looked at them.
"Was it you two?" she asked. "Did you take my money?"
"No," one of the girls said. "We're not crooks. Come on, Jill, let's get out of here."
"Yeah." Her friend giggled. "Before she accuses us of something else!"
The two of them laughed and walked off. Maggie glared at them, and then looked around again.
"Maybe it was Ryan!" she said. Ryan had finished chugging his lemonade. Now he was jumping his skateboard on and off the curb.
"Did you steal my money when I wasn't looking?" Maggie asked.
He stopped and stared at Maggie. "Dude, I didn't take your money. Maybe you should have watched it better," he said. Then he skated off down the street.
"Hey! Get back here!" Maggie yelled. But Ryan ignored her, skidding around the corner.
Nathan and his little sister Nora were listening to everything. "It wasn't me," Nathan said before Maggie could say anything to him. "I promise."
"Are you sure?" Maggie said. "It had to be someone!"
Nora poked her brother. "I think I hear Mommy calling us," she said.
"I didn't hear anything," Henry said.
"Me neither. But I'd better go check," Nathan said. "Come on, Nora, let's go home."
"No!" Nora said. She loved to argue. "I don't want to!"
Nathan was used to her, so he just ignored her. But when he rushed off toward their house, she hurried after him.
Maggie was looking around for more possible thieves. "Where did Mrs. Martin and Marty go?" she asked.
"They left." Cole pointed down the block.
Henry looked and saw Mrs. Martin wandering away. Her cell phone was still pressed to her ear. Little Marty was skipping along after her.
"I don't think you need to accuse Mrs. Martin of being the thief," Henry said. "She's a police detective, remember?"
Cole nodded. "She catches thieves—she's not one herself," he said.
"Maybe you're right." Maggie frowned. "But someone stole my money, and I want to know who it was."
"Calm down," Henry told his cousin. "You're not going to figure it out by yelling at everyone."
"How else am I going to get an answer?" Maggie asked.
"Think about it logically," Henry said. "Whoever took that money is a thief, which means he or she is probably a liar too."
"Good point," Cole said with a nod. "Guess you'd better say good-bye to that money, Maggie."
Maggie scowled at him. "Be quiet, Cole!"
"She doesn't need to give up," Henry told his friend. "We just need to think like detectives. I bet if the three of us work together, we can figure out who took the money."
"We're just kids," Maggie said. "How are we supposed to think like detectives?"
"I know!" Cole said. "I watched a mystery movie on TV last week. The detective started by figuring out who the suspects were."
"We already know that," Maggie interrupted. "It had to be someone who was nearby when the money disappeared."
Henry smiled. "See? We're already thinking like detectives," he said. "Okay, so we know approximately when the money disappeared. Who was nearby during that time?"
"You just saw them," Maggie said. "Nathan and Nora, Mrs. Martin and Marty, Ryan, and those two teenage girls. Oh, and you two of course."
"Nobody else stopped by before Henry and I got here?" Cole asked. "Like a stranger or a suspicious-looking deliveryman?"
Maggie shook her head. "Nope. Just the people you saw."
Cole bit his lip. "That means the thief had to be someone we know."
They all looked at each other.
"It's someone from our very own neighborhood!" said Henry.
"It's weird to think that someone from our neighborhood is a thief," Cole said.
"I know," Henry agreed. "But Maggie's money is gone, which means that someone stole it. All we have to do now is figure out who it was."
"Who are the suspects again?" Cole asked.

Maggie sighed. "Weren't you listening?" she said. "There were only a few people close enough to the lemonade stand to grab the money. They were Nathan and Nora, Mrs. Martin and Marty, Ryan, and those two teenage girls."
"I doubt it was Nathan," Cole said. "He's a nice kid."
Henry nodded. Nathan was the same age as him and Cole, and everyone liked him. Kids liked him because he was always smiling and loved to have fun.
"That little sister of his is kind of weird though," Maggie pointed out. "She's always making up crazy stories and dressing up in funny costumes and stuff."
"Nora is a bit strange," Henry agreed. "But being weird isn't the same as being a thief. Plus she's only five years old. That's pretty young to steal money from a cashbox."
"What about Ryan, that kid who skateboards all the time?" Maggie said. "He's always getting in trouble at school."
Ryan was three years younger than Henry. Henry had seen him around, but he didn't know Ryan very well.
"What kind of trouble?" Henry asked Maggie.
She shrugged. "Mostly teachers get mad at him for goofing off and not paying attention in class."
"I heard he skateboarded into his neighbor's flowers," Cole said. "He got in big trouble for that!"
"That doesn't make him a thief," Henry said. "But he seems like a better suspect than the others. Let's go find him and talk to him."
Maggie put a cover on her pitcher of lemonade so bugs wouldn't get in it. Then the three kids headed down the block in the direction that Ryan had gone.
"What are we going to say when we find him?" Cole asked.
"I know what I want to say." Maggie frowned. "I want to tell him to give me back my money! Otherwise I'll break his skateboard in half!"
"I don't think that's a good idea, Maggie," Henry told her. "We're not going to threaten Ryan. We're just going to ask him a few questions, like my dad does when he's interviewing someone."

Henry's father was a journalist who wrote stories for the local newspaper. He liked to say that his job was one part writing, one part asking questions, and three parts listening. That was because he spent so much time interviewing people and listening to their answers.
"Wait. We're going to ask Ryan a few questions?" Cole said. "I can only think of one question: Did you take the money?"
"Yeah," Maggie said. "And I already asked him that."
Henry had just spotted Ryan up ahead. The skateboarder was practicing kick flips. His baggy shorts fluttered when he jumped, and his sneakers squeaked when he landed.
"Just listen and play along," Henry whispered to Cole and Maggie. "I'm going to interview Ryan, just like Dad would. We might learn something by listening to his answers."
The other two looked skeptical. But Henry hurried forward.
"Hi, Ryan," he called out. "Can I talk to you for a second?"
Ryan finished his flip, and then rolled over to Henry on his skateboard. "Sure, dude. What do you want to talk about?" He grinned, shoving both hands in his pockets.
Henry smiled back. "We're just trying to find out what happened to Maggie's money. Since you were there, we thought you might have seen who took it."
"Nope. Sorry." Ryan shrugged.
"Okay," Henry said. "Then did you see anyone hanging around the lemonade stand? Maybe a stranger or something?"
"I already told you there was nobody else around, Henry," Maggie interrupted. Then she glared at Ryan. "I know you stole my money. Why don't you just admit it?"
"No way." Ryan glared back at her. "Why should I admit to something I didn't do? I didn't take your money!"
"Well, somebody did," Cole pointed out.
"It was probably her." Ryan laughed and pointed at Maggie.
"What?" Maggie screeched. "Don't be ridiculous! Why would I steal my own money?"
Ryan shrugged again. "How should I know?"

Henry looked away, thinking. He still believed that Ryan was the most likely suspect, but this interview wasn't going well so far. Henry tried to think of another question. What would his dad ask? He couldn't think of anything. Besides he was pretty sure that Ryan wouldn't answer any more questions. Not after Maggie had just accused him of the crime again.
So how could they figure out if Ryan had done it?
"Are you guys ready to stop accusing me of stealing your money?" Ryan asked. "Because I'm not going to stand here all day. See you later."
Without waiting for an answer, he skated off. He stopped about half a block away and went back to practicing skateboarding tricks on the sidewalk.
"Well, that was a waste of time," Cole said.
Maggie watched Ryan do a fancy flip. "I still think he did it," she muttered.
Henry was thinking hard. "If Ryan took that money, there must be a way to prove it."
"I know." Cole cracked his knuckles. "Ryan's a lot smaller than us. We could hold him down and Maggie could search him."
"Great idea!" Maggie's eyes lit up. "Let's go get him!"
"Hold on." Henry grabbed Maggie's arm before she could rush down the block. "We can't do that."
"Why not?" Maggie said. "He took my money!" For a second it looked as if she were about to cry. "I need that money for horseback-riding lessons."
"We don't know for sure that he's the thief," Henry reminded her. "And it's not fair to gang up on him. If he didn't take your money, we'll get in big trouble."
Maggie sighed. "I'm starting to think this investigation isn't worth it. Maybe I should just go back to the lemonade stand and start over."
Cole nodded. "And maybe you should put a lock on your cashbox," he suggested.
"Good idea," Maggie said.
Henry couldn't believe his ears. "You mean you guys are ready to give up already? But we're only on our first suspect!"
Maggie shrugged. "Like you said, the thief is never going to admit to it. So what's the point?"
"There has to be a way to figure out what happened." Henry turned to look at Ryan.
Ryan was still ignoring them and practicing his skateboard tricks. He did a couple of flips, and then jumped the skateboard off the sidewalk.
Henry stared at the shorts. He could see the pockets open every time Ryan moved.

"If Ryan did take the money, he must have stuck it in his pockets," he murmured. "There's nowhere else he could be holding it. And he probably didn't have time to hide it anywhere between then and now."
"Good point." Cole nodded. "Does that mean you want to hold him down and search him after all?"
"No. I have a better idea."
Henry hurried off toward Ryan before Maggie and Cole could respond. Ryan stopped skating when he saw him coming.
"Oh, it's you again," he said, not sounding very happy.
"Don't worry. I'm not here to ask you any more questions." Henry smiled at the younger kid. "Actually I was just watching you skate. You've got some nice moves."
"Thanks, dude." Ryan looked suspicious but a little proud too.
"So can you do some of the harder tricks?" Henry asked. "I saw a kid from Oakview School do some awesome tricks last weekend."
Maggie and Cole had caught up to him by now. "Who cares what tricks he can do?" Maggie muttered.
"I can do tons of cool stuff," Ryan bragged. "Way more than anybody from Oakview."
"I saw that kid do a handstand on his skateboard," Henry said. "Can you do that?"
"Sure. Watch me." Ryan skated a short distance away from them. Then he turned around and headed back toward them, kicking off with one foot to build up speed.
"Who cares if he can do a handstand?" Maggie said.
"Shh." Henry hushed her. "Just watch."
As he got closer, Ryan leaned down and grabbed the edges of the board with his hands.
A second later, he was upside-down with his legs in the air.
"Awesome!" Cole cheered, clapping. "You're really good."
"Thanks." Ryan flipped back onto his feet and stood up. His face was red, and his pockets were turned inside out.
"I think you lost the stuff that was in your pockets," Henry said. "I'll help you pick it up."

Henry stepped forward. A little pile of stuff lay in the spot where Ryan had flipped himself upside down. There was a peppermint candy, a house key, and a couple of snail shells. Henry grabbed it all and handed it back to Ryan. Then he said good-bye and hurried off around the corner.
His friends followed. "What was that all about?" Cole asked.
"Don't you get it?" Henry smiled. "I just proved that Ryan isn't our thief. If he'd stolen Maggie's money, it would have fallen out of his pockets along with all that other stuff."
Cole's eyes widened. "Whoa! You're right!"
Maggie looked impressed too. But she didn't look happy.
"So now what?" she said. "If Ryan didn't take my money, then who did?"
Henry, Maggie, and Cole stood on the sidewalk staring at one another. They'd just proven that Ryan hadn't stolen Maggie's cash. But they weren't any closer to solving the mystery.
"I guess we should check out some of our other suspects," Henry said to Maggie and Cole.
"What about those two teenage girls?" Cole suggested. "They left the scene of the crime pretty fast."
Maggie nodded. "True. Plus they were whispering together the whole time they were at the lemonade stand, like they were planning something."
"Do you think they could have taken the money when you weren't looking?" Henry asked her.
"Sure," Maggie said. "I had my back to the cashbox while I was talking to Nathan. Anyone could have grabbed the money then."
"Okay, let's see if we can track down those girls," Henry said.
They walked back to the lemonade stand. There was no sign of the two teenagers.
"I think they walked away in this direction," Cole said. He pointed down the street.
The three of them walked to the end of the block, and then stopped.
"Which way should we go now?" Maggie wondered.
Henry looked around and spotted Mrs. Smith watering flowers on her front porch. She smiled and waved when she saw them.
"Hot day, isn't it?" she called.
"It sure is," Henry replied politely. "Mrs. Smith, did you happen to see two teenage girls walk past here recently?"
"Do you mean Jill and Ashley?" Mrs. Smith nodded. "Yes, they passed by about ten or fifteen minutes ago. They were heading toward town."
"Thanks," Henry said. Then he looked at his friends. "Come on. Let's go."
They walked another few blocks until they reached Main Street. Lots of people were going in and out of the shops and restaurants.
"How are we supposed to find those two girls now?" Cole asked, looking around. "They could be anywhere."
"Not really," Henry said. "I doubt they're in the dry cleaner's or the hardware store. Teenage girls don't usually go to stores like that."
"True." Maggie was looking around too. "And it's the middle of the afternoon, so they're probably not at any of the restaurants."
"I bet they're in the drugstore or the bakery," Cole said. "Maybe we should check the bakery first," he added, licking his lips.
Henry grinned. He knew that Cole loved the bakery's doughnuts more than almost any other food.

But Henry didn't want to waste any time. "The drugstore is closer," he pointed out. "Let's go there first, and then we'll look in the bakery. If they're not in either place, we could start checking some of the other stores."
The three friends headed across the street to Herman's Drugstore. As soon as he stepped inside, Henry heard loud giggles.
"Listen! That sounds like them," he whispered to his friends.

He followed the giggling sounds to the makeup aisle. Jill and Ashley were halfway down the aisle, looking at a display of brightly colored nail polish and lip gloss. They didn't notice Henry watching them because they were too busy grabbing stuff from the shelves.
"This is nice," Jill exclaimed, tossing a bottle of sparkly nail polish in a shopping basket.
"It's kind of expensive, isn't it?" Ashley said. Then she giggled. "Oops, never mind. Who cares if it's expensive? We have plenty of money!"
"Yeah." Jill giggled and reached for some lip gloss. "I think I'll buy this too."
Ashley grabbed two more tubes of lip gloss. "We might as well get a few extras. After all we can afford it!"
"True," her friend agreed with another loud giggle. "After we finish here, let's go pick out some candy."
"And then I want to look at the magazines," Ashley said.
Henry's eyes widened. The teenagers were acting as if they had lots of money to spend!
"I knew it! Those two did it!" Maggie said from behind him. "They stole my money!"
Her voice was kind of loud. The two older girls heard her and looked over.
"Hey, it's that girl with the lemonade stand," Jill said. "Shouldn't you be home squeezing lemons or something?"
Ashley started giggling all over again.
Maggie marched over and pointed into their shopping basket. "Where'd you get the money to buy all that stuff?" she demanded.
Ashley shot a look at Jill.
Jill frowned and looked down at the floor.
For a second neither of them answered.
Henry traded looks with Cole. "Is it my imagination," he whispered, "or are those two acting awfully suspicious?"
It wasn't Henry's imagination. The two teenage girls were definitely acting suspicious. They grabbed their shopping basket and rushed away, disappearing around the end of the aisle.
"Hey, wait!" Henry called after them. "Come back here! We want to talk to you."
He rushed after the girls, with Maggie and Cole right behind him.
"They did it!" Maggie exclaimed. "They stole my money! I should have known it was them!"
"Just hold on," Henry told her over his shoulder. "Don't start accusing them of stealing your money until I get a chance to ask them some questions."
They caught up to Jill and Ashley near the back of the store. The two girls seemed annoyed when they saw the younger kids coming again.
"Why are you following us around?" Ashley demanded.
"We just wanted to say hi," said Henry. "Maggie likes to keep in touch with her best customers. Right, Maggie?"
"Right," Maggie said, glaring at the older girls. Henry was afraid she was going to say something rude to them. But she kept quiet.
"So you guys are doing a lot of shopping today, huh?" Henry said, glancing into the girls' shopping basket.
"Not really." Jill shot a look at Ashley. "We were just kidding around."
"That's right," Ashley agreed quickly. "We're not really buying all this stuff. See? We're putting it back."
She reached into the basket, grabbed lip gloss, and stuck it back on the shelf. Jill did the same thing with a pack of gum.
"That's weird," Cole said. "Why would you pick up all that stuff if you weren't planning to buy it?"
Ashley shrugged. "I told you. We were just goofing around, having fun."
"That doesn't seem like much fun to me," Cole commented.
"Well, playing basketball doesn't seem like fun to me," Ashley snapped. "And boys do that all the time, right?"
Cole was surprised. "What do you mean? Basketball is a blast!"
Henry glanced over at Maggie. She was getting that impatient look on her face again.
"You two aren't fooling me," she burst out. "I know what you were doing. You were getting ready to spend my money!"
"What are you talking about?" Jill asked.
"You know what I'm talking about!" Maggie went on. "Someone stole the money from my lemonade stand!"
Ashley laughed. "Oh, right. I forgot about that."
"You mean you never found that money?" Jill added. "Did you ask Ryan, that kid who's always skateboarding? He's a troublemaker. He crashed into my mom's flowers a couple of weeks ago."
"It wasn't Ryan. It was you two!" Maggie insisted.
"No, it wasn't," Ashley said. "Why would we need a few dollars? We already have—"
"Quiet!" Jill hissed, elbowing her friend in the ribs.
"Oops." Ashley had a guilty expression on her face. Then she shrugged. "But what's the big deal?" she asked Jill. "We already agreed we're not going to use it."
"Use what?" Henry asked, feeling confused. What were the girls talking about?
Jill had a guilty expression too. She reached into the shopping basket and grabbed a candy bar. She stuck it on a nearby shelf.
"It's nothing," she said.
"Maybe you'd better tell us," Cole suggested. "Because you two are acting pretty suspicious."
"It's no big deal," Ashley said. "Jill's mother gave us a fifty-dollar bill. We were supposed to use it to buy sunscreen and some other stuff we need for summer camp."
Jill nodded. "We thought my mom wouldn't notice if we bought a few extra things. But I guess we got carried away."
"Yeah. We realized it when you guys started asking us all those annoying questions." Ashley shrugged. "So thanks, I guess."
Henry smiled. "You're welcome," he said.
Maggie was staring at them. "You mean you really didn't take my money?"
"Nope," Jill said. "Besides we could buy a lot more with my mom's fifty dollars than we could with your two or three dollars."
"It was much more than that," Maggie corrected her. "That's why I want to get it back! I need it so I can take horseback-riding lessons."
"Oh. Good luck," Ashley said. She sounded more sympathetic now.

Jill seemed thoughtful. "I just remembered something," she said. "I saw that little girl Nora grabbing something off the table while you were busy talking to her brother. I thought she was just getting a napkin or something, but she was pretty close to that cashbox. And she was acting kind of sneaky."
"Really?" Maggie said.
Henry and Cole looked at each other. "I guess we know who to investigate next," said Henry.
"Do you really think Nora took the money?" Cole asked.
"I don't know," Henry said. "She's just a little kid. And she has always seemed pretty honest to me. Remember? She even told the bus driver that his hairpiece looked fake."
Cole laughed. "I almost forgot about that," he said. "Good thing the bus driver has a sense of humor!"
Maggie was several steps ahead of them. She was in such a hurry to reach Nathan and Nora's house that she was almost jogging.
"Hurry up!" she called over her shoulder. "I want to get my money back and open up my lemonade stand again."
Henry walked a little faster until he caught up with Maggie. "I wonder why Nora would steal your money," he said. "She seems pretty young to do something like that."

"That's true." Cole had caught up by then too. "It's hard to believe that Nora suddenly decided to rob Maggie's lemonade stand all by herself." He looked worried. "I just thought of something. What if Nora and Nathan were in cahoots?"
"In cahoots?" Maggie echoed. "What the heck does that mean?"
"I heard it on that detective movie I saw on TV," Cole said. "When someone's in cahoots, it means they're working together."

Henry nodded. "I see what you mean. If Nathan and Nora were in cahoots, then Nathan could have distracted Maggie on purpose by talking to her. He kept her distracted long enough for Nora to grab the money out of the cashbox. Then once they got away, the two of them could have split the cash between them."
Maggie's eyes widened. "Do you really think that's what happened?"
"No," Henry said. "I don't think Nathan is like that."
"Yeah, I don't either," Cole agreed. "Maybe it was just Nora after all. We already know she's a weird kid. Nathan says she acts sneaky and secretive all the time. Maybe she's a thief too."

"Maybe." Henry still had a hard time believing Nora was the culprit. Something was bugging him about the whole situation, though he couldn't figure out what it was. Then again those teenage girls had seen Nora grab something off the table. That definitely made the little girl seem guilty. Besides they were almost out of suspects.
Soon they were turning the corner onto Nathan and Nora's street. From halfway down the block, they spotted Nora talking and laughing with another girl.
"Looks like Nora has a friend over," Cole commented.
"I don't care," Maggie said. "I'm going to get my money back."
"Slow down." Henry grabbed her by the arm. "You can't just march up to her and demand your money back."
"Oh yeah? Says who?" Maggie said.
"Think about it," Henry said. "We already know that Nora likes to argue. If you accuse her of being the thief, she'll just argue, whether she did it or not."
"Well, what else can I do?" asked Maggie.
"She and her friend haven't seen us yet. Let's hide and spy on them for a little while," Henry suggested.
"Yeah. Like a stakeout!" Cole grinned. "The detectives in that mystery movie did that. They sat in their car in front of a suspect's house all night!"
"I don't want to sit around here all night." Maggie still sounded a little grumpy. But she followed the boys as they tiptoed behind a hedge that ran along the side of the yard.
The three of them crouched down behind the hedge. They could see Nora and her friend through the branches, but the little girls couldn't see them.
"What are they doing?" Cole whispered.
Henry watched the two little girls. Nora was holding a stick in one hand. The other girl had a crown made of vines on her head.
"It looks like they're playing princesses," Maggie whispered.
Nora and her friend still didn't see them. The friend was picking dandelions to weave into her crown.
"I am the prettiest princess in all the land," she said with a giggle.
"So what? I'm the richest princess in all the world!" Nora cried. "I have more jewels than all the other princesses!"
That was all Maggie needed to hear. "Give it back!" she hollered, jumping out from behind the hedge. "You took what's mine, and I want it back right now!"
Nora and her friend glanced up in surprise.
The friend looked confused—and a little scared.
But Nora instantly burst into tears. "I'm sorry!" she sobbed. "I didn't mean to take it!"
"Wow," Cole said as Nora started crying even harder. "It looks like we just solved the mystery."
"Yeah," Henry agreed.
"So my funny feeling was wrong," he thought. He'd been convinced that Nora was too little to be the thief. But now, here she was, confessing to the crime.
"I'm sorry, Maggie!" Nora blurted out between sobs. "I didn't think you'd mind if I took it."
"You didn't think I'd mind?" Maggie echoed in disbelief. "Are you crazy? Why wouldn't I mind? You took my money!"
"Huh?" Nora blinked and sniffled. "What money?"
"The money you grabbed from the cashbox," Cole said. "Those two older girls saw you take it."

Henry was starting to get that funny feeling again. "Wait," he said. "The girls didn't say that. They just said they saw Nora grabbing something from the table and looking sneaky. What did you take, Nora?"
"None of your business," Nora said. She wasn't crying anymore. Now she was starting to look stubborn.
Henry stared at her. Something about this didn't make sense. He just wished he could figure out what it was.
"You'd better tell me right now, Nora!" Maggie exclaimed.
"You can't make me," Nora yelled back.
"Yeah!" Nora's friend added. "You can't order her around. She's a princess!"
Just then Nathan hurried out of the house. "What's going on out here?" he asked.
"Hi, Nathan," Henry said. "We were just talking to your sister."
"No, they weren't!" Nora started to cry again. "They were trying to drag me off to jail!"
"What?" Now Nathan looked really confused.
"She's exaggerating," Maggie said. "We were just trying to get my money back. Nora stole it!"
Nathan shook his head. "Nora didn't take that money."
"Yeah!" Nora stuck out her tongue at Maggie. "I didn't take your money."
"Yes, you did!" Maggie said. "You just confessed, remember?"
"No way." Nora looked stubborn again. "I didn't take any money. All I took was an extra cup of lemonade!"
Everyone looked surprised. "Extra lemonade?" Cole said.
"Oh . . ." Henry nodded. "That must be what those teenage girls saw her doing. Nora wasn't sneaking around to steal the money. She was just sneaking some extra lemonade."
"How do we know she didn't do both things? She just admitted that she's a lemonade thief," Maggie said. "She might be a money thief too!"
"Come on, Maggie," Nathan said. "Nora might be sneaky enough to grab some extra lemonade. But she wouldn't steal your cash."
"Maybe not on her own," Maggie said, glancing from Nora to Nathan and then back again.
Nathan folded his arms across his chest. "What do you mean?" he asked.
"Cole was right. It was probably all your idea!" Maggie burst out.
"Wait, I didn't say that!" Cole chimed in.
Maggie didn't pay any attention to him. She was still staring at Nathan. "You two were wandering past and saw that I was making tons of money at my lemonade stand," she said. "So you got greedy."
She narrowed her eyes and looked around.
Henry could tell she was pausing to make her story sound more dramatic.
It was definitely a dramatic story. But Henry still wasn't convinced that it was true. That funny feeling inside him was stronger than ever, and he needed time to think about it.
"Maggie . . . ," he started to say.

"That's when you made your plan," Maggie went on, glaring at Nathan and ignoring Henry. "You walked over and bought some lemonade for yourself and Nora. You even borrowed money from Mrs. Martin to pay for it!"
"They did?" Henry was surprised. He hadn't known that.

Maggie was still staring at Nathan. "Then you started talking to me, distracting me on purpose. That gave your sneaky little sister time to grab the money out of the cashbox while my back was turned. Then all she had to do was hide it and pretend she didn't know anything. I think she—"
"Hold on, Maggie," Henry interrupted. "I just realized something. Nora couldn't have taken your money."
Maggie, Cole, Nathan, and even Nora all turned to stare at him.
"What are you talking about, Henry?" Maggie said. "Of course she did! Who else could have done it?"
"I don't know." Henry shrugged. "But it wasn't Nora. You said it yourself. All she had to do was hide that money after she took it."
"Right," Maggie said. "So?"

"So don't you see?" Henry continued. "She couldn't hide it because she had nowhere to put it. Remember? Nora and Nathan stopped by the lemonade stand on their way home from the swimming pool. All they had on were their bathing suits!"
Maggie gasped. "Oh my gosh," she said. "You're right, Henry! I forgot that Nathan and Nora were only wearing bathing suits when they stopped at the lemonade stand."
"Me too," Cole said.
"But I remember now," Maggie went on. "Nathan dripped all over my shoes while I was talking to him."
"Sorry about that," Nathan said sheepishly. "We forgot to bring towels to the pool. Good thing it was a hot day."
"That's why you had to borrow money to buy lemonade, right?" Henry said.
Nathan nodded. "We didn't bring anything with us to the pool," he said. "But Mrs. Martin let us borrow enough money to buy two cups of lemonade."
"So you guys really didn't take my money?" Maggie asked. She sounded kind of disappointed.
"You said yourself there was lots of money in your cashbox," Cole said to Maggie. "Was there too much for Nora to hide in her hands?"
"Definitely," Maggie said. "There were a bunch of dollar bills and lots of change too. Way too much for anyone to hide in their hands."
"I guess that proves it," Henry said. "Nathan and Nora couldn't have done it."
"Yeah," Cole added. "Sorry we accused you guys."
"It's all right," Nathan said with a smile.
"Cool," Henry said, glad that Nathan wasn't angry.
"Sorry I took the extra lemonade, Maggie," Nora said. "I was just really thirsty after swimming."
"That's okay," Maggie told the younger girl. "But please remember to ask next time, okay?"
"I promise!" Nora said.
"So now what?" Cole shrugged. "Nora and Nathan didn't take the money. Those two teenage girls didn't do it either. Neither did Ryan."
Cole stared at Henry and Maggie. They stared back.
Henry knew they were all thinking the same thing. "So who did it?" he asked. "We're all out of suspects."
"No, we're not," Maggie said. "What about Mrs. Martin? She was hanging around when the cash went missing."
"Mrs. Martin?" Cole said. "We already talked about that, remember? She couldn't be the thief. She's a police officer."
Nora wasn't paying attention anymore. She and her friend were already back to arguing about who was a better princess. But Nathan was still listening to Henry and his friends.
"Not right now she isn't," he pointed out. "Mrs. Martin took time off from the police force. She's going back to work when Marty gets a little older."
"I forgot about that!" Maggie exclaimed.
"Me too, but that's not the point," Henry said. "Mrs. Martin is an honest person and a mother. She wouldn't steal money, especially not from a kid."
"How do we know that for sure?" Maggie said. "What if she's short of cash right now since she isn't working?"
"Don't be silly," Cole said. "Mr. Martin still has a job. He's a teacher at the college."

"But what if he doesn't make enough money?" Maggie said. "They used to have two salaries to pay the bills, and now they only have one. Plus they have a kid who's growing and needs stuff all the time." She stared around at all of them. "Maybe they barely have enough to get by, and she's desperate. Desperate enough to steal any money she can find!"
Henry sighed. "That sounds more like something from a movie than real life, Maggie."
"Besides I don't think Mrs. Martin is that desperate," Nathan added. "She bought lemonade for Nora and me, remember? Plus she bought two cups for herself and one for Marty."
"Marty?" Nora looked up suddenly at the sound of Marty's name. "Yuck! I don't like Marty Martin one bit!"
Maggie, Nathan, and Cole didn't even look over at her. But Henry did.
"What do you mean, Nora?" he asked. "Why don't you like Marty Martin?"
Nora scowled. "When my mom babysits him at our house, he's always grabbing my stuff and saying it's his," she complained. "He even tried to take my microphone so I couldn't play rock star anymore!"
"No way!" her friend cried. "That's mean!"
Henry hardly heard the other little girl. "That's it!" he cried.
"That's what?" Cole asked.
"It was that little kid, Marty Martin!" Henry exclaimed. "He's our thief!"
"Are you crazy?" Maggie said. "How could Marty be the thief?"
"Yeah," Cole agreed. "Marty is only three years old. He doesn't even know what money is yet!"

"It doesn't matter." Henry grinned, certain that he was right this time. "He probably doesn't know what a microphone is either, and Nora just said he took hers. Now come on, guys. Let's go get Maggie's money back!"
Henry and his friends said good-bye to Nathan and Nora, and then hurried down the street toward the Martins' house. On the way Henry explained how he'd realized that Marty was the thief.
"It's the only possibility," he said. "We already proved that none of our other suspects did it. Besides it makes perfect sense."
"It does?" Cole said.
"Sure," Henry said. "Everyone else at the lemonade stand was distracted, remember? Those two teenage girls were giggling together."
Maggie grinned. "They were probably planning their shopping trip to the drugstore!"
"Probably," Henry agreed. "And Ryan was busy chugging his lemonade and doing tricks with his skateboard."
"And I was talking to Nathan and Nora," Maggie remembered.
"Even Mrs. Martin was distracted by her cell phone," Henry said. "While nobody was paying attention, Marty must have grabbed the cash."
"And then what?" Cole asked. "Like Maggie said, there was too much money to hide in Nora's hands. And Marty's hands are even smaller."
"He didn't need his hands," Henry said. "He stuffed it in that toy suitcase he was holding."
Maggie gasped. "Henry, you're a genius!" she shrieked. "It's the perfect hiding place! Why didn't I think of that?"
"There was no reason to remember it," Henry pointed out. "Little kids always have toys, right?"
"So how come you remembered?" Cole asked.
"I didn't at first," Henry admitted. "But when Nora was talking about Marty, I started thinking about him. That's when I remembered the suitcase and realized what must have happened."
They had almost reached the Martins' house. Henry could see Mrs. Martin out in the yard with Marty.
She saw them coming. "We were just about to go back to your house, Maggie!" she called out. "I discovered something very interesting in Marty's suitcase."
"You did?" Maggie hurried over. Henry and Cole were right behind her.
Marty's suitcase was lying open in the front yard. Cash was spilling out of it!
"My money!" Maggie cried happily.
"So Marty was the thief," Cole exclaimed.

Mrs. Martin smiled. "I just discovered Marty playing with all this cash. At first I couldn't imagine where it came from, but then I figured out what must have happened," she said. "Sorry, Maggie. Marty likes to grab everything these days. He must have grabbed your money while I wasn't looking."
"We just figured that out ourselves," Henry said.
"Yeah," Cole chimed in. "Henry put together all the clues and solved the mystery."
"You did?" Mrs. Martin looked impressed. "Good work, Henry. Maybe you'll be a police detective when you grow up."
"It wasn't just me," Henry said. "These guys helped."
Cole grinned. "Yeah, solving mysteries is fun. It's sort of like solving the puzzles on the Puzzle Pirates website, only better."

Mrs. Martin smiled back. "Well, keep up the good work," she said. "Now I'd better get Marty inside and explain to him why we don't steal other people's things. It would be awfully embarrassing to have to arrest my own son!"
"Don't worry, Mrs. Martin." Maggie started gathering up her money. "I won't press charges."
Mrs. Martin chuckled. Then she picked up Marty and went into the house.
Maggie kept scooping up her money. Cole watched her.
"Aren't you going to share some of that with us?" he asked with a grin.
Maggie looked up. "Share my money?" she said. "Why would I do that?"
"Usually when people solve a mystery, they get a reward," Cole pointed out.
Maggie didn't say anything for a second. She had a thoughtful look on her face.
"What's the matter?" Henry asked her. "Are you trying to figure out how much our reward should be?"
"No," Maggie said. "But I am thinking about rewards. What if we turned the lemonade stand into a detective agency? That might be a faster way to earn money for my riding lessons!"
Cole laughed. "The Lemonade Detectives?" he joked.
"Why not?" Maggie smiled. "We did a great job solving this mystery. We could solve other mysteries for people, and they could pay me."
"Pay you ?" Henry said.
"Okay, okay. Pay us ," Maggie said. "You guys could each get 10 percent of our rewards."
Henry and Cole traded a look. Without a word they turned and started to walk away.
"Wait!" Maggie ran after them. "I meant to say 15 percent."
Henry and Cole kept walking.
"Fine!" Maggie sounded annoyed. "We can split the money evenly."
"That's more like it." Henry stopped and turned around.
So did Cole. "If you throw in all the free lemonade we can drink, you have yourself a deal," he agreed.
"Okay." Maggie nodded. "So let's have a cheer. Hooray for The Lemonade Detectives!"
"Hooray!"
Henry grinned. He liked the sound of The Lemonade Detectives. "Now all we need is another case!"
"Hi! I heard you guys are detectives."
Henry glanced up from pouring a cup of lemonade. So did his cousin, Maggie, and his best friend, Cole. It was a hot summer day in Belltown, and the kids' lemonade stand was busy.
A girl named Gail was standing there. Gail was a year ahead of Henry and Cole in school and three years ahead of Maggie.
"Yes, we are detectives!" Maggie told her. "We solve all mysteries, large and small. See our new sign?"
There were two handmade signs hanging by the lemonade stand. The first sign was about the lemonade. The second sign was about the stand's latest business. It said:
The Lemonade Detectives
All Mysteries Solved, Guaranteed
No Problem Too Large or Too Small
$5 per case plus expenses

Henry thought the new sign looked great, but so far it hadn't brought any customers with mysteries to solve. The other sign, however, had brought plenty of people looking for a cold glass of lemonade.
"Do you have a mystery for us?" Cole asked Gail eagerly.
"No, my sister just told me that you three are detectives now," Gail said. "I'd like to buy some lemonade though."
Maggie looked disappointed. "Are you sure you don't have a case for us? Hasn't anything mysterious happened to you lately?"
"Nope. Sorry," Gail said.
Henry reached for the lemonade pitcher. He poured some into a cup and handed the cup to Gail.
"That will be 25 cents, please," he told her. "Enjoy your lemonade."
"Thanks." Gail handed him a quarter. "Good luck with your detective agency."
After she left, Henry sighed. "I'm starting to think that there are no more mysteries to solve in Belltown."
"We've been sitting here all morning, and haven't gotten a single case!" Cole added. "We could have been playing soccer instead."
"At least we're making money." Maggie fanned herself with her hand. "It won't be long before I have enough to start horseback-riding lessons!"

Maggie had started the lemonade stand because she wanted to take riding lessons. Her parents had told her they would only pay half the cost. She needed to earn enough money to pay the other half herself.

The lemonade stand was a success right from the start. Maggie had made plenty of money selling her delicious lemonade. But then all her money had disappeared right out of her cashbox! Henry and Cole had helped her track down the thief. That was when the idea for The Lemonade Detectives was born.
"We'd be making a lot more money if we had a case," Cole grumbled. "Besides Henry and I never agreed to be lemonade salesmen. We want to be detectives!"
"Detectives need to be patient," Maggie shot back. "Sooner or later we'll get a case and then—"
"Stop arguing, you two," Henry said. "Here come some more customers."
A group of boys was heading their way.
"Four lemonades, please," one boy said, holding out a dollar bill.
"Here you go." Maggie poured their lemonade. "Did you know that we offer detective services now as well as lemonade?"
The first boy squinted at the new sign. "How can you guys be detectives?" he asked. "You're just kids."
A boy named Ryan, who never went anywhere without his skateboard, was standing there too. "I bet it's because they figured out who stole Maggie's money," he said. "They thought it was me at first!"
He began telling his friends about how he'd been a suspect as the boys walked away sipping their lemonade.
"At least people are hearing about our detective agency," Maggie said, watching them go.
"That's good," Henry said. "But I don't think all three of us need to stay here for the whole day."
Cole nodded. "Henry and I could go play soccer, and you could call us if someone shows up with a mystery."
"No way!" Maggie said. "I need you to help me with the lemonade."
"If we aren't here, it means you get to keep all the lemonade money," Henry reminded her.
Maggie hesitated, thinking about that.
"Here comes your next lemonade customer, Maggie," Cole said, pointing down the street. "He's all yours."
Henry glanced at the boy hurrying toward them.
"Hey, it's Nathan," he said. "Maybe we should see if he wants to play soccer with us."
Nathan was a kid in Henry and Cole's class who lived nearby. Everyone liked him because he was always friendly, nice, and happy.
When he got closer, though, Henry saw that Nathan didn't look very happy right now. In fact, he was frowning and looking worried.
"What's up, Nathan?" Cole asked when Nathan reached the lemonade stand.
Nathan pulled a five-dollar bill out of his pocket and slapped it down on the table. "I've got a mystery for you!" he announced.
"Really? You have a mystery for us to solve?" Maggie asked Nathan eagerly.
Henry stared at the five-dollar bill that Nathan had just slapped down on the lemonade stand. He felt a flutter of excitement.
"Cool!" he said.
"What's the mystery?" Cole sounded excited too.
"It's about my little sister Nora," Nathan told them. "She's been acting weird lately."
Henry's excited feeling faded. He traded a look with Maggie and Cole. Cole looked disappointed. Maggie rolled her eyes.
"What's the mystery about that?" Maggie asked Nathan. "No offense, but Nora always acts kind of weird."
"Yeah." Cole laughed. "Remember when she wore those pink pants every day for a week, and wanted everyone to call her Princess Pretty Pants?"
"That's nothing," Maggie said. "What about the time she pretended she was an alien from outer space?"
Henry nodded. Nora was only five years old, but she was famous in the neighborhood for doing strange stuff.
"She argues with everybody about everything," Henry added. "And she's always dragging her stuffed animals around and pretending they're real."
Nathan grinned. "She pretends her stuffed animals are real because she wants a pet so badly. She begged for a puppy for her fourth birthday, but Mom and Dad said no pets."
"So it's no mystery that she's acting weird," Cole told Nathan again.
Nathan shook his head. "This is different," he said. "Mom and Dad are really worried. They think Nora has been sleepwalking! They've caught her a couple of times walking around outside after dark."
"Nora's been sleepwalking?" Henry said. "That sounds kind of serious, but it's not really a mystery."
"I said they think she's been sleepwalking," Nathan said. "I think she's faking!"
"Why do you think that?" Henry asked.
"It's just a feeling," Nathan said. "I think she's up to something sneaky, but I'm not sure what it is."
Maggie shrugged. "So what? Why do you care if she's pretending to sleepwalk?"

"I just want to find out the truth," Nathan said. "Like I said, my parents are really worried about her. They're planning to take her to the doctor next week. If she's really sleepwalking, that's okay. But if she's faking it, she's making them worry for nothing! That's not fair."

Henry still wasn't sure that this counted as a mystery. But Nathan was their friend, and he seemed pretty worried. Besides, investigating a mystery was better than sitting around pouring lemonade all day.
"We can look into it, I guess," Henry said.
Cole picked up the five-dollar bill. "But you should take this back for now," he told Nathan.
"What are you doing, Cole?" Maggie cried. "This may not be much of a mystery, but that doesn't mean we'll solve it for free!"
"I know." Cole gave the bill back to Nathan. "But The Lemonade Detectives have a guarantee, remember?"
He pointed to the line on their sign that read "All Mysteries Solved, Guaranteed."
Maggie looked at it. "So what?" she said.
"A guarantee means Nathan only pays us when he's satisfied with our work," Cole replied. "That's what my dad always tells his customers, and he's a businessman."
"Well, we're not businessmen," Maggie said with a frown. "We're just kids. And I need that money for my riding lessons!"
"We'll get the money as soon as we solve the case," Cole said.
"Cole has a point, Maggie," Henry said. "It doesn't make sense for Nathan to pay us now. If we can't solve the case, we'll just have to give the money back."
Maggie still looked unhappy. But she nodded. "Fine," she said. "I guess it doesn't matter as long as we solve this case fast."
Nathan tucked the five-dollar bill back into his pocket. "So does this mean you'll try to solve my mystery?" he asked.
"Yes," Henry said. "The Lemonade Detectives are on the case!"
"Let's go to your house and talk to Nora," Cole said.
There were no customers waiting for lemonade just then. Maggie took out a small sign that said "Back in a While" and set it on the table. Then they all walked over to Nathan and Nora's house.
"Do you know where Nora is right now?" Maggie asked Nathan.
"She's probably in the playroom," Nathan said. "It's at the back of the house so we can go in the back door."
He led the way around the side of the house. They turned the corner just in time to see a window slide open. A second later Nora climbed out and tiptoed across the backyard!
"Hey!" Nathan yelled, rushing after Nora as she tiptoed across their yard. "What are you doing? Why'd you climb out that window?"
"Come on," Henry said to Cole and Maggie. "Let's catch up to them."
The Lemonade Detectives ran across the yard after Nathan. By the time they reached him, Nora had stopped and spun around. She glared at her brother.
"It's none of your business!" she yelled at him.
"Where were you going?" Cole asked Nora, glancing around the yard.

Henry looked around too. Nathan and Nora's backyard was really nice. There was a big maple tree in the middle where Nathan and his dad had built a tree house. On the left there was a short picket fence between their yard and the one next door. A tall hedge on the right blocked the view of the other neighbors' house. There were no neighbors at all at the back of the yard, just a thick forest. Henry was pretty sure Nora was headed there when they'd caught her.
"Yeah," he said. "Where were you going, Nora?"
Nora stared at Henry, then at each of the others. She looked suspicious. "Who wants to know?"
"The Lemonade Detectives, that's who," Maggie replied. "We want to know what you're up to!"
Henry winced. He didn't think it was a very good idea to tell Nora that they were investigating her. But Maggie was impulsive. She often spoke before she thought.
Nora stared at them all again. For a second she didn't answer.
"Well?" Nathan demanded.
"I was just walking across the backyard," Nora said at last. "What's wrong with that?"
"Why did you climb out the playroom window instead of using the door?" Nathan pointed to the back door of their house. "It's right there, you know!"
"I was in a hurry," Nora said. "I, um, saw a butterfly and I wanted to catch it."
Henry glanced at Cole. He could tell his friend was thinking the same thing he was. Nora was lying.
But how were they supposed to get her to tell the truth now? She knew they were watching her. That was going to make their job as detectives much harder.
"It's okay, Nora," Henry said. "Go ahead and do whatever you were doing."
"I wasn't doing anything," Nora said. "I was just about to go back inside."
She ran over and climbed back inside through the window. Maggie stared after her.
"You were right," she told Nathan. "She is acting even weirder than usual."
Cole shrugged. "So what do we do now? She didn't seem very eager to tell us anything."
"We'll have to figure out what's going on in a different way," Henry said.
"Maybe we should try a stakeout," Maggie suggested. "That worked last time we were suspicious of her."
"No it didn't," Cole said. "Last time we staked out Nora's house, she turned out to be innocent."
"True, but Maggie's right," Henry said. "If we hide and wait for Nora to sneak out again, we'll be able to follow her. Then we can see where she's going and what she's doing."
"You mean we have to sit around here all day?" Maggie suddenly didn't look very happy about the stakeout idea. "What about my lemonade stand?"
Henry glanced at Nathan. "You said she's been sneaking out at night, right?"
"Sort of," Nathan said. "Her bedtime is at seven, so it's not usually very late when she sneaks out."
"Perfect." Henry smiled. "All we have to do is come back at seven and wait!"
That evening at exactly seven o'clock, The Lemonade Detectives met behind the hedge along Nora's yard. Nathan was waiting for them there.
"Perfect timing," he whispered. "Nora just went to bed."
Henry nodded. He peeked through the hedge. It hid them from view, but allowed them to see Nora's house.
"Does she usually sneak out the back door?" he asked.
"She used to," Nathan replied. "But Mom and Dad started locking it once all this started."
"Maybe she'll climb out the playroom window again," Cole said.
Nathan nodded. "Or she might use her bedroom window," he said. "It's upstairs, but she knows how to climb down the house. It's part of our family's fire-safety plan."
"Okay, let's watch both windows," Henry said.
They all settled down behind the hedge to wait. But they didn't have to wait very long. About twenty minutes later, they heard a window slide open.
Maggie peeked through the hedge. "It's Nora!" she whispered. "She's climbing out her bedroom window."
Henry looked too. He saw Nora climb out her bedroom window and jump to the ground. She glanced around, and then scurried across the yard.
"She sure doesn't look like she's sleepwalking," Henry whispered. "Come on, let's follow her!"
Henry pushed his way through the hedge as quietly as he could. Nora was halfway across the backyard by now.
"Shh!" he warned the others. "Don't make too much noise, or she'll know we're here. And try to stay hidden!"
He realized that it wasn't going to be easy to follow Nora without being spotted. They would have to be very careful.

Luckily, there were plenty of tall shrubs in the backyard. Henry rushed out and ducked behind the closest one. A second later Cole joined him behind the shrub. Maggie and Nathan were right behind him.
"Where's she going?" Cole whispered in Henry's ear.
Henry peeked at Nora. She hadn't heard or seen them yet. But she sure didn't look as if she were sleepwalking. She stopped every few steps to look around.

"I can't tell for sure, but it looks like she's heading toward the woods at the back of the yard," Henry whispered back. "Come on, let's try to get closer. We don't want to lose sight of her if she goes into the woods."
They all dashed across the yard to another shrub. When they were safely hidden behind it, Henry peeked out again. Nora had stopped and turned around. She had a suspicious look on her face.
Henry yanked his head back behind the shrub. Whew! Nora hadn't spotted him. He put a finger to his lips to warn the others to be quiet.
They waited silently for a few seconds. Then Maggie peeked out.
Her eyes widened. "Hey," she said, sounding excited. "It looks like she might be heading for Nathan's tree house!"
Henry winced. In her excitement Maggie had forgotten to whisper. And her voice was always pretty loud.
A second later he heard the sound of running feet. When he jumped out from behind the shrub, he saw Nora running away.
"She heard us," he called to his friends. "Come on, let's catch her!"
"Nora!" Nathan yelled as they all started running. "Stop!"
But Nora didn't stop. That was no surprise, at least to Henry. As far as he could tell, Nora hardly ever did anything anyone told her to do!
Nora was a pretty fast runner for a little kid. She raced across the yard and disappeared through the hedge.
"She's in the neighbors' yard," Maggie said. "Hurry!"
Henry ran as fast as he could toward the hedge. It was too thick to see anything on the other side. But he kept his eyes on the spot where Nora had pushed through.
Cole was the fastest of all of them, so he got there first. "Ahh!" he yelled as he pushed through the hedge. "Hey, where'd she go?" he called from the other side.
Henry pushed through the hedge too. He looked around and saw Cole standing there. A second later Maggie and Nathan appeared.
But there was no sign of Nora.
"Uh-oh," Cole said. "Do you think she's hiding?"

Nathan was out of breath after all the running, so it took him a second to answer. "Probably," he said. "She likes to hide. Once she hid in the basement and my parents couldn't find her for over an hour."

Henry looked around the neighbors' yard. It was smaller than Nathan and Nora's yard, but there were plenty of places to hide. There was a large vegetable garden with lots of big tomato plants, a patch of corn, and teepees covered with bean vines. The rest of the yard had shrubs and flowers, a birdbath, and a sculpture of a dog. At the back of the yard was the same forest that ran behind all the houses on the block.

"Let's spread out and search for her," Henry decided. "Nathan, you go that way and search the neighbors' flower beds. Maggie, check the front yard and the other side of the house. Cole, make sure she's not hiding out in the woods. I'll check the vegetable garden."
"Okay," Nathan said, and the others nodded. Then they split up.
Henry hurried over to the vegetable garden. He peeked behind every tomato plant and bean teepee. He looked into the corn patch. He even checked under the wheelbarrow.
But there was no sign of Nora. By the time he finished searching, his friends were coming back.
"I didn't see her," Maggie reported.
"Me neither," Cole said. "What about you, Nathan?"
"Nope," Nathan said. "Did you find anything, Henry?"
Henry shook his head and sighed. "It looks like Nora got away from us."
Henry could hardly believe that Nora had outsmarted them. She had led them into the neighbors' yard and then disappeared. But he wasn't ready to give up yet.

"I have an idea," he told Maggie, Cole, and Nathan. "Nora probably waited for us to start looking for her. Then she sneaked back through the hedges. If we hurry, we might be able to find her before she makes it to the house."
Nathan nodded. "Let's go," he said.
He led The Lemonade Detectives through the hedge into his own yard. They got there just in time to see Nora racing toward the house.
"Stop right there!" Nathan yelled loudly. "We caught you, Nora!"
They ran toward her. Just then the back door flew open and Nora's parents rushed out.
"Oh no!" Nora's mom exclaimed. "She got out again!"
Nora's dad looked worried. "Hush, don't wake her," he told his wife. "Someone told me you're never supposed to wake a sleepwalker."
"She's not really sleepwalking, Dad!" Nathan said.

Henry had been watching Nora. As soon as she'd seen her parents, she'd closed her eyes and held out both arms in front of her. Henry thought she looked more like a zombie than a sleepwalker. But her act seemed to be fooling her parents.
"That's not a nice thing to say, son," Nathan's father scolded. "Your sister could get hurt if she keeps sleepwalking like this. I wonder how she got outside this time."
"She climbed out her bedroom window," Nathan said.
"That's enough, Nathan," his father said. "This is no time for jokes."
"Come with me, sweetie," Nora's mother said softly as she started guiding Nora toward the house. "Let's get you safely back to bed."
"It's time for you to come inside too," Nathan's father told Nathan. Then he glanced at Henry, Maggie, and Cole.
"And you kids had better head home. It's getting late."
"Late? It's not even eight o'clock yet," Maggie said.
Henry grabbed his cousin by the arm and pulled her toward the front of the house.
"Yes, we'd better go," he told Nathan's dad politely. "See you tomorrow, Nathan."

Now that Nora had been caught "sleepwalking" again, Henry guessed that her parents would watch her very closely. She probably wouldn't be able to sneak out again that night. That meant any more detective work would have to wait until the next day.
The following morning Henry was eating breakfast when Maggie hurried in through the kitchen door.
"Good morning, Maggie," said Henry's mother, who was also Maggie's aunt. "Would you like some scrambled eggs?"
"No thanks, Aunt Susan. I already ate." Maggie sat down at the table across from her cousin. "Hurry up, Henry," she said. "I want to go back to Nora and Nathan's house and investigate."
"Okay," Henry said. "Let's call Cole and tell him to meet us there."
Nathan was waiting in front of his house when the three detectives got there. "What's the plan for today?" he asked. "Do you have any theories about what Nora is doing when she sneaks out?"
"Not yet," Henry admitted. "But at least we know she's not sleepwalking."
Cole nodded. "She was wide-awake when she ran away from us, that's for sure."
"I still think she was heading for the tree house when she heard us," Maggie said. "Maybe we should search for clues up there."
Nathan seemed doubtful. "Why would she sneak around just to go to my tree house?" he asked. "She's allowed to climb up there whenever she wants, as long as she tells someone where she's going."
"Really?" Cole said. "My friend Bruce never lets his little sisters in his tree house."
"Nathan must be much nicer than your friend Bruce," Maggie said with a laugh. "Anyway, I still think we should look in the tree house."
"You're right, Maggie," Henry agreed. "It's worth checking out, just in case."
All four of them hurried past the house to the backyard. Then they climbed up the ladder leading into Nathan's tree house.
"Wow," Cole said, looking around. "This place is really cool, Nathan! You can see half the neighborhood from up here."

Henry wasn't very interested in the view. He was busy looking around for anything suspicious. But all he saw were some empty candy wrappers and Nathan's favorite comic books. There was no sign that Nora had been in the tree house recently.
"Oh well," Henry said. "I guess this idea isn't working. Maybe we'll have to wait until tonight to try another stakeout."
"Okay," Maggie said, and Nathan nodded.
Cole wasn't listening. He was still looking out the window.
"Hey, check it out!" he said. "Nora just climbed out the playroom window again and is sneaking across the yard!"
Henry rushed over to the tree house window. Cole was right! Nora was tiptoeing across the backyard. She stopped every few steps and stared around in every direction.
"Shh!" he warned the others. "Don't let her hear us up here!"
Nora didn't look up as she passed beneath the tree house. She turned left and hurried toward the picket fence at the side of the yard.
"Where's she going?" Maggie whispered.
Nora reached the fence and stepped over it. Then she kept walking.
"It looks like she's cutting across the Smiths' yard," Nathan said. "Let's follow her!"
They all climbed down from the tree house as fast as they could. Henry led the way as they hurried after Nora.
"Will your neighbors mind that we're in their yard?" Cole asked Nathan as he hopped over the fence.
Nathan shook his head. "They're really nice. They said we can play over here anytime we want."
Henry was glad to hear that. But he was more focused on keeping Nora in sight.
"She's heading for the woods," he whispered to his friends. "Let's go!"
They raced to the edge of the forest. There was a trail just inside the tree line. Henry and his friends followed the trail as quietly as they could.
"Do you see her?" Maggie asked quietly.
"Not yet. Let's stop and listen," Henry whispered.

They all stopped and listened for a few seconds. There were a lot of sounds in the woods. Birds chirped in the branches overhead. A squirrel rustled against pine needles as it scampered up a pine tree. Bees buzzed around looking for flowers.
Then Henry heard something else: the crack of a twig somewhere deeper in the forest!
"Did you hear that?" he whispered.
The others nodded.
Henry spotted a smaller trail that turned off the main one. Following the new trail, he walked toward the spot where he'd heard the cracking sound. His friends were right behind him.
Then they all heard another sound: Thump!
"What was that?" Maggie whispered.
Henry didn't answer. He was already running toward the sound. It had to be Nora!

He burst out into a small clearing. There was an old toolshed in the middle of it. Its rickety door was open—that was what had caused the thumping sound. Standing in the doorway, with her back to them, was Nora!
"She's here!" Henry cried.
"Eek!" Nora spun around and let out a squeak of fright. "What are you doing here?"
"We were following you." Henry walked toward her, glad that she wasn't running away this time. "What are you doing out here?"
"None of your business," Nora said.
Maggie, Cole, and Nathan rushed into the clearing.
"There she is!" Maggie exclaimed.
"You guys should stop sneaking around like that!" Nora cried loudly. "You scared me! I had no idea you were following me!"
Henry stared at her. "Why isn't she trying to run away?" he wondered. Last night she'd seemed desperate to get away from them.
"What's going on?" he demanded. "Are you really surprised to see us, or are you faking?"
"What are you talking about, Henry?" Maggie pushed past him. "Let's see what's in that shed."
Henry was still watching Nora suspiciously. But he was curious about the shed too. He followed the others inside.
"Aha!" Nathan pointed to something in the corner. "That explains everything!"
It was dark inside the shed. Henry had to lean forward to see what Nathan was pointing at.
"Soda cans?" he said when he got a good look. "I don't get it."
"Nora isn't allowed to drink soda," Nathan explained as he picked up a can. "She must have been sneaking out here to drink it."
Cole laughed. "I'm not allowed to drink soda either. But I never thought of sneaking into the woods to drink it!"
Henry opened the shed door wider. That let in more light so it was easier to see. He counted three more empty soda cans lying in the corner.
"Please don't tell Mom and Dad!" Nora begged Nathan. "I'll be in big trouble!"
Nathan sighed. "All right. But only if you promise not to do it anymore."
Nora crossed her heart. "I promise I won't sneak out here to drink soda anymore," she said. Then she dashed out of the shed and disappeared into the woods.
"Case closed!" Cole grinned. "It looks like The Lemonade Detectives solved another tough mystery!"
"That's right." Nathan pulled a five-dollar bill out of his pocket. "Here's your payment. Thanks!"
"Wait." Henry stepped forward and stopped Maggie from taking the money.
"What's the matter this time?" Maggie said.
"Keep your money for now, Nathan," Henry said with a frown. "Because I don't think we've really solved your case."
"What do you mean, Henry?" Cole looked confused. "We just solved the case! Nora was sneaking out here to drink soda!"
"Nora confessed," Maggie agreed. "We should be happy that she didn't argue for once."
"But that's just it." The more Henry thought about it, the more certain he was that he was right. "Since when does Nora give up so easily?"
"It does seem strange." Nathan frowned. "But she does love soda. And we caught her in the act."
"Did we?" Henry looked at each of them. "Or is Nora even sneakier than we thought? Maybe she saw us go up in the tree house so she sneaked past on purpose."
"Why would she do that?" Maggie asked.
Henry shrugged. "To make us think we'd solved the case. That way, once we stop paying attention to her, she can go back to doing whatever she's really doing."
"But Nathan said she's not allowed to drink soda," Maggie said. "So it makes sense that she'd sneak around for something like that. Remember how she sneaked an extra cup of lemonade from my stand?"
"Yes," Henry said. "But this still doesn't make sense to me. Why would she hide the soda this far from her house?"
"So her parents wouldn't find it," Cole said. "That's obvious."
Henry shook his head. "There are tons of closer hiding places."
"I guess so." Maggie looked around. "But this shed is a pretty good spot. She could sit inside and drink the soda, and nobody would ever see her."
Nathan frowned again. "Now that I think about it, she hates places like this shed." He stepped inside. "It's dark in here, and there are a ton of spiders and other bugs. Nora does not like bugs!"

"I forgot about that," Maggie said. "When she bought lemonade from me, she double-checked to make sure there were no bugs in it." She shrugged. "But so what? Maybe she decided soda was more important than bugs."

"Maybe," Henry said. They started walking through the woods, still talking about the case. "But why would she sneak out after her bedtime just to drink soda? She could do it just as easily during the day."
"I guess that's true," Nathan agreed, looking thoughtful.
Maggie still didn't look convinced. "We already know that Nora is weird," she said. "Nothing she does makes a lot of sense."
"It does seem strange that there are only four empty cans in the shed," said Cole. "How many times has she sneaked out?"
"More than four times," Nathan said.

Henry could tell that his friends were starting to believe him. "Also, when we saw her sneaking out yesterday, she wasn't heading toward the Smiths' yard," he said. "Remember? She was walking straight past the tree house toward the back of her own yard."
"You're right!" Maggie's eyes widened. "Do you really think she tricked us into following her here?"
"But why?" Cole looked more confused than ever. "What's she really doing?"
"That's what we still have to figure out before we accept Nathan's money," Henry said.

Maggie sighed loudly. "Maybe you're right," she told Henry. "Mom says you're the most logical person she knows. And Nora is definitely the sneakiest kid in the neighborhood. We should make sure she's not tricking us."
"Yeah," Cole agreed. "But how?"
"Good question," Nathan said.
They all turned to look at Henry. He smiled.
"Nora is sneaky," he said. "That means we have to be sneakier than she is."
"Okay," Cole said. "But how?"
Henry thought for a second. The bad news was that they still had no idea what Nora was really doing when she sneaked out. Their investigation had failed so far.

But the good news was that Nora thought she'd tricked them. She wouldn't expect them to keep investigating after they'd solved the case. That meant she wouldn't be as careful next time she sneaked out.
"I have a plan," Henry told his friends. "It's time for another stakeout."
Maggie groaned. "Again?" she said. "But my favorite horse show is on TV tonight! I don't want to miss it, especially since it seems like I'll never earn enough money for riding lessons!"
"You'll have enough money before long, Maggie," Henry said, smiling. "And you can record your show and watch it later. It'll be worth missing it tonight."
Cole looked doubtful. "Are you sure?" he said. "Even if Nora thinks we gave up, she'll still be sneaking around so her parents don't catch her. How are we supposed to follow her without being seen?"
"Don't worry," Henry said. "I told you I have a plan. This isn't going to be an ordinary stakeout."
"What do you mean?" Nathan asked.
Henry winked. "This time our stakeout is going to have an extra-special, detective twist!"
"Are you ready?" Henry asked Maggie.
It was later that day. The Lemonade Detectives were hiding behind a car parked near Nora's house. They were getting ready to put the first step of Henry's plan into action.
Maggie made a face. "Why do I have to be the one to distract Nora?" she complained.
"You're the only one who can distract her well enough," Henry said.
"Yeah." Cole laughed. "Nora would never believe it if Henry and I suddenly wanted to play princesses with her!"
"I guess you're right," Maggie said. "But being a detective is harder than I thought!"
"Good luck." Henry peeked out from behind the car. "She just came outside. See if you can keep her in the front yard, okay?"
"Okay." Maggie stood up and waved at Nora. "Hi, Nora! What are you doing?" she called in a super-friendly voice.
"Wow," Cole whispered. "She's a pretty good actress."
Henry grinned. "Mom always says Maggie is very dramatic. I guess she's right."
He looked out from behind the car again. Nora was twirling on her tiptoes while Maggie watched.
"It looks like Nora is distracted," he told Cole. "We should be able to sneak through the neighbors' yard so she won't see us."
Cole nodded. "Don't forget the flour."
Henry picked up the bag of flour sitting by his feet. Nathan had borrowed it from his family's kitchen. It was an important part of Henry's plan.
"I've got it," Henry said. "Let's go."
That evening Henry and Maggie met Cole at Nora's house again. They all hid behind the hedge. It was time for step two of Henry's plan.
"Is Nathan coming?" Cole whispered.
Henry shook his head. "I told him to stay inside and act normal. That might keep Nora from getting suspicious."
"Good idea," Maggie said. "If he's home when she goes to bed, she'll never think we're still investigating her."
Henry nodded. "Let's get to the tree house."
Soon all three of them were in Nathan's tree house. Cole went over to the window. "All we have to do now is wait," he said.
"We can take turns watching for Nora to come outside," Henry suggested.
"I'll go first," Cole said. "You two probably won't even have to take turns. Last time Nora sneaked out right after she went to bed."
Maggie nodded, looking hopeful. "Maybe I'll get home in time to see my TV show after all," she said. "It's not on until eight-thirty."
"I thought you were recording it," Cole said.
"I am," Maggie replied. "But I'd rather see it live."
They all settled down to wait. Cole sat by the window watching the house while Henry and Maggie played cards.
Half an hour passed. Cole stretched. "I'm bored," he said. "It's time for somebody else to take a turn."
"I'll do it," Henry offered.
He traded places with Cole. When he looked out, the yard was quiet. From the tree house, it was easy to see the back door, the playroom window, and Nora's bedroom window.
Another half hour went by. Henry's eyes were getting tired from staring at the house.
"Maybe Nora isn't going to sneak out tonight," he said.
Cole looked up from flipping through one of Nathan's comic books. "Or maybe she was telling us the truth," he said. "Maybe she really was sneaking out to drink soda in that shed."
Henry still didn't believe Nora's story about the soda. It didn't seem logical. But Nora wasn't a very logical person. Could Cole be right?
"It's probably after eight o'clock by now," said Maggie. "I'll have to leave soon if I want to watch my show."
"Let's just wait another few minutes," Henry said. "Maybe Nora is being extra careful. Her parents are probably checking on her a lot."
He looked out again. It was getting darker, and there were deep shadows in the woods. But it was still easy to see Nora's house.
Finally Maggie stood up. "I'm going home. There's no point in missing my show if Nora's not going to sneak out tonight."
Henry was disappointed. He and Cole had spent a long time setting up their special detective trick. They'd used the whole bag of flour!
"Maybe you're right and she's not going to sneak out tonight," he said with a sigh. He glanced at the house one more time. Then he gasped. "Wait!" he whispered. "Here she comes!"
"Really?" Maggie said.
She and Cole rushed to the window. They all watched Nora climb out her bedroom window and hurry across the backyard.
"She's heading straight for the woods," Maggie whispered.
Cole nodded. "She's definitely not heading toward the soda shed!"
Henry smiled. His feeling had been right! Now all they had to do was figure out what Nora was really doing.
"Let's go after Nora!" Maggie whispered. She sounded excited now. "She's almost reached the woods!"
"No, let's wait for a few seconds," Henry said. "We don't want her to hear us following her."
He watched Nora until she disappeared into the woods. A few seconds later there was a glow from just inside the tree line.
"It looks like she brought a flashlight," Cole said.
Henry nodded. "That should make it a lot easier to spot her. Come on, I think it's safe to climb down now. She's too far away to hear us."
He led the way down from the tree house. The three detectives hurried across the yard toward the woods.
"It's getting kind of dark," Maggie said, peering at the trail that led into the forest. "I hope we'll be able to see."
"Don't worry. I brought a flashlight too." Henry pulled it out.
He stepped onto the shadowy trail. It was time to put step three of his plan into action.
Henry waited a second longer, and then turned on his flashlight. He shined it around until he found the flour that he and Cole had sprinkled on the ground earlier that day.
"Wow," Maggie said. "You guys sure used a lot of flour."
