Cole grinned. "We used the whole bag. I hope Nathan's parents don't decide to bake a cake anytime soon."
"Using a lot of flour was the only way my plan would work," Henry explained to Maggie. "We had to sprinkle enough on the ground so that Nora would be sure to step in it."
Cole nodded. "Now all we have to do is follow her footprints," he said. "I always knew Henry was smart, but this has to be the coolest plan ever!"
"I hope Nora didn't see the flour and jump over it," Maggie said, worried.
"I thought about that," Henry said. "That's why we made sure to put it here in the woods, under the trees, instead of out in the yard. It gets dark here a lot sooner than it does out there."
"Good thinking!" Maggie was impressed. "Nora didn't turn on her flashlight right away. So she probably didn't see the flour."
Cole grinned. "That's what we were hoping she'd do."
Henry was shining his flashlight up and down the line of flour. "There!" he cried, spotting some powdery, white footprints leading deeper into the woods. They had to be Nora's!
He followed the footprints, keeping his flashlight aimed at the ground.
His friends crept along behind him.
"The footprints are getting fainter already," Maggie whispered. "I guess it didn't take long for most of the flour to come off Nora's shoes. What if the footprints run out before we catch up to her?"
"If that happens, at least we'll know what direction she's going," Henry whispered back.
"And it's definitely not toward that shed where she pretended she was going before," Cole added. "It's a good thing that Henry was too smart to fall for that!"
"Are you saying I wasn't smart enough?" Maggie asked, sounding insulted.
"Shh!" Henry hushed them. "I don't want her to hear us coming!"

Maggie and Cole stayed quiet after that. The three friends tiptoed through the woods, following the faint flour footprints. It was getting so dark that the woods seemed a little spooky. Insects and frogs chirped all around the kids, and an owl hooted in the distance.
But Henry stayed focused on the footprints. They were getting fainter and fainter. Finally they disappeared completely.
"Uh-oh," Cole whispered. "It's the end of the trail!"
Henry turned off his flashlight and looked around. It was hard to see anything in the darkness. But then he saw something up ahead—a light!
"Look!" he whispered. "That must be Nora's flashlight."
"Let's go get her!" Maggie whispered eagerly.
The three of them hurried toward the light, moving as quietly as they could.
Henry was in the lead as they emerged into a clearing. On the far side was a huge oak tree. The light was coming from the base of the tree.
Nora was there, leaning over. Her back was to the detectives. She hadn't heard or seen them yet. Henry squinted, trying to see what she was doing, but he couldn't tell.
He was about to whisper to his friends that they should hide behind the trees and watch Nora. But Maggie was already pushing past him.
"Freeze, Nora!" she said loudly. "We caught you!"
Nora spun around and gasped. "Oh no!" she cried in surprise.
Henry hurried toward Nora, who was huddled against the tree. "What are you doing over there?" he asked.
"None of your business!" Nora cried, looking upset.
"Do you guys hear something?" Maggie asked.
A high-pitched sound was coming from the tree trunk. At first Henry thought it was an insect or a frog. Then he heard it again.
"It sounds like—," he began.
"Kittens!" Maggie cried. "Look, there's a mother cat and a bunch of adorable kittens!"
Nora burst into tears. "Please don't tell anyone!" She sobbed. "If Mom and Dad find out, they'll take Patches and her babies to the shelter! They said I couldn't have any pets!"
Henry glanced at his friends. He remembered what Nathan had told them about Nora wanting a pet. She must have found this cat and her kittens and decided to take care of them in secret.
"It's okay, Nora," Maggie said. "We'll make sure nothing bad happens to Patches and her kittens. I promise."
"Really?" Nora wiped her eyes.
"Really." Maggie reached in and tickled a kitten under its chin. "Aw, they're so cute!"
"Come on, Nora," Henry said. "We'd better get you home."
The next day Henry met Cole at the lemonade stand.
"Where's Maggie?" Cole asked. "I was hoping for some lemonade."
"She'll be here soon," Henry said. "She offered to walk over to Nathan's house to pick up our five-dollar fee."
"Cool! I already know how I'm going to spend my share." Cole grinned. "I want glow-in-the-dark laces for my soccer shoes."

"We definitely earned our fee this time," Henry said. "That was a tricky case! At least now we know why Nora sneaked out mostly at night. She didn't want anyone to see her carrying cans of tuna into the woods."
Cole nodded. "I feel sorry for her. She seemed really upset about losing her new pets."
"Actually she's not losing them," Henry said. "I talked to Nathan this morning. He said his parents aren't against having a pet after all."
"Really?" Cole looked surprised. "But Nathan said they told Nora she couldn't have one!"

"That was a year ago," Henry reminded him. "They didn't think she was ready to take care of a pet then. But she's older now. They said if she promised to be good from now on, she could keep Patches. And Patches' kittens can stay until someone adopts them."
"Awesome!" Cole said. Then he pointed down the street. "Here comes Maggie with our money. That's even more awesome!"
Maggie hurried over, carrying a plate covered in foil.
"Hi, guys," she said. "Ready to sell more lemonade? I'll run inside and get the pitchers."
"First things first," Cole said. "Did you get our fee from Nathan?"
Maggie hesitated. "Um, sort of."
"What do you mean, sort of?" Henry said.
Maggie smiled sheepishly. "Did you notice how adorable those kittens were?"
"Yeah, they were cute," Cole said impatiently. "But where's my money? Did Nathan pay you or not?"
"He paid me," Maggie said. "But not with money. I, um, told him I'd take two kittens instead of the five dollars."
"What?" Cole shrieked. "Are you kidding?"

"Sorry," Maggie said quickly. "I know I should have checked with you guys first. But the kittens are so cute, and they need homes . . . I just couldn't resist, even if it means waiting longer to start riding lessons."
Cole looked annoyed. "Okay, you got two kittens for solving the case," he complained. "What do Henry and I get?"
"You can split our next detective fee, just the two of you," Maggie said. "I promise."
Henry smiled. It hadn't been fair for Maggie to give away their fee without asking. But if she was willing to give up her share of the next one, she must really want those kittens.
"It's a deal," he said before Cole could respond.
"Great!" Maggie seemed relieved. "And look, Nathan's mom gave us these to thank us!"
She uncovered the plate. It was full of chocolate chip cookies.
"Yum." That made Cole a little happier. "Just ask next time, Maggie, okay?"
Maggie nodded. "Sorry."
Meanwhile Henry had spotted Gail and her older sister walking toward them.
"Uh-oh," he said. "I think our first customers of the day are coming. We'd better get some lemonade."
"Be right back." Maggie dashed into the house and returned a few seconds later carrying two pitchers of lemonade.
By then the girls had reached the lemonade stand. "Two lemonades please," Gail's sister said.
"We heard you solved another case," Gail added.
"You heard about that already?" Cole looked excited.

The three friends grinned at each other. Henry was glad that word was spreading about The Lemonade Detectives. That would bring them more cases. He couldn't wait to find out what the next one would be!
"Here's your lemonade," Henry said. He handed a cup of ice-cold lemonade to a teenage girl.
"Please come again," Henry's cousin Maggie added. "And let us know if you have any mysteries for us to solve."
"Okay." The girl took a sip of her lemonade. "But nothing mysterious ever happens here in Belltown."
Henry grinned. "That's what you think!" he said. "The Lemonade Detectives have solved five mysteries so far."

He pointed to two signs on the lemonade stand. One of the signs was about the lemonade they were selling. The other sign was about The Lemonade Detective Agency. Henry, Maggie, and their friend Cole had started the agency a couple of weeks ago.

At first it had been just a lemonade stand. Maggie had started selling lemonade to earn money for horseback-riding lessons. Her parents had promised to pay half of her lesson fees, but she had to pay the rest herself.
Maggie's lemonade stand had been a big success from the start. On her very first day, she'd made a lot of money.
But then the money had disappeared from her cashbox! Henry and Cole had helped her figure out who had taken it. After that the three of them had decided to open the detective agency.

The teenage girl looked at the signs. "Oh right. I heard you helped my neighbor figure out how a groundhog was getting into his garden. That doesn't sound like a very exciting mystery to me," the girl went on. "But if anything mysterious happens, I'll let you know."
"Okay," Henry said. "Enjoy your lemonade."
"Thanks." The teenage girl took another sip, and then walked away.
"She's right, you know," Maggie told Henry. "Our last few mysteries have been kind of boring."

"I know," Henry said. "Finding Mr. Flinn's lost keys wasn't very interesting. Neither was the groundhog case, or the one about the missing library book. But we still got paid our detective fee each time, so we shouldn't complain."

"That's true," Maggie agreed. "If we solve a few more cases, and keep selling lots of lemonade, I'll have enough money for lessons soon." She dropped the quarter from the teenage girl into the cashbox. "That's another 25 cents for my horseback-riding fund."
"You mean one-third of 25 cents," Henry corrected her. "You have to split the money with Cole and me."
Maggie shook her head. "Cole doesn't get to split the lemonade money when he's not here. So I get to keep one-half of 25 cents."
"Oops, you're right," Henry said. "I forgot that Cole has swim-team tryouts again today."
"Why does he want to be on the swim team?" Maggie wondered. "Hanging out at the lemonade stand seems a lot more fun than swimming laps all day long."
"Cole loves sports," Henry reminded her. "And he's a really good swimmer."
"He's lucky that someone on the team just moved away," Maggie said. "Otherwise he wouldn't have a chance to try out until next summer."
Henry nodded. "Cole is the youngest kid trying to make the team," he said. "But it sounds like he did really well on the first day of tryouts. I bet he'll make the team."
"I know why he's such a good swimmer," Maggie said with a laugh.
"Why?" Henry asked her.
"Because he spends so much time watching his pet frogs swim around their tank!"

Henry grinned. Cole was crazy about reptiles and amphibians. He had several large tanks in his bedroom. One tank was full of frogs. Another tank was for his turtles, and a third one held a snake. Cole took very good care of all his pets.
"Yeah," Henry said, still smiling. "Frogs are good swimmers, and so is Cole!"
"Hey, here comes Cole now." Maggie pointed down the street.
Henry was surprised to see Cole running toward them from the direction of the town pool.
"I wonder why he's back so soon," Henry said. "Tryouts just started a few minutes ago. They shouldn't be over for hours."
Maggie shrugged. "Maybe the coach already told him that he didn't make the team."
"I doubt it," Henry said, still watching Cole. "I don't think they even started swimming yet today. Look! Cole's hair isn't wet."
"That's a smart observation, Detective Henry," Maggie said with a laugh.
Cole was closer by now. Henry could see that he was very upset.
"What's wrong?" Henry asked. "Why aren't you at the pool?"

Cole skidded to a stop in front of the lemonade stand. "I need your help!" he cried. "Someone dumped a bunch of frogs into the pool right before tryouts started. And everyone thinks I'm the one who did it!"
"What do you mean, someone dumped frogs in the pool?" Maggie asked.

"I mean just what I said," Cole replied. "All the swimmers were helping the coach carry some stuff to the pool from his car. When we got to the pool, we saw the frogs. About twelve of them were swimming around."
"Are you sure the frogs didn't hop into the pool by themselves?" Henry asked.
Cole nodded. "I'm sure. These aren't the kind of frogs you see around here."
"Okay. If you say so," Maggie said with a shrug. "You're the frog expert."

"That's the problem!" Cole looked more worried than ever. "A few of the other swimmers know I like frogs. That's why they think I did it. But I would never throw a bunch of frogs into pool water. It's not healthy for them."
"Why not?" Maggie asked. "I thought frogs liked water."
"They do," Cole said. "But pool water has chlorine in it. That can be bad for them."
"Did you tell everyone that?" Henry asked.
"Yes, but most of them still think I did it," Cole said. "I need The Lemonade Detectives to help me clear my name!"
"We're on the case!" said Maggie.

Henry and Maggie closed down the lemonade stand. Then they walked to the pool with Cole. When they arrived, a bunch of kids were in the pool with nets, still chasing the frogs. Someone had put buckets of fresh water near the edge of the pool. Whenever the swimmers caught a frog, they put it into a bucket.
"Are the frogs okay?" Cole called, rushing over and looking into the buckets. "Do any of them look sick?"
A girl named Daisy looked at him. She was two years ahead of Henry and Cole in school.
"I think we got them out fast enough," she said.
An older kid named John gave Cole a dirty look. "Yeah. No thanks to you, frog boy!" he said.
Coach Phillips stepped forward. He was a cheerful man, who was almost always smiling. But Henry could see that he wasn't smiling now.
"That's enough," the swim coach told John. "Everyone is innocent until proven guilty."
"Okay, Coach." John shrugged. "But everyone knows who the frog lover is around here."
A couple of kids nodded. Others stared at Cole suspiciously or looked confused.
"Uh-oh," Henry whispered to Maggie. "Cole was right. He's the main suspect! We'd better start investigating!"
"How are we supposed to figure out who put the frogs in the pool?" Maggie asked. "We can't check the frogs for fingerprints!"
"Good point," Henry said with a grin. "But we can split up and start talking to people. Maybe someone saw what really happened."
"Okay," Maggie said. "I'll go question Daisy."

She walked away. Henry looked around. Belltown was pretty small, so he knew almost everyone at the pool. A kid who lived across the street from him was standing in the water. His name was Arnold, but everyone called him Tiny. The nickname was a joke because Tiny was the tallest kid in the tenth grade.
"Hi, Tiny," Henry said, walking over.
"Hi, Henry," Tiny said. "Did you come to help us catch these frogs?"
Henry smiled. "Sorry, I just came to watch the tryouts. So I don't have my swimsuit on."
"That's okay." Tiny looked around the pool. "I think we got most of them already."
Henry looked around too. He saw two frogs still swimming around. The rest were already in the buckets.
"Is everyone here trying out for the team?" he asked Tiny.

"Not exactly." Tiny shrugged. "There are only six spots on the team, and five of them are already taken. I've been on the team all summer, so I have one of the spots. The Farley twins, Mary Martinez, and John Miller are already on the team too."
Just then Henry saw a frog swim past. "There's one!" he cried.
Tiny swam after the frog. He chased it halfway to the other end and finally caught it.
Henry carried a bucket closer. Tiny swam over to him.
"How many people are trying out for the last spot on the team?" Henry asked as Tiny put the frog in the bucket.
"Four," Tiny said. "Your friend Cole and three other people."
"Wow," Henry said. "Four swimmers trying out for one spot. That's a lot of competition."
"If you ask me, Cole is the best swimmer of the four," Tiny said. "He'll probably get the spot."
Just then a young girl walked past. She was one of the few kids that Henry didn't recognize. She stopped when she heard what Tiny had just said.
"Don't be so sure!" the girl said, glaring at Tiny. "Cole definitely won't be getting a spot on the team if I have anything to say about it!"
"Who was that?" Henry asked Tiny as the girl stomped away.
"Lauren," Tiny said. "She's in college. Coach Phillips hired her to be his assistant coach."
Henry was surprised. "I thought she was a high-school student. She looks really young."

"That's what Cole said when he met her yesterday," Tiny said. "I guess Lauren doesn't like being called young. She got really insulted when he said it, and she's been giving Cole dirty looks ever since."
"Hey, Tiny!" someone called from the other end of the pool. "There's one last frog over here that we can't catch."
"See you later, Henry," Tiny said. Then he swam away.

Henry returned the frog bucket while he thought about what he'd just learned. It sounded as if Cole had accidentally insulted Lauren and she was still mad about it. Could she be angry enough to try to ruin Cole's chances of making the team?
Soon Tiny and the others caught the last frog. Coach Phillips looked relieved.
"All right, people," he called out. "Time to get back to tryouts. Everyone in the pool!"
Maggie walked over to Henry. "Daisy says she didn't see a thing," she reported. "But she thinks that Cole did it. Mostly because he put a plastic toad in her lunch once."
"I remember that," Henry said. "Cole loves joking around. I'm sure that's another reason why some people believe he did this."
Maggie nodded. "Did you find out anything useful?" she asked.
"I was talking to Tiny when the assistant coach walked past . . ." Henry went on to describe what Lauren had said. Then he told Maggie what Tiny had said afterward.
"Wow," Maggie said when he finished. "Lauren must be really sensitive about looking young. Do you think she was mad enough at Cole to do this?"

"I was wondering the same thing," Henry said. "But how would she know that Cole liked frogs? She only met him yesterday. We shouldn't assume it was her until we know more. Maybe we can talk to other people when the team takes a break."

The two of them sat down to watch as tryouts continued. The coach had all the swimmers do laps for a while. Then he told Tiny and the other team members to get out of the pool and rest. Cole and the other three kids who were trying out had to stay in the water. The coach asked them to swim all the different strokes.
"Wow. Cole really is a good swimmer," Maggie commented.
"Daisy and Kyle are pretty good too," Henry said.
"But that last kid is terrible," Maggie said. "Who is he? He looks familiar."
"That's Tommy Miller," Henry said. "He's one year ahead of Cole and me in school."
Maggie shook her head. "He really stinks. Why would he try out for the swim team?"

"Maybe it's because his older brother is one of the stars of the team." Henry looked over at John Miller. Tommy's older brother was sitting with Tiny and the others. John was bragging about getting his driver's license soon, when he turned sixteen.
"I guess John got all the swimming talent in the family," Maggie said.

Henry went back to watching Tommy. He was swimming the backstroke. But by the time he was halfway across the pool, he looked like he was about to drown. He had to dog paddle to finally get to the other end.
"I just remembered something," Henry said. "Tommy's parents own the pet store at the mall. That's where Cole buys food and supplies for his pets."
"So?" Maggie said.
"So Tommy knew about Cole's interest in frogs. Maybe he's trying to frame him."
"Frame him? What does that mean?" Maggie asked.
"It's a detective word," Henry said. "It's when someone tries to make it look as if someone else committed a crime."
"So you think Tommy framed Cole for the frog prank?" Maggie looked doubtful. "Why would he do that?"
"Because Cole's such a good swimmer," Henry said. "And Tommy really wants the spot on the team."
Maggie thought for a second. "Yeah, but even if Cole got kicked out of tryouts, there's no way Tommy would make the team. Daisy and Kyle are both better than him too."

Henry realized she was right. Just then the coach ordered Cole and the others out of the pool for a rest. All four of them climbed out and hurried toward the chairs where they'd left their towels and sports drinks.
"Maybe Daisy and Kyle should be suspects instead of Tommy," Henry said to Maggie. "Do you think they knew that Cole likes frogs?"
Before Maggie could answer, there was a loud shriek.
"Help!" Daisy screamed. "I'm being attacked by ants!"
Henry spun around when he heard Daisy scream. He saw her throw a towel onto the ground. Tiny black insects were crawling up her arms! She raced toward the pool and jumped in.
A second later she came up from underwater. "Whew!" Daisy said. "There was a swarm of ants on my towel! Luckily I rinsed them off before they could bite me."
Henry hurried over to look at the towel Daisy had dropped. Sure enough, dozens of ants were crawling all over it!
"That's weird." Cole looked over Henry's shoulder. "How did those ants get there?"

Henry was wondering the same thing. He shook off the ants, and then took a closer look at the towel. It was white, but there was a purple stain on it. When he sniffed the stain, it smelled sweet, like grape juice.
"What is it?" Maggie asked.
"Daisy must have spilled her sports drink on her towel," Henry said. "Ants love sweet stuff."
He went over to where Daisy was talking to Coach Phillips.
Henry showed them the stain. "Did you spill something on your towel earlier?" he asked Daisy.
"It's not my towel," Daisy said. "I forgot mine, so I borrowed that one from Tiny."
"Let me see that, Henry." Coach Phillips looked at the towel with an anxious frown. "I hope someone didn't spill their drink in the locker room. There will be ants everywhere! I'd better go check."
"I have an extra towel in the office," Lauren told Daisy. "We'll be right back, everyone."
Coach Phillips, Lauren, and Daisy headed toward the pool building.
"Do you think the ants are connected to the frog prank?" Maggie asked Henry.
"I'm not sure," Henry said. "Let's go ask Tiny about his towel."
Henry and Maggie walked over to Tiny. "Did you know there was grape drink on that towel you loaned to Daisy?" Maggie demanded.
Tiny shook his head. "That towel was clean when I put it in my locker this morning. Maybe Tommy accidentally dragged it in something when he took it out of my locker."
"You mean Tommy was the one who brought the towel to Daisy?" Henry asked. "Why didn't you get it yourself?"
"I was busy stretching, so John said he'd ask Tommy to get it," Tiny said. "But I still feel terrible about what happened."
"Maybe Cole isn't the only swimmer that Tommy wanted out of tryouts," Henry murmured to Maggie as they walked away. "Maybe Tommy is trying to chase away all of his competition, including Daisy!"
"That's the only way he could ever make the team," Maggie said. "Let's go question him!"
She raced toward Tommy. "Why did you give Daisy that towel?"
Tommy looked confused. "Because Daisy forgot hers, and Tiny had an extra one," he said.
"How did that grape stuff get on there?" Maggie demanded. "And all those ants?"
"I don't know," Tommy said.
Henry couldn't tell if Tommy was lying or telling the truth. Either way Henry was afraid that Maggie's questions might make him mad. He quickly changed the subject.
"Hey, Tommy," he said. "Why did you decide to try out for the swim team?"
"My parents wanted me to get some exercise this summer," Tommy said. "I thought it would be fun to swim with my brother. Too bad I stink at swimming!" He laughed.
Just then John came over to give him some swimming tips. Henry and Maggie wandered away.
"Do you think Tommy's telling the truth?" Maggie asked.
"I'm not sure," Henry said. "Let's go see what Cole thinks."
Cole was checking on the frogs. "Did you solve the mystery yet?" he asked.
"Not yet," Henry said, keeping his voice low. "But we have a couple of suspects. One of them is Tommy Miller."
"We think he might be trying to get you kicked out of tryouts," added Maggie. "That way he'll have a better chance to make the team."
"Tommy?" Cole shook his head. "No way. He's a nice kid. Plus he's not competitive like his older brother. Tommy doesn't care if he makes the team or not."
Just then Kyle marched over. He was two years older than Henry and Cole.
"You should go home and take your frogs with you, Cole," Kyle said loudly. "Fifth-grade nerds don't belong here! You should have tried out for the junior swim team."
"I'll be in sixth grade in the fall," Cole told him. "That means I can try out for either team."

Kyle took a sip of the purple sports drink he was holding, and then smirked. "Oh yeah?" he said. "I just heard Coach Phillips talking to Lauren. She's trying to talk him into kicking you out of tryouts!"
"What?" Cole exclaimed, staring at Kyle.
"No way!" Maggie said. "Does Lauren really want Coach Phillips to kick Cole out of tryouts?"
"That's what I just said," Kyle said with another smirk. He took one more sip of his sports drink, and then wandered away.
Cole looked upset. "I have to go talk to the coach! I have to beg him to give me another chance!"
"Wait a minute, Cole," said Henry. "Everyone knows that Kyle likes to cause trouble. What if he's just trying to make you worry?"
Maggie nodded. "He's probably upset because you're doing better than him in the tryouts. He could be another one of our suspects!"
"She's right," Henry said. "Did you notice that Kyle was sipping a sports drink? I'm pretty sure it was grape."

"Really?" Maggie said. "That proves it! Kyle must have poured the grape drink on the towel. Then he dragged it through an anthill to try to scare Daisy away. He probably framed Cole for the frogs too!"
Cole shrugged. "I guess it's possible. Kyle really wants the spot on the team. He's been teasing me all day, saying I'm too young and stuff like that."
"Case closed!" Maggie exclaimed. "Let's go tell the coach!"

"Wait," Henry said. As usual Maggie was rushing things. "The case isn't closed yet. We don't know for sure that Kyle did it. What if he's telling the truth about what he heard? Lauren was already one of our suspects. Maybe she wants to get Cole kicked out because he insulted her yesterday."
Cole made a face. "Yeah, my big mouth sure got me in trouble with her," he admitted. "I tried to apologize, but she wouldn't listen."
"Maybe we should go ask Coach Phillips if what Kyle said is true," Henry said. "If it is, then Lauren should be our main suspect. Otherwise it should be Kyle."
Cole looked around the pool area for the coach. "He must still be inside. Let's go!"
Henry, Cole, and Maggie headed toward the pool building. Just as they reached the door, Lauren came out with Daisy. Lauren saw Cole and frowned.
"Where are you going?" she demanded.
"Inside," Cole said. "We need to talk to the coach."
"You don't have time right now," Lauren said. "I'm in charge until Coach Phillips comes back outside. And I want everyone to run laps around the pool building. Now!"
She raised her voice for the last part so everyone could hear. A few of the swimmers groaned. But she ordered them to put on their sneakers and start running.
Henry and Maggie watched as the swimmers disappeared behind the pool building. Lauren jogged away with them, leaving the pool area deserted.
"It makes me feel hot just watching people jog in this weather," Maggie said. "Let's go stand in the shade."
"Okay." Henry followed her around the corner of the building. There was shade there from some large trees, and they could see some walking trails too.
Henry tried to glance back at the pool. But he couldn't see it from where they were standing.
"Lauren seems really mad at Cole," he said. "She made everyone jog so he couldn't go inside and talk to the coach. Do you think she guessed that we suspect her?"

"Maybe," Maggie said. "But I still think Kyle could be the bad guy. He really wants to get on the team. Cole and Daisy are the only two people who might stop him. And the two pranks today were aimed at them."
"We shouldn't forget about Tommy though," Henry said. "He was the one who gave Daisy that towel. That means he's still a suspect too."
Maggie looked doubtful. "Cole thinks it couldn't be Tommy."
Henry was about to answer when he heard a shout. It came from near the pool.
"That sounded like Coach Phillips!" he said. "Let's go!"
Around the corner the coach was staring into the pool. A few of the joggers, including Cole, had made it back to the building by then.
"What's wrong, Coach?" Cole called.
Coach Phillips pointed to the water. "The frogs!" he exclaimed. "They're in the pool again!"
Henry gasped when he saw the buckets tipped over at the edge of the pool.
The rest of the joggers appeared around the corner. When they saw what had happened, everyone started talking at once.
"Quiet!" the coach hollered. "I want to know who did this!"
Nobody said a word. Lauren hurried toward the edge of the pool and picked up something on the ground near the buckets.
"Look!" she cried. "Whoever did it left a pair of flip-flops behind."
She held up two blue-and-white flip-flops. Cole let out a gasp.
"Those are mine!" he blurted out.
Henry stared at Cole in shock. So did everyone else.
"Your flip-flops were at the scene of the crime," Kyle said, pointing at Cole. "That means you dumped the frogs back in the water!"
John nodded. "I bet he did it the first time too."
"I knew it!" Lauren muttered.
Henry didn't know what to think. Those flip-flops were a big clue. Could Cole be the culprit? After all, Cole did love a good joke.
But Cole was shaking his head, looking more upset than ever. "I didn't do it!" he told Coach Phillips. "I swear!"
That brought Henry back to his senses. Cole might be a joker, but he wasn't a liar. If Cole said he was innocent, then Henry believed him.
But he could tell most of the others didn't. Even Coach Phillips had a doubtful frown on his face.
"We'll talk about it later," the coach said. "First we'd better get those frogs rounded up again."
The swimmers all jumped in the pool and started catching frogs. Henry and Maggie watched.
"This doesn't look good for Cole," Maggie whispered.
"I know," Henry whispered back. "If we don't solve this mystery fast, Cole will never make the swim team!"
"Someone must have put Cole's flip-flops by the buckets so he'd get the blame," Maggie said. "Who could have done that?"

"I don't know." Henry tried to remember who had been near the pool when he and Maggie had returned. The coach had been there of course. So had a few of the faster joggers, including Cole. But Henry couldn't remember who else was in the fast group.
Maggie was staring at Lauren. The assistant coach was watching the swimmers retrieve the frogs.
"Lauren was the one who spotted the flip-flops," Maggie said. "Maybe that's because she was the one who put them there."
"Maybe," Henry agreed. "Let's go talk to her. But let me ask most of the questions, okay? We don't want her to know we're suspicious of her."
Maggie frowned. But she nodded. "Okay," she said.
They walked over to Lauren. "Hi," Henry said. "I'm Henry, and this is my cousin Maggie."
"Nice to meet you. I'm Lauren," Lauren said. "Are you here to try out for the team? Because we usually recommend wearing a swimsuit."
Henry laughed. "No, we're just here to watch our friends try out."
"You didn't bring your pet frogs with you, did you?" Lauren asked, smiling a little.
Henry's dad was a reporter who had a lot of experience interviewing people. Henry suddenly remembered his dad's advice: A good way to start an interview is to ask people about themselves.
"We heard you're a student at Bellville College," Henry said to Lauren. "Do you like it there?"
"Sure, it's great," Lauren said. "I've been there for three years. I'll graduate next spring."
"Really?" Maggie blurted out. "Wow, you look much younger than that!"
Lauren's friendly expression instantly changed to a frown. "Excuse me," she snapped. "I have work to do."
Henry sighed as Lauren stomped away. "You already knew she was sensitive about looking young," he said to Maggie. "Why did you have to mention it?"
"Sorry." Maggie shrugged. "I couldn't help it."
Henry knew better than to get annoyed at his cousin. She had a habit of saying whatever was on her mind without thinking about it first.
"Forget about it," he murmured, thinking hard.
Maggie was thinking too. "Lauren is so sensitive about her age. She's probably still mad at Cole. Maybe even mad enough to try to get him kicked out of tryouts!"
"Right," agreed Henry. "Let's go see what Cole thinks."
Cole was putting a frog into one of the buckets. Henry and Maggie hurried to Cole before he could swim away.
Henry bent down to talk to him. "We were just talking to Lauren. We think she might still be mad at you."
"That makes her our top suspect for everything, including dumping the frogs again," Maggie added. "Especially since she was the one who spotted your flip-flops."
Cole shook his head. "She might have done the earlier stuff," he said. "But I know she didn't tip over the buckets."
"How can you be so sure?" Henry asked.

"She was near me the whole time we were jogging," Cole said. "She ran right behind me, yelling at me to go faster. She only slowed down to check on the others when I was almost all the way around the building."
"Are you sure?" Maggie asked.
Cole nodded. "Lauren's definitely still mad at me," he said with a sigh. "But she's definitely not the one who dumped those frogs back in the pool."

"So Lauren wasn't the one who dumped the frogs back in the pool," Maggie said. "But that doesn't mean she didn't do the other stuff. Like put the frogs in the pool the first time. Or put ants on Daisy's towel."
"True," Henry agreed. "But why would she do that to Daisy? Did Daisy say something about her looking young too?"
"I don't think so," Cole said.
"Then Lauren probably didn't do the ant prank either," Henry said. "Let's talk about our other suspects."
"You mean Kyle and Tommy?" Maggie asked.
"I still don't think Tommy did it," Cole said. "He's my friend."
"Okay," Henry said. "But he does have a good motive. If you get kicked out of tryouts, he has a better chance of making the team."
"It didn't seem like he really cares about making the team," Maggie said.
"Don't forget that his brother is a star," Henry said. "What if Tommy cares more about the team than he's showing? And it would be easy for him to get the frogs from his parents' pet store."
Maggie's eyes lit up. "Plus Tommy was the one who gave Daisy that towel. He might have poured grape drink on it, and then dragged it through an anthill."
"That doesn't sound like something Tommy would do," Cole said. "Aren't there any other suspects?"
"Sure," Henry said. "The other two people with good motives are Kyle and Daisy."
"Daisy?" Maggie said. "But she's the one who got attacked by ants!"
"She could have set that up herself," Henry said. "That way nobody would suspect her of the frog prank."
"Maybe." Cole looked unsure. "It doesn't seem very likely though. She almost got bitten. And ant bites really hurt."
Just then Lauren wandered past. "Hey," she said, pointing at Cole. "Aren't you supposed to be the frog expert around here?"
He nodded.
"Then help catch those frogs!"
"Okay." Cole waved to his friends and swam away.
"I guess Lauren knows that Cole likes frogs," Maggie said to Henry. "Are you sure she's not the culprit?"
Maggie's voice was pretty loud. Henry didn't want everyone to hear them talking, so he led her over to the playground. The two of them sat down on the swings.
"I'm pretty sure," Henry told Maggie. "Lauren had no reason to make those ants swarm Daisy."
"What if the ant prank was just a coincidence?" Maggie asked. "Maybe Tiny spilled grape juice on his towel, and then Tommy dragged it through an anthill without noticing."
"It's possible," Henry said. "But I'm still pretty sure about Lauren. She couldn't have dumped the frog buckets while she was jogging behind the pool building."
"I guess that's true." Maggie said. "It had to be one of the joggers who finished first. Who's the fastest runner out of our suspects?"
"Probably Kyle," Henry said. "He was on the track team at school."
"And we saw him with a grape sports drink," Maggie said. "Plus we know he really wants the spot on the swim team. He has to be the culprit!"
"We have to be able to prove it's Kyle," Henry reminded her. "Let's go talk to him and see what we can find out."
They found Kyle chasing a frog in the pool. "Hi, Kyle," Henry greeted him. "Can you believe those frogs got in the water again?"
"I can't believe it!" Kyle said. "Your friend Cole is a troublemaker. I hope the coach kicks him out this time!"
Maggie scowled. "Cole didn't do it!"
"That's not what everybody else says." Kyle grinned and puffed out his chest. "Once Cole's gone, that spot on the team will be all mine!"
Henry traded a look with Maggie. He could tell they were thinking the same thing. Kyle sounded guilty!
"You're a chicken, Kyle!" Maggie said angrily. "You're afraid Cole will beat you."
"No way," Kyle said. "I'm not afraid of anybody! Having Cole out of the way just makes it easier. Maybe he should take some of these frogs home with him so they can teach him how to swim."
Kyle laughed loudly, as if that was the funniest thing anyone had ever said. But Henry frowned.
"What do you mean?" he asked Kyle. "Cole already has a bunch of pet frogs."
"Really?" Kyle looked surprised. "So that's why John called Cole 'frog boy.'"
Henry was still watching Kyle closely. "You didn't know that Cole has frogs?"
Kyle shrugged. "I don't pay much attention to fifth-grade nerds," he said. "Speaking of which, why am I standing here talking to you?"
He smirked and then swam away.
"What a jerk," Maggie muttered.
"He might be a jerk," Henry said. "But he's definitely not our culprit."
"What are you talking about?" Maggie asked Henry in surprise. "I thought we agreed that Kyle was our top suspect."
"He was," Henry said. "But he's not anymore. He just told us that he didn't know Cole was interested in frogs. That means he wouldn't know that Cole would be blamed for the prank!"
"I didn't think of that," Maggie said.
"Plus it would be stupid for Kyle to use grape sports drink for the ant prank," Henry added. "Everyone saw him drinking it all day."
Maggie shrugged. "Maybe he's not very bright. Or maybe he was lying about not knowing Cole liked frogs."

"Maybe," Henry said. "But I don't think so. We'd better check out our other suspects. Starting with Tommy. He definitely knew Cole liked frogs because of his parents' pet store. Plus Tommy could have gotten the frogs there."
"Sure," Maggie said. "But Cole isn't the only one who's a better swimmer than Tommy. Why didn't Tommy try to ruin Daisy and Kyle's chances too?"

"Maybe that's why Tommy did the ant prank," Henry said. "He was trying to get rid of the other two swimmers that way. If Daisy got bitten by ants, she might not want to try out anymore. And using grape sports drink meant Kyle might get the blame."
Maggie gasped. "Henry, you're a genius!" she exclaimed. "That makes perfect sense! Let's go tell the coach!"
"Hold on," Henry said. "It's just a theory. We haven't proven anything yet."
"How are we going to prove it?" Maggie asked.
"I'm not sure yet. Let's go talk to Tommy."

Henry looked over at the pool. Most of the swimmers were chasing the last few frogs. Lauren was watching them. Coach Phillips seemed to be counting the frogs that were already in the buckets. But Tommy was nowhere in sight.
"Where is he?" Maggie wondered.
"I don't know," Henry said. "But there's his brother John. Let's go ask him if he knows where Tommy is."

John was climbing out of the pool. He had an annoyed expression on his face. Henry wondered if that was because tryouts had been disrupted again. Everyone in town knew that John was a very talented swimmer.
"Hi, John," Henry said. "We're looking for your brother. Where did he go?"
"That's a good question." John looked more annoyed than ever. "I was just looking for him myself."
"Why?" Maggie asked.
"Tryouts will start again in a few minutes, and he needs all the practice he can get," John said. "Tommy isn't taking these tryouts very seriously."
Then he stomped away.
Maggie watched him go. "John sounded mad," she said. "And did you hear what he said about Tommy? Maybe John suspects his brother of causing all the trouble!"
Henry shrugged. "Brothers get mad at each other all the time. John is probably just embarrassed because his brother is a terrible swimmer."
"Yeah, you're probably right," Maggie agreed.
Henry noticed Cole putting another frog in one of the buckets. Most of the other swimmers were climbing out of the pool and grabbing their towels.
"It looks like they caught all the frogs," Henry said. "We'd better hurry if we want to talk to Tommy before tryouts start again."
"There's Daisy. Let's ask her if she's seen him," Maggie said.
"I saw Tommy heading toward the pool building a few minutes ago," Daisy told them a second later. "He probably went inside to use the bathroom."
"Thanks," Henry said. He wondered if he should ask Daisy more questions. She was still a suspect too. "Hey, Daisy," he said. "When Lauren made you jog, did you make it around the building first?"

Daisy smiled. "Not this time," she said. "At first I was keeping up with Cole, Kyle, and John. But then I saw a pretty flower growing beside the running trail, and I stopped to look at it. I thought I might want to come back and paint it later. So I was one of the last ones to make it back."
"Oh." Henry remembered that Daisy liked art. He'd seen some of her paintings displayed at school.
Daisy walked away. "Why were you asking her about jogging?" Maggie asked Henry. "I thought we were in a hurry to talk to Tommy."
"I'm still trying to figure out who dumped those frogs the second time," Henry said. "It had to be the first person who got back from that jog. So Daisy's probably not our culprit."
"I could have told you that!" Maggie rolled her eyes. "Our top suspect is Tommy now, remember?"
"Okay. Let's go find him."
Before they could move, Henry and Maggie heard an angry howl.
"Hey!" Kyle yelled. "Someone poured paint in my gym bag!"
"Let's go!" Henry said to Maggie.
Without waiting for her, he rushed over to Kyle. Coach Phillips was hurrying toward him too. Everyone else had stopped whatever they were doing and turned to stare.
"What happened?" Henry asked when he reached Kyle.

Kyle's large blue gym bag was sitting on a chair near the pool. Its zipper was halfway open. When Henry looked down into the opening, he saw a puddle of green. The green paint was all over Kyle's sneakers, T-shirt, and other belongings.
"All my stuff is ruined!" Kyle complained.
The coach reached them. "This is outrageous!" he exclaimed as he looked into Kyle's bag. Then he spun around. "Someone had better confess right now! Otherwise I'm going to cancel these tryouts!"
"Oh no!" Daisy exclaimed.

Kyle glared at Cole, who was standing a short distance away. "It was him!" he said, pointing. "Everyone knows he's the one who dumped those frogs in the pool. He must have done this too! He's afraid I'll beat him for that spot on the team!"
"Cole didn't do anything!" Maggie said. "You probably put that paint there yourself, Kyle! If there's any paint in your bag, that is."
Henry realized that nobody could see the paint except for him, Kyle, and the coach. "There's really paint in here, Maggie," he said. "The only question is how it got there."
"Yes," Coach Phillips agreed. "And I want an answer to that question right now! I also want to know who brought those frogs to the pool."
Just then Tommy came out of the pool building. When he saw everyone staring at Kyle, he looked confused.
"What's going on?" he asked, hurrying over.
"That's a very good question," Coach Phillips said. "We're trying to figure out who's responsible for all of today's pranks."
"I know the answer," Maggie declared. She pointed at Tommy. "He did it!"
"What?" Tommy exclaimed.
Henry winced. He thought Tommy was probably the culprit too. But they still had no way to prove it. Why did Maggie have to have such a big mouth?
John looked angry. "How dare you accuse my brother of something like that!" he yelled at Maggie. "Tommy didn't have anything to do with this!"
Maggie didn't back down, even though John was a lot older. "That's not what we think!" Maggie yelled back. "Right, Henry?"
"I don't understand," Tommy said, looking confused. "What happened? Are the frogs in the pool again?"
"No," Tiny told him. "Someone poured paint in Kyle's bag."
"You want to make everyone think that Cole did all these pranks," Maggie went on. "How did you do it?"
"That's ridiculous." John scowled. "It was Cole. Everyone knows he has pet frogs."
"Right!" Lauren jumped in.
"You probably poured that green paint in Kyle's bag too," John went on. He looked around. "Or maybe it was Daisy. Everyone knows she likes to paint!"
"What?" Daisy cried. "I didn't do anything!"
"And like I keep telling everyone, I didn't put those frogs in the pool!" Cole added. "I would never do something like that. Pool water isn't good for frogs!"

Everyone started yelling at once. Maggie was yelling at Coach Phillips about evidence. John was yelling that Tommy was innocent. Kyle was yelling about his bag being ruined. Cole and Daisy were yelling that they hadn't done anything wrong. Everyone else was yelling out questions.
But Henry wasn't yelling. He was thinking. Something someone had just said didn't make sense. That was a clue. A big one! Suddenly he realized who was behind all the trouble.
"Hold on," he said. "I know who did this."
Nobody heard him. Everyone else was still yelling. So Henry stuck his fingers in his mouth and let out a loud whistle.
Everyone fell silent for a second. They all turned to look at Henry.
"I know who did this," he said again.
"You do?" Maggie asked.
"Of course he does," Kyle said. "Henry is friends with Cole. He probably even helped Cole. Why else would he hang around the pool all day?"
"Yeah." John rolled his eyes. "Why are we even listening to him? He doesn't know anything."
"He might," Daisy said. "Haven't you heard about The Lemonade Detectives? Henry and his friends helped my neighbor find his lost keys last week."
"Really?" Tiny asked. "That's cool. Can you guys find my lost cell phone?"
"Quiet!" Coach Phillips shouted. "Henry, do you really know something about all this?"
Henry nodded. "Cole didn't have anything to do with the pranks," he said. "Neither did Daisy or Kyle or Tommy."
"Then who did it?" Maggie asked.
Henry looked over at Tommy's brother. "It was John."
"How dare you accuse me!" John exclaimed as everyone else gasped. "You can't prove anything!"

"I can't prove you dumped those frogs," Henry said. "But I know you poured the paint in Kyle's bag. Kyle, Coach Phillips, and I were the only ones who looked at the paint. But you just said it was green paint. How would you know that unless you poured it in there yourself?"
Daisy gasped. "He did say it was green!"
"That was just a lucky guess," John protested. "Daisy is always painting pictures of trees and stuff. I figured she'd use green paint!"
But the coach was frowning. "Did you have anything to do with those frogs, John?" he asked.
"His parents own a pet store," Tiny spoke up. "I bet he got the frogs there and dumped them in the pool when we weren't looking!"
"I just remembered something," Cole said. "John was the fastest jogger. He got back to the pool before the rest of us."
"I remember that too," Kyle said. "Cole and I got there next. But it took us a few more minutes than John. He had plenty of time to dump the frogs back in the water."
"And place my flip-flops near the buckets," Cole added.
Tommy stared at his brother. "Is that why you said you'd go inside and get Tiny's towel for Daisy, John?"
"Aha!" Henry said. "So John was behind the ant trick too!"

Finally John hid his face in his hands. "Okay, you're right. It was all me!" he blurted out. "I stained the towel and dragged it through an anthill. Then I folded it so nobody would notice the ants until Daisy used the towel. I dumped the frogs in the pool too. I'm sorry. I thought if I got rid of everyone else, Tommy might make the team."
Tommy stared at John. "Why would you do that? You know I don't care much about swimming."

"If you don't make the swim team, Mom and Dad will let you take tennis lessons instead," John said. "I heard them talking about how expensive that is. They might not have enough money to buy me a car for my birthday!"
"Wow," Maggie whispered to Henry. "John had a motive we didn't know about!"
The coach looked very serious. "Come with me, John," he said. "We'd better call your parents."
The next day Maggie and Henry were at the lemonade stand. "The last day of tryouts is almost over," Maggie said. "I wonder if Cole made the team."
Suddenly they heard a shout.
"That sounds like Cole," Henry said.
Cole raced toward them, grinning. "I made it!" he cried. "I'm on the swim team!"
"Congratulations!" Henry and Maggie exclaimed.
They each gave him a high five.
"Kyle must be mad that you got the spot," Maggie said.
"Nope," Cole said. "He made it too! There was an extra spot after Coach Phillips kicked John off the team."
"Then Daisy must be mad," Maggie said.
Cole shrugged. "Not really. Her parents said she could take horseback-riding lessons instead."
"What about Lauren?" Maggie asked next. "Is she mad that you made the team?"
"Not anymore," Cole said. "I apologized again for saying she looked young. This time she listened."
"That's great," Henry said.

"Another great thing happened," Cole went on. "John's parents gave me the frogs John brought to the pool! They wanted to apologize for John trying to get me in trouble. They even gave me free frog food for one month!"
"That's really generous," Henry said.

Cole put his hand in his pocket and pulled out a five-dollar bill. "I almost forgot. Coach Phillips was really grateful that The Lemonade Detectives solved the mystery. He offered to pay our detective fee."

Maggie looked away for a second. Then she looked back at Cole. "You didn't really do much to solve the case. Plus you got all those free frogs. So Henry and I should just split the money between the two of us."
"What?" Cole protested. "That's not fair!"
"The Lemonade Detectives are a team, Maggie," Henry reminded her.
"But I've almost got enough money to start horseback-riding lessons!" Maggie argued.
"I need money too!" said Cole.
While they were arguing, a man walked over. "Would you like to buy some lemonade?" Henry asked.
"No, thanks," the man said. "My son Kyle told me you three are pretty good detectives."
"That's right," Maggie said. "Do you have a case for us?"
The man sighed. "Yes. My wife's birthday is this weekend, and I forgot where I hid her gift."
Henry smiled. Finding a lost birthday gift wasn't the most exciting case in the world. But that didn't matter. The Lemonade Detectives solved all mysteries, large or small!
"Here, kitties," Henry said. "Fetch!"
He tossed a cat toy across the family room. Two kittens ran over and pounced on it. Henry laughed as the tiny cats batted the toy under the sofa.
Henry was at his aunt and uncle's house. They lived next door to him and his parents. It was a nice summer day, and the two families were having a barbecue in the backyard.
"The kittens are cute, Ellen," Henry's mother said as she picked up a plate of hot dogs in the kitchen.
Henry's aunt Ellen sighed. "Yes, they are," she said. "But they get into everything! I'll be glad when they're a little older."

One of the kittens started rolling on the rug. The other one jumped onto the sofa. Henry smiled as he watched them. They were really playful! The kittens belonged to his cousin Maggie. She was nine years old, two years younger than Henry.
"Should we head outside?" Henry's father asked. "I could start grilling the food while we wait for Uncle Bruce and Maggie to get home."
Henry's father and Uncle Bruce both loved to cook on Uncle Bruce's fancy grill. Whenever the families had a barbecue together, the two dads did most of the cooking.
"Good idea," Henry told his father. "I'm hungry!"
"Henry, would you please put the kittens in Maggie's room before we go outside?" Aunt Ellen asked. "They can't get into too much trouble there. All her clothes are already covered in cat hair!"
"Sure," Henry said. He scooped up one kitten in each hand. They wriggled and meowed, trying to escape. But soon they were safely shut inside Maggie's bedroom.
Henry headed outside. His parents and Aunt Ellen were setting food on the picnic table. They were having hot dogs and hamburgers, corn on the cob, and Henry's favorite—watermelon.
"I hope Maggie gets home from her riding lesson soon," Henry's father said as he walked over to the grill. "I want some of her delicious lemonade."
"Watch out, Dad," Henry joked. "She'll probably charge you 25 cents per cup!"

Everyone chuckled. Maggie had started a lemonade stand a few weeks ago to earn money for horseback-riding lessons. Her parents had told her they would pay half the lesson fees if she paid the other half herself.
"I wonder what's taking them so long," Aunt Ellen said, looking at her watch. "Bruce left to pick Maggie up from the barn almost an hour ago. They should be home by now."
"Uh-oh," Henry's dad joked. "Sounds like a mystery for The Lemonade Detectives!"

Henry grinned. A few weeks ago, Maggie, Henry, and their friend, Cole, had started The Lemonade Detective agency. They'd already solved quite a few cases. Some cases were interesting, like figuring out who'd dumped frogs into the town pool. Other cases were kind of boring, like finding people's lost keys or library books. But so far The Lemonade Detectives had solved them all. They were even making money, which was helping to pay for Maggie's horseback-riding lessons.

"That's not much of a mystery, Dad," Henry said. "We already know that Maggie loves being at the barn. We also know that she's really talkative. She's probably giving Uncle Bruce a tour and making him meet all the horses before they leave."
"But I thought this was her third riding lesson," Henry's father said. "Hasn't Uncle Bruce been to the barn before?"
"Yes," Henry replied with a shrug. "But that wouldn't stop Maggie from dragging him all over the place!"
Aunt Ellen smiled. "Good detective work, Henry," she said. "If you're right, will we owe you five dollars for your detective fee?"
"No," Henry said with a laugh. "I'll give you the family discount. Just don't tell Maggie!"
"It's nice that Maggie is enjoying her lessons," Henry's father said. "She worked so hard to earn the money for them."
"Yes, she's definitely enjoying them," Aunt Ellen said. "I think she'd move into the barn if we'd let her!"
Henry grinned. "It's easy to imagine Maggie sleeping in a stall like a horse," he said. "But I can't imagine her eating hay. She doesn't even like salad!"
Just then the back door swung open. Maggie came stomping into the backyard, still dressed in her riding clothes. Her face was bright red, and she did not look happy.
"There's a rotten thief at the barn!" she cried. She pointed at Henry. "And I need the other Lemonade Detectives to help me figure out who it is!"
"A thief at the barn?" Henry said. "What are you talking about, Maggie?"

By now Maggie's father, Henry's uncle Bruce, had come into the backyard. "There's no need to be so dramatic, Maggie," he said with a sigh. "Mom and I have talked to you before about this. You need to be more careful with your things."

"But I was being careful!" Maggie exclaimed. "I left the check on my bag, right on top of my sandals. It was definitely there when I led my pony outside for our lesson. But when I got back, the check was gone!"
"Wait a minute," Aunt Ellen said. "Are you saying you lost the check we wrote for today's lesson?"
"Don't worry, I wrote another one," Uncle Bruce told his wife. "And I called the bank to cancel the first check."
"Oh, Maggie." Aunt Ellen shook her head. "I can't believe you were so careless, especially after what happened last week."
Henry was surprised. Maggie could be careless about some things. But she was really careful with her money.
"What happened last week?" he asked.
"Maggie lost a few other things at the barn," Uncle Bruce said.
"Oh dear," Henry's mother said.
"I didn't lose anything!" Maggie protested. "Someone has been stealing things!"
"Really? What else disappeared?" Henry asked.
"At my first lesson, I took off my charm bracelet and left it in the barn," Maggie said. "I didn't want to lose it while I was riding. When I came back inside after my lesson, it was gone!"
"I don't know why you were so worried about losing it," her mother said. "You always let those kittens of yours use it as a cat toy!"
Maggie frowned. "That's different. The kittens just bat it around. I always know where it is."
"Did anything else disappear?" Henry asked. He was already thinking like a detective. The first thing a good detective needed to do was find out the facts of the case.

Maggie nodded. "At my second lesson, my brand-new horse grooming brush disappeared," she said. "It happened the same way. It was in the barn when I went outside for my lesson, but gone when I got back."
"Don't forget about your gloves," her father said.
"Oh, right," Maggie said. "I didn't wear my riding gloves today because it was so hot. I left them with my stuff in the barn. Whoever took that check must have taken the gloves too."
"Maggie!" Aunt Ellen looked shocked. "Those gloves were expensive!"
"Everything about horseback riding is expensive," Uncle Bruce agreed. "We can't afford to keep replacing things."

Henry could tell that Maggie's parents thought she'd lost all those things. But he wasn't so sure. Maggie was too careful with money to misplace a check. She was so excited about riding that he couldn't believe she'd lose a horse brush or her riding gloves. And he knew she loved that charm bracelet.
"Is anyone allowed inside the barn while there's a lesson outside?" he asked Maggie.

"Sure, I guess so," Maggie said with a shrug. "I mean, they don't close the doors or anything. Any rotten thief could just walk in." She clenched her fists. "I can't believe someone is doing this to me!"
She sounded so dramatic again that all the adults looked at each other. But Maggie's words made Henry think of another question.
"Has anything else disappeared?" he asked her. "I mean, anything belonging to other people. Or is it only your stuff?"
"How should I know?" Maggie frowned. "That's what I need you to find out! Dad made me leave the barn before I could investigate."
Uncle Bruce shook his head. "We were already late for this barbecue," he said. "Besides, I don't think there's a mystery here. It just means that you have to be more careful with your things."
"That's right," Aunt Ellen said. "I had to pull your favorite horse T-shirt out from under your desk this morning. The kittens were using it as a bed. It was absolutely covered in cat hair."
Henry's mother cleared her throat. "Should we eat? Everything smells delicious, and I'm hungry," she said.
"Good idea, Susan," Uncle Bruce agreed. "Go sit down at the picnic table, everybody. I'll help Kevin bring the food over from the grill."
The adults were obviously ready to change the subject. But later, while everyone was eating, Maggie was still thinking about her missing things.
"I didn't lose my stuff at the barn!" she said loudly. "Somebody stole it! And The Lemonade Detectives will figure out who it was!"
Aunt Ellen glanced up from her corn on the cob. "I hope so, Maggie," she said. "Because if this keeps happening, you might not be able to keep riding."
"Ah-choo!" Cole sneezed.
"Bless you," Henry said.
"Thanks." Cole sniffed. "I'm allergic to cats."

It was two days after the family barbecue. Henry was in the car with Cole and Maggie. Uncle Bruce was driving them to the barn. Maggie had another riding lesson, and the boys were going along to investigate the mystery of her missing stuff.
"Sorry, Cole," Uncle Bruce said. "Maggie's kittens have never been in the car. But their hair gets all over everything, especially Maggie's clothes."
"At least the car doesn't smell like horses," Henry told Cole with a smile. "Uncle Bruce makes Maggie put on her riding boots at the barn."
He pointed to a bag on the seat beside Maggie. Her boots and socks were inside, along with her helmet and other riding gear.
Cole was the first one out of the car when they reached the barn. "Fresh air!" he cried happily. "I can breathe again!"
Maggie rolled her eyes. "Don't get too excited. There's a barn cat who lives here. Look, there she is." She pointed to a cat who was sleeping in the sun on top of a hay bale.
"That's okay," Cole said. "I don't usually sneeze when a cat is outside."
They waved good-bye to Maggie's dad and hurried into the barn. "The pony I ride is over here," Maggie said. "His name is Spot."
She stopped in front of a horse stall and set down her bag. A pony looked out at them. When Maggie patted him, he nibbled on her hair.
Maggie giggled and gently pushed his head away. "Stop that, Spot!"
Henry heard a bark. A dog came running toward them. His tail was wagging.
A girl Henry didn't recognize came running too. "Come back here, Spot!"
"Hey! This dog has the same name as Maggie's pony!" Cole exclaimed. He stooped to pat the dog. Cole wasn't allergic to dogs, just cats.
Maggie nodded. "Everyone calls the pony Big Spot and the dog Little Spot," she explained. "Little Spot belongs to Eleanor. She's one of the other riders in my group lesson."
By now Eleanor had reached them. "Hi," she said breathlessly. "Sorry about that. But Little Spot is friendly."
"We don't mind," Cole said. "He's cute."
"Thanks." Eleanor picked up Little Spot. "See you later. I need to get my pony ready."
She hurried off.
"Shouldn't you be getting Big Spot ready?" Cole asked Maggie.
"I want to show you around the barn first," Maggie said. "That way you can start investigating."
"Good idea," Henry agreed.
He and Cole followed Maggie down the aisle. A horse or pony looked out of each stall they passed.
Then they saw a pony standing in the aisle. A boy was brushing it while a teenage girl watched. The girl was holding a pitchfork.
"You're not doing that right, Zach," she complained. "You're supposed to move the brush in circles."
"Leave me alone, Jill," the boy said.
Henry recognized them from his neighborhood. Zach was in Maggie's class at school. Jill was Zach's older sister. She and her friend Ashley sometimes came to the lemonade stand.
"Hi, Zach," Henry said. "I didn't know you rode horses."
"I just started." Zach frowned. "My parents are making me because my sister has a dumb part-time job here."
"You'd have fun if you had a better attitude," Jill told him.
Just then a woman walked toward them. "Did you finish cleaning the stalls, Jill?" she asked.
"Not yet, Ms. Wood." Jill hurried off to finish her chores.
Maggie introduced Henry and Cole to Ms. Wood. "She owns the barn and teaches all the lessons," Maggie explained.
Ms. Wood smiled. "Nice to meet you, boys," she said. "Maggie, it's time to get Big Spot ready. And you need to change into your riding boots. It's not safe to wear sandals in the barn."
"Sorry, I was just about to do that," Maggie said. "Come on, you guys."
They headed back down the aisle. On the way, they passed another girl. Henry recognized her too. Her name was Daisy, and she was two years ahead of him at school.
"Hi, Maggie," Daisy said. "Am I late for our lesson?"
"Not yet," Maggie told her. "But you'd better hurry."
Daisy rushed away. "I didn't know Daisy was a rider," Cole said.
"She started taking lessons at the same time I did," Maggie explained.
"How many people are in your lesson?" Henry asked.
"You just met them all," Maggie said. "It's Daisy, Zach, Eleanor, and me."
Henry nodded. So far he hadn't seen anything suspicious. But he wanted to keep track of all the possible suspects.
They turned the corner and saw Big Spot's stall. Maggie hurried to her bag and pulled out her riding boots.
"Oh no," she moaned. "One of my socks is missing!"
"Are you sure your sock is gone?" Henry asked. "Maybe it fell into the bottom of your bag."
Maggie dumped her bag out on the bench. "No, it's not here. Someone stole it! Just like all my other stuff!"
"Why would someone steal one sock?" Cole wondered.
Maggie didn't answer. She was already stomping down the aisle of the barn.
"Uh-oh," Henry said. "We'd better follow her."
He knew that his cousin had a quick temper. If she started yelling about her sock, she might accidentally warn the thief that the boys were investigating.
Maggie stopped in front of a horse stall. Daisy was standing in the doorway holding a saddle.
"My sock is missing!" Maggie said. "Did you take it?"
Daisy gave her a surprised look. "Why would I take your sock? I have my own." She pointed to her feet. Two pink socks were sticking out above her boots.
Henry grabbed Maggie's arm as Daisy went into her horse's stall.
"Wait," he said. "Yelling at people won't get your sock back."
"Or any of the other stuff," added Cole. "Let us investigate."
For a second Henry didn't think Maggie would agree. But finally she nodded.
"Okay," she said. "But how am I supposed to ride with only one sock?"
Cole kicked off his sneakers. "You can borrow one of mine," he said.
"Yuck. Boys' socks stink." Maggie made a face. But she took the sock Cole handed her. "I guess I'll have to suffer if I want to ride."
Then she stomped back toward Big Spot's stall. Cole took off his other sock and stuck it in his pocket. Then he put his shoes back on.
"Are we really going to investigate a missing sock?" he asked Henry. "She probably just left it in the car or something."
"You could be right," Henry admitted. "Did you notice if she had both socks in her bag when we came in?"
Cole laughed. "No. I don't usually go around counting people's socks, especially when they're not even on their feet."

That gave Henry an idea. "I know what we can do," he said. "Let's go see what socks everybody else is wearing. For example, we know Daisy isn't wearing Maggie's missing sock. Her socks are pink, and Maggie's are white."
"Do you really think someone took that sock?"
"Who knows?" Henry shrugged. "Maybe someone forgot a sock and decided to borrow Maggie's since she wasn't watching it."
"Even if someone did borrow a sock, that doesn't mean that person is the barn thief," Cole said.
"True," Henry agreed. "But we can watch for other suspicious behavior while we check everyone's socks."
They walked back to Zach. By now he was putting a saddle on his pony.
"What do you want?" he asked when he saw Henry and Cole. He sounded kind of grumpy.
"Nothing." Henry looked at Zach's feet. He was wearing athletic socks with stripes on them. "Do you know where Eleanor is?"
"Nope." Zach adjusted the pony's saddle.
Henry and Cole walked away. "Wrong socks," Cole whispered.
Henry nodded. "Two suspects down, one to go."
"Only one?" Cole said. "What about Jill and Ms. Wood?"

Henry thought about that. "I don't think Ms. Wood is a good suspect," he said. "Why would an adult steal a kid's stuff? Plus she was going to get the check from Maggie anyway. But we probably should investigate Jill."
They wandered around until they found Eleanor. She was leading a pony out of its stall.
Henry looked at her feet. She was wearing short boots, just like the others. But her pants completely covered her socks. Now what?
Cole had an idea. "Hey, Eleanor," he said. "Is that a bug crawling up your pant leg?"
"What? Which leg?" Eleanor shrieked. She dropped the pony's reins and yanked up both pant legs. Her socks were brown.
"Sorry, I guess I was wrong," Cole said.
Eleanor gave him an angry look. Then she grabbed her pony's reins and hurried off.
"Good trick," Henry said with a grin. "I guess it proved that nobody is wearing that sock. Maybe Maggie did leave it in the car."
"Or maybe Big Spot grabbed it," Cole suggested. "Maggie left her bag sitting right by his stall."
"Yeah. Let's go check."
They hurried back to Big Spot's stall. The pony was gone. So was Maggie.
"I guess the riding lesson started," Henry said.
Cole looked into the pony's stall. "I don't see the sock in here. Maybe Spot ate it. He wanted to eat Maggie's hair, remember?"
Henry shrugged. "Maybe. But he definitely didn't eat that brush that disappeared or Maggie's charm bracelet. We have to find that thief!"
"Let's go outside and watch Maggie's riding lesson," Henry suggested. "Someone might do something suspicious."
"Okay. Maybe you should bring Maggie's sandals so they don't get stolen," Cole said.
Henry was pretty sure Cole was joking. But he picked up the sandals anyway. "That's a good idea," he said. "If these sandals disappear, Maggie's parents will freak out."
Cole nodded. "I think Maggie said the riding ring is this way." He headed toward the back door.
On their way out, the boys passed Jill. She was trying to yank a wheelbarrow out of a stall. It was piled high with horse manure.
"Ugh!" Jill cried as the wheelbarrow almost tipped over. Then she spotted the boys. "Hey," she said. "Will you two help me? My wheelbarrow is stuck."
"Sure." Henry put down the sandals. Then he and Cole grabbed the wheelbarrow. Working together, they soon pulled it into the aisle.
"Whew! Thanks." Jill wiped sweat off her forehead. "I thought I'd never get it out of there."
"Cleaning all these stalls must be hard work," Henry said.
"It is." Jill frowned. "And Ms. Wood doesn't pay me very much."
"So why do you do it?" Cole asked.
"Because it's the only way to pay for extra riding lessons." Jill sighed. "I wish I had a way to earn more cash! Then I could ride every day and not have to clean a bunch of stinky stalls first."
Henry and Cole said good-bye to Jill and headed outdoors. "Are you thinking what I'm thinking?" Cole asked as they sat down on a bench outside the riding ring.
"Yes, if you're thinking that Jill should be a suspect." Henry put Maggie's sandals on the bench. "It sounds like she'd do anything to get more money for riding."
"Including steal stuff?" Cole asked.
"Who knows?" Henry said. "She could probably sell Maggie's gloves and charm bracelet. And she might have thought she could cash that check."
"Okay, we'll put her on the suspect list," Cole said. "But we'd better not let her know she's on there. If she turns out to be innocent again, she'll be really annoyed!"
Henry laughed. The Lemonade Detectives had suspected Jill of stealing during their very first mystery. She'd turned out to be innocent in that case. But that didn't mean she was innocent now too.
Henry glanced at the riding ring. "We should be watching our other suspects."

He and Cole watched the lesson for a while. Ms. Wood stood in the middle of the ring and told the riders what to do. First she had them walk their horses around in a big circle. Then she told them to trot. Henry noticed that trotting was faster, and it looked kind of bouncy.
"This is no fun!" Zach complained loudly. "Every time my pony trots, I almost fall off."
"That kid really doesn't want to be here, does he?" Cole whispered.
"It's easy, Zach!" Daisy called out. "Just watch me."
As Daisy trotted past the others, Eleanor's pony slowed to a walk. "Ms. Wood, my pony is lazy!" Eleanor called out. "I have to squeeze him so often, my leg muscles are tired!"
"You're doing fine, Eleanor," Ms. Wood said. "Daisy, please come back and join the others."
"But I was just showing Zach how to trot," Daisy said. "I was doing it right, wasn't I?"
"Daisy is pretty competitive," Cole whispered to Henry. "She tried out for the swim team, remember?"
Henry nodded. "Maybe she's afraid Maggie is a better rider. Daisy could be taking Maggie's stuff so Maggie will get in trouble and have to quit."
"Zach has a good motive too," Cole said. "He hates this place. Maybe he's stealing stuff just to cause trouble."
"Or he could be trying to get his sister in trouble," Henry said. "If she gets fired, his parents probably wouldn't make him ride anymore."

Cole looked out at the ring again. Eleanor was still whining about her pony being too slow. "What about Eleanor?" he said. "She's the only one who doesn't seem to have a motive. Maybe she thought that jingling Maggie's charm bracelet at her pony would make him go faster."
Henry laughed. "I doubt that. We don't know Eleanor very well," he reminded Cole. "Maybe she has a motive that we haven't figured out yet."
Cole nodded. "All we know is that she's kind of lazy and she has a dog."
"Speaking of her dog, there he is." Henry saw Little Spot wandering toward them. The dog stopped to sniff at something on the ground. Then he came toward them.
"Here, Little Spot." Cole held out his hand.
Little Spot ignored him. He grabbed one of Maggie's sandals and took off!
"Hey!" Henry cried.
"Aha!" Cole said. "I think we just caught the thief!"

"I wish Little Spot had turned out to be the thief after all," Maggie said with a sigh. "Then the mystery would be solved. And I wouldn't still be worried that Mom and Dad are going to make me stop riding."
Henry, Cole, and Maggie were at the lemonade stand talking about what had happened yesterday.
"We thought Little Spot was guilty at first," Cole said. "But then Henry started thinking logically again."

Henry smiled. "Little Spot did grab your sandal," he reminded Maggie. "But then I thought of something. Why would a dog steal things only from you? It didn't make sense. The other riders leave their stuff sitting around too."
"That's why we questioned everyone after your lesson," Cole went on. "We wanted to make sure the thief wasn't stealing stuff from everyone."
"Nobody else is missing anything," Henry said. "Well, except for Ms. Wood."
Cole nodded. "She said the barn cat's bed has been missing for a few days. But she's pretty sure a raccoon took that."
"We also did an experiment to see if Little Spot would try to grab anything else," Henry said. "We used Cole's sock. Little Spot sniffed it, but he didn't pick it up."
"So we decided that Little Spot just likes to grab shoes," Cole said. "My neighbor's dog is the same way, except he only steals TV remote controls."

Maggie sighed again. "Well, it definitely wasn't Big Spot either," she said. "He might have been able to grab my sock. But he couldn't have taken my bracelet. I put it in my bag as I led him out, and it was missing as soon as I got back."
"Really? Then I guess we can rule out all of the animal suspects," Henry said.
Cole laughed. "Yeah. The barn cat couldn't have picked up your grooming brush."
"So who are our human suspects?" Maggie asked.
"All the other riders in your class," Henry said. "Plus Jill."
"Right," Cole said. "We found out that Jill wishes she had more money for riding. What if she stole your stuff so she could sell it?"
"Who would buy one sock?" Maggie asked.
"Nobody," Henry answered. "We figured you might have lost that on your way into the barn."
Maggie frowned. "You're as bad as my parents! I didn't lose that sock. I know it was in my bag when I put the bag down!"

Henry wasn't so sure. He still didn't think Maggie was careless enough to lose the check or the other stuff. But it would be easy for her to drop a sock without noticing, especially when she was excited about going riding.
He didn't say that though. He didn't want to make Maggie angry.
"How well do you know Eleanor?" he asked instead.
"Not that well." Maggie shrugged. "We've only had four lessons together. But I doubt she's the thief."
"Why?" Cole asked. "You just said you don't know her very well. How do you know she's not sneaky?"
"Because she takes such good care of her dog," Maggie said. "She's just as crazy about Little Spot as I am about my kittens. Someone like that has to be a good person."
"Okay," Henry said. "But what about the others? We noticed Daisy was acting kind of competitive."
"Yeah, she's always like that." Maggie rolled her eyes. "She wants to try everything first. And she thinks she's the best at whatever we do."
"Then there's Zach," Cole said. "He was complaining about everything. What if he's stealing stuff because he hates riding?"
"I still think his sister, Jill, is a better suspect," Henry said. "She has the best motive. She needs money."
"I agree, Henry. But here come some customers." Maggie pointed to several people heading toward the lemonade stand. "We'll have to finish talking about this later."
"I hope we can solve the mystery today," Maggie said. "Otherwise Mom said this might be my last lesson for a while." She sounded upset. Henry didn't blame her.
It was a few days later, and The Lemonade Detectives were back at the barn.
"Do you have both of your socks today?" Cole asked.
Maggie made a face at him. "You already asked me that twenty times," she said. "I told you, I stuck them in my boots today. There's no way they can fall out."
Henry noticed Ms. Wood hurrying toward them. The barn owner had an anxious expression on her face.
"Maggie!" Ms. Wood said. "There you are. I need to speak with you about something serious."
"I'm not late, am I?" Maggie asked.
Ms. Wood shook her head. "It's not that," she said. "We have a problem. Right after you left the barn the other day, I realized something: Big Spot's saddle pad is missing!"
"Big Spot's saddle pad is missing?" Maggie said. "What do you mean? I put it back in the tack room, just like always!"
"What's a tack room?" Cole whispered to Henry.
"I think it's where they keep the horses' equipment," he answered.
"Are you sure?" Ms. Wood was asking Maggie. "Because the other pads were there. But yours wasn't with them."
"I'm positive!" Maggie insisted. "I remember because it was kind of damp from Spot's sweat. I could feel it through my shirt when I carried everything back to the tack room."
Ms. Wood didn't look convinced. "Well, I haven't seen it since your last lesson. If it doesn't turn up soon, I'll have to speak to your parents about replacing it."
Henry looked at Cole, worried. Had the thief struck again?
"I put a different pad under Spot's saddle," Ms. Wood went on. "You can use that one for today."
The barn owner hurried away. Maggie stomped toward Big Spot's stall. The boys followed.
"I can't believe this!" Maggie cried. "It's bad enough that my parents might not let me ride anymore. Now I have to worry about Ms. Wood kicking me out of the barn too!"
"How much does a saddle pad cost?" Henry asked.
"Why?" Maggie looked hopeful. "Are you going to buy Ms. Wood a new one so she doesn't tell my parents?"
"No. I'm trying to figure out whether the thief could sell that pad for a lot of money."

"Probably not." Maggie started changing into her riding boots. "The pad was kind of old. And saddle pads only cost about 15 dollars when they're new. I looked at some when Mom took me to the store to buy my riding clothes."
"This case doesn't make sense," Cole said. "The thief is stealing really weird stuff."
Henry nodded. "It's weird that only Maggie's stuff has disappeared. And it's even weirder that some of the missing stuff is valuable and some isn't."
"A thief could sell Maggie's bracelet or her new riding gloves," Cole said. "And the check was worth money too, of course. But why steal one sock? Or a sweaty old saddle pad?"
"Who cares why someone did it?" Maggie said. "We just need to figure out who did it. And fast!"
"Don't worry," Henry told her. "I have a plan, remember?"
"Good. I hope it works."
Maggie started getting her pony ready, and the boys wandered off. "Do you think your plan will work?" Cole asked.
Henry stooped to pat Little Spot as the dog ran up to them. "I don't know. But it's the best plan I can think of right now."
