"True." Henry nodded. "Plus, he was alone with the booty while Nathan ran to get us, remember?"
Cole's eyes widened. "You're right! What if Luke opened the box while Nathan was gone? He could have hidden the tickets somewhere and tossed the gum into the container."
Maggie gasped. "Yes! Especially since he said it's his favorite flavor."

"Wait," Henry said. "I just remembered something else. When we got to the tide pool, William was already waiting there with Luke. Do you think Luke had enough time alone to grab the tickets before William showed up?"
"I almost forgot about that!" Cole said. He frowned. "I wonder why William went to that tide pool instead of finding me. We were supposed to be a team."
Henry shrugged. "I don't know. But we should ask him what time he got there."
"I have another idea," Maggie said. "What if Luke and Nathan took the tickets? They're both obsessed with pirates. And they're both dying to see that movie."
"Why would they do that?" Cole asked. "They would get to see the movie either way. There were enough tickets in there for all of us."
"True. But maybe they wanted the extra tickets so they could invite some other friends," Maggie said.
"I don't know." Henry stopped and looked up at the Pirate Ship rock. "Nathan has been acting a little bit strange today," Henry went on. "But he's such a nice kid. I can't believe he'd—"
Just then someone stepped out from behind the rock. "What are you kids doing here?" he asked in a gruff voice. "Talk, or I'll make you walk the plank!"
The man was Roger Redbeard!
"W-what do you mean, you'll make us walk the plank?" Maggie asked nervously.
Roger Redbeard grinned. "I'm just joking around, kids," he said. "I like to practice my pirate voice. Aargh! "
Henry glanced at his friends. He could tell they were thinking the same thing he was. Had Roger taken their tickets?
"Excuse me, Mr. Redbeard," he said. "Can we ask you a question?"
"Sure." Roger took a sip from the plastic cup he was holding. "Is it about pirates?"
"Not exactly." Henry cleared his throat. "We're just wondering where you've been since the last time we saw you."
Roger looked surprised. "I walked downtown to get lunch." Henry noticed that Roger was holding a plastic cup. It had a logo printed on it that said SCGS. "Why do you ask?"
"No reason." Henry traded another look with his friends. "Um, did you see anyone else on the beach while you were walking?"
Roger shrugged. "It's pretty quiet at this end of town. It's mostly private land. The only person I passed out here was the Jones girl."
"The Jones girl?" Maggie said. "Who's that?"
"Sorry, I don't remember her first name," Roger said. "But her parents own the general store in town."
Henry realized Roger must be talking about Anna. "Did she see you?" he asked Roger.

"I doubt it," Roger replied. "She was running through the surf." He took another sip of his drink. "Is that all you want to know? Because if you don't have any questions about pirates, I'd better move along."
"Okay. Bye," Henry said.
Roger wandered away, disappearing soon behind some rocks. Maggie checked to make sure he was gone.
"Do you think he's telling the truth?" she asked.
"He wasn't carrying that cup when we saw him before," Henry reminded her. "So he probably is telling the truth."
"That means he couldn't have stolen our tickets," Cole said.
"Not necessarily," Maggie argued. "How far away is the town? It might only take five minutes to walk there. We should ask William or Anna."
"Speaking of Anna, shouldn't she be a suspect?" Henry asked. "Roger said he saw her running down the beach. That's kind of suspicious."
"Not really," Maggie said. "She was looking for booty, just like the rest of us."

Henry nodded. "But she was alone, while the rest of us had partners. And she knew exactly where all the tide pools were. What if she grabbed the tickets before Luke and Nathan reached the tide pool?" he asked.
Maggie gasped. "You could be right! Nathan said he and Luke had trouble finding their tide pool."
"But why would she want the tickets?" Cole wondered. "She's not even interested in pirates."
"That's true." Henry thought back. "She said the legends were stupid."
Just then they heard a shout. Luke was running toward them.
"What is it?" Maggie called. "Did you find the booty?"

"Maybe," Luke replied breathlessly. "We didn't find anything at the marina. I told the others I'd run and see if you guys found anything. But on the way here, I noticed something interesting. Come on!"
He led the way back to the bay. A rowboat was bobbing in the water just offshore. A skull-and-crossbones flag was flying from it.
"That's a pirate flag!" Cole exclaimed. "You guys pull in the boat. I'll run and get the others."
The rowboat was tied to a small dock with strong rope. Henry, Maggie, and Luke pulled on the rope as Cole ran off. By the time Cole returned with Nathan, William, and Anna, the boat was on the beach.
"There's a pirate chest on board!" Luke called.Cole helped Luke lift the chest out of the boat. Then Henry opened it.
"Wow!" he cried when he saw what was inside. "Handheld video game players! There are seven of them, one for each of us!"
"Are you kidding?" Maggie exclaimed. "Let me see!"
She grabbed one of the players and turned it on. A picture of a pirate ship appeared on the screen.
"Whoa!" Luke peered over Maggie's shoulder. "It's already loaded with the Revenge of the Pirate's Ghost game!"
"No way!" Nathan yelled.
"Can I have one?" Cole asked.

The kids each grabbed one of the players. Anna was the last to take one. "I've been dying to get one of these," she said slowly. "My parents said they're too expensive, but I've been saving my allowance all summer."
That made Henry stop and think. "You're right, Anna," Henry said. "These game players are expensive, a lot more expensive than a bunch of movie tickets, even for a premiere."
"Yeah." Nathan sounded distracted as he played with his game. "So what?"
Henry shrugged. "So why would someone steal the tickets, but not this booty?"
"I know why someone would take the movie tickets but not these games," Cole said. "It's simple. The thief stumbled across that plastic container. But he didn't find this treasure chest."
"Yeah," Luke agreed. "William's parents said that's probably what happened."
"I still think Roger Redbeard stole our tickets," Maggie added. "He probably didn't notice the clue in the box."
"It's a good thing he didn't know about this booty," Nathan said. "We wouldn't have our awesome new game players right now!"

Henry didn't say anything. He still wasn't sure that Roger was the thief. They needed more evidence. Henry was still thinking as they started to walk back to the beach. He had to find out if Roger had really walked to town.
"Hey, Anna," he said. "Did you see Roger walking by the surf while we were all checking the tide pools?"
Anna blinked. "Excuse me?" she said.
Henry repeated his question.
She shook her head. "I didn't go down by the surf," she replied. "My tide pool wasn't close to the water."
"Really?" Maggie said. "Because Roger said he saw you running through the surf."

"He did?" Anna said. Then she gave a quick smile. "Oh, I know. I bet he saw my sister. She's only two years older than I am. A lot of people think we look alike. She was probably jogging. She loves to exercise."
Henry thought of another question for Anna. "How long does it take to walk to town from here?"
"About fifteen or twenty minutes," Anna replied.
Cole wasn't paying much attention to the conversation. He was staring at the next clue. "It's a drawing of some buildings," he said. "Close to a park or something."
"I think we have to go into town," said Luke. "We can play our games on the way."

Everyone started walking up the beach toward town. When they passed William's house, William stopped. "I'll catch up with you in a few minutes," he said. "These sandals are giving me blisters. I want to put on different ones."
Without waiting for an answer, he ran ahead and disappeared into his house. The others stared after him.
"What's wrong with William today?" Nathan said with a frown. "He seems grouchy. It's almost like he wishes we weren't here."
Henry had been thinking the same thing. He just shrugged. "I'm not sure."

They all kept walking. Everyone except Henry was focused on their video game players. Soon Henry poked Cole and Maggie, gesturing for them to slow down. He wanted The Lemonade Detectives to whisper to one another without anyone else overhearing.
"What do you guys think?" Henry asked quietly. "If Roger really walked to town and back, it took him at least half an hour."
"Plus however long it took him to go into a store and buy that soda," Cole pointed out.
"That means he didn't have time to steal our tickets," Maggie added. " If he's telling the truth, that is."
Cole nodded. "We still don't know for sure. Anna said she didn't see him, remember?"
"I know." Henry glanced forward to make sure the others weren't listening. "When we get to town, let's try to find out if he really bought that soda there."
"How are we going to do that?" Cole asked.
"There was a logo on the cup," Henry replied. "It said SCGS. Maybe we can find a business with that name."
"Okay," Cole said. "But what about our other suspects?"
"Like William, for instance," Maggie said. "It's pretty suspicious that he ran off by himself."
"This is the second time he's done that," Cole said. "He left when he and I were supposed to be searching together too."
"That is suspcious," Henry agreed. "We should pay attention to William. And to Anna, Luke, and Nathan."
"I still don't think Nathan would steal anything," Cole said. "I know he's acting kind of grouchy today, but—"
Cole stopped short. Henry saw why. Luke was dropping back to join them.
"Keep up, you guys," he said with a smile. "Otherwise we might not share the next pirate booty with you!"
Henry chuckled. Since Luke was there, he decided to try to question him.
"It's too bad about those missing movie tickets, huh?" he said. "You're such a big fan of pirates, I bet you'd love to go to that premiere."
Luke didn't answer. Henry looked over at him. To Henry's surprise, Luke wasn't smiling anymore. His face was turning bright red.
"Um, actually, about those movie tickets . . ." Luke muttered.
Henry's eyes widened. Was Luke about to confess to the crime?
"I have a confession to make," Luke went on.
"I knew it!" Maggie exclaimed. "You took those tickets, didn't you?"

"What?" Luke looked confused. "No, wait. My confession is that I already saw Revenge of the Pirate's Ghost . My uncle owns a movie theater in my hometown. He held an early screening, and I got to go."
Henry was surprised. That wasn't the confession he'd expected!
"Wait," Henry said. "You already saw the movie? Why didn't you tell us?"

Luke shrugged. "I didn't want to give away any secrets about the plot. Especially anything important, like Captain Green is actually the main pirate's brother . . . Oops!" He clapped one hand over his mouth. Then he pulled it away, looking sheepish. "Don't tell Nathan I just said that, okay? He's really excited to see the movie. I don't want to ruin the surprise for him. Sorry I just ruined it for you guys."
"It's okay, and don't worry, we won't tell Nathan," Cole promised while Henry and Maggie nodded. "But does this mean you didn't take our booty?"
"Of course not!" Luke said. "Why would I do that? I'm not a thief."
He hurried to rejoin the others. Henry looked at Maggie and Cole.
"I guess Luke's innocent," he said. "If he already saw that movie, he has no motive for stealing the tickets."
"Yeah," Maggie agreed. "Especially since his uncle owns a movie theater. He can see any movie whenever he wants."

A few minutes later the whole group reached the town of Sea Cove. Maggie hurried over to Anna and Luke, who were looking at the drawing. Cole was about to go over there too. But Henry grabbed his arm.
"Look," he said, pointing to a shop nearby.
"Sea Cove General Store," Cole said, reading the sign on the front. "That must be Anna's family's store."
"That's not all," Henry said. "Look at the initials—SCGS. That's where Roger got that soda cup. Let's go find out!"
They hurried toward the store. When they got closer, Henry could see it wasn't just a store. There was a sandwich shop, a catering business, and a soda fountain.
"Wow, Anna's family sure must be busy," he commented.
Cole didn't answer. He was looking in another direction. "Here comes William."
Henry looked and saw William walking toward them. "Let's try to question him while he's alone," he whispered to Cole.
When William got closer, Henry smiled. "Hi, William. Are your new shoes more comfortable?" he said.
They all looked down at William's feet. He was wearing the same shoes he'd had on all day.
"I couldn't find my other sandals," William mumbled. "So I just left these on."
"Are you sure that's what happened?" Cole said. "Or were you really hiding something in your room?"
"Hiding something? What do you mean?" William asked.
Henry elbowed Cole. Henry didn't want Cole to give away their suspicions.
But Cole ignored him. "Did you take those movie tickets, William?"
"What?" William looked confused. "Of course not! Why would I do that?"
"We don't know," Henry spoke up. "But we've noticed that you don't seem very happy to have us here. Maybe you changed your mind about inviting us."
"Yeah," Cole added. "Maybe you're trying to ruin the treasure hunt so we'll leave early."
William looked upset. "No way!" he blurted out. "I'm glad you guys are here!"
"Then why have you been in such a bad mood all day?" Cole asked.

William sighed. "Sorry about that. It's because of my parents. They're used to spending lots of money entertaining people for Dad's job. I didn't want them to do that this weekend. I just wanted us to have a fun, normal weekend at the beach." He shrugged. "But they planned this whole expensive treasure hunt without even telling me! I was afraid you'd all think I was showing off."
"Is that why you kept disappearing?" Cole asked.
William nodded. "I was trying to get them to tell me what else they have planned. But they wouldn't tell me anything."
Henry could tell William was being truthful. "Don't worry. We didn't think you were showing off."
"Yeah. The treasure hunt is fantastic." Cole clapped William on the shoulder. "Anyway, we like you no matter what."
Henry nodded. "We don't care how much money your parents spend," he added. "We came because you're our friend."
William looked relieved. "Thanks. In that case I'll be in a better mood from now on," he promised.
"Good." Henry smiled. Then he realized something. "This means we still don't know who took those tickets."
"Is Roger Redbeard still a suspect?" William asked. "Because when I was leaving my house just now, I saw him lurking around outside!"
"Roger Redbeard was hanging around outside your house?" Henry asked William. "Why?"
"I don't know. I only saw him for a second." William looked around. "Hey, where's everybody else?"
"I think they're over there." Cole pointed.
William took a few steps and then paused. "Aren't you guys coming?"
"We'll be there in a minute," Henry said.
After William left, Cole shrugged. "That's weird," he said. "Why is Roger hanging around William's house? Is he looking for more booty?"
"Maybe." Henry glanced at the general store. "Come on, let's go inside and ask if Roger was really here earlier. Maybe he found that cup on the beach and used it for his alibi."
Henry and Cole hurried into the general store. A woman was behind the cash register. She had a friendly smile and hair the same color as Anna's.
"Hello, boys," she greeted them. "I haven't seen you around here before. Are you William's new friends from Belltown?"
Henry guessed that the woman was Anna's mother. He also guessed that Anna had told her about their visit. "Yes, we are," he told her.
"Welcome to Sea Cove," Anna's mother said. "I hope you're enjoying the treasure hunt."
"It's great," Cole said.
"We were wondering something," Henry added. "Did a man named Roger Redbeard come in here a little while ago?"
"Roger?" Anna's mom smiled. "Why yes. He did come in earlier today."
Just then another customer came toward the register. Henry and Cole stepped away to talk.
"I guess Roger does have a good alibi after all," Cole said. "If he was here earlier, he couldn't have taken those tickets."
"Yeah." Henry bit his lip. If Roger hadn't done it, that meant one of their friends was the thief. "Let's go."
"Hold on." Cole stepped toward a shelf. "Seeing that gum earlier made me want some. I think I'll buy some now." He grabbed a pack of cherry gum from the shelf.
Henry and Cole waited for the other customer to finish. Then they stepped up to the counter again. Cole set down his pack of cherry gum.
"Do you need anything else, boys?" Anna's mom asked as she rang up the sale.
Cole handed over a dollar. "No, thanks."

Henry was staring at the gum, still thinking about what William had just told them about seeing Roger again. Something didn't seem quite right about Roger's story. Why did they keep seeing him everywhere?
"Excuse me," Henry said to Anna's mom. "Is Anna's sister around?"
If Roger had really seen Anna's sister on the beach, maybe she'd seen him too. Or maybe she'd seen something else suspicious while she was out jogging.
Anna's mom looked surprised. "Do you mean Josie?" she said. "She's not here right now. She's spending the whole weekend with friends out of town."
"Really?" Henry said. "Is that Anna's only sister?"
Anna's mom laughed. "Yes. And trust me, two kids in one family is plenty!" she said with a wink.
"Okay, thanks." Henry wandered toward the door along with Cole, still thinking hard. Had Roger lied about seeing "the Jones girl" on the beach? Or was something else going on?
He kept thinking as he and Cole left the general store. "We'd better find the others," Cole said.

"Uh-huh." Henry didn't say anything else. He just kept thinking as he followed Cole across the street. He thought about everything that had happened so far, and everything everyone had said all day. Someone was lying. And Henry was starting to figure out who it might be . . .
Cole and Henry found the others standing at the edge of a small but pretty park.
"We've been looking all over for you!" Maggie cried when she spotted them.
"Yeah," Luke added. "We think we know where the next booty is hidden."
Maggie nodded and pointed. "We're pretty sure it's in the old bandstand over there."
"What are we waiting for?" Cole exclaimed. "Let's go!"
"Wait," Henry spoke up before they could rush off. "First I need to ask Luke something. Remember when you and Nathan found the treasure in the tide pool and were waiting for the rest of us?"
"Yeah," Luke said. "So?"
"So exactly when did William get there?" Henry asked.
William frowned. "I just told you guys I didn't take those tickets!" he cried. "I thought you believed me!"
"Don't worry, I do believe you," Henry assured him. He continued to look at Luke. "Well?"
Luke shrugged. "Actually, William was already there when Nathan and I found the tide pool."
Nathan nodded. "Yeah."
"Do you have a theory, Henry?" Maggie demanded. " Did William steal those tickets? Or was it Nathan and Luke?"
"No, it wasn't any of them," Henry replied. "It was Anna."
"What?" Anna cried as everyone else gasped.
"Why do you think Anna stole the tickets, Henry?" Nathan asked.

"She's the only one with the motive and the opportunity," Henry said. "She's been saving to buy a game player, so we know she needed money. When she got to that tide pool first, she decided to go grab the booty for herself."
William turned to Anna. "Is that true?"
Anna's shoulders slumped. "I didn't mean to do it! It was an accident."
Maggie scowled. "How can you steal something by accident?"
"Yeah!" chimed in Luke.
Anna sighed. "I was about to check one tide pool when I realized that another one is shaped like a teardrop. Just like the clue!" Anna went on. "So I got excited and ran to that one."
"That must be when Roger saw you running on the beach," Cole said.
"When I got to the tide pool, nobody else was there yet," Anna went on. "I spotted the box in the water and grabbed it. I thought the envelope had money inside."
"So you decided to steal it?" Maggie demanded.

"I was thinking about taking some of it," Anna admitted. "Enough to buy myself a game player. I had gum in my pocket," she went on. "So I dropped that in the box. I thought the gum might make up for taking some of the money." Tears filled her eyes. "I know it was wrong—really wrong."
Luke was staring at her in disbelief. "I can't believe you stole our stuff!"

Anna bit her lip. "Once I realized that the envelope didn't have money, I wanted to put it back in the box. But I heard someone coming. I panicked and stuck the envelope in my pocket. Then I tossed the box back in the water and sneaked away before anyone saw me."
Nathan frowned at Anna. "How could you do something like that?"

"I'm sorry." Tears rolled down Anna's cheeks. She pulled an envelope out of her pocket and gave it to Henry. "I never meant to ruin anyone's fun. I just wasn't thinking, and now I feel terrible. I don't even want a video game player anymore!"
Henry couldn't help feeling a little sorry for Anna.
"I made a terrible mistake," she went on. "And I owe your parents a big apology too, William."
He nodded coolly. "You sure do, Anna."
Looking miserable, Anna headed back to the beach house to apologize to William's parents.
"Come on, you guys," Maggie said to the others. "We have one more treasure to find!"
They all ran to the bandstand. A cooler with a skull and crossbones sat there. Henry read the note that was taped to it.
"We're supposed to carry the cooler back to William's beach house," he informed his friends. "It will get filled up with something there."
As they hurried back to William's house, The Lemonade Detectives talked about the case. "How did you figure out that Anna was the thief?" Maggie asked Henry.
Henry shrugged. "It was the only answer that fit all the clues."
"A few things still don't make sense though," Cole said. "Why was Nathan acting weird all day?"
They looked at Nathan. " Ah-choo! " Nathan sneezed.
Henry smiled. "Another case closed," he said. "Nathan caught his sister's cold and isn't feeling well. That's why he's grumpy today!"
"Okay," Maggie said. "But I have another question. Why was Roger hanging around us all day?"
They'd just come within view of the beach house. Henry pointed. "I think we just solved that mystery too."
There was a party set up on the deck with pirate decorations!
Roger stood there, dressed in a pirate costume. "Ahoy, mateys!" he called, waving. "Come and enjoy your final booty—it's a pirate party!"
They brought the cooler over, and Roger immediately filled it with ice and soda for them. Henry could see Anna standing off to the side, talking with William's parents in low tones.
Henry and Maggie were watching her. "Do you think Anna and William can still be friends?" asked Maggie softly.
"I'm not sure," Henry replied. "Anna seems pretty sorry about what she did, but friends don't steal from friends."
"And cousins don't steal from cousins," Maggie added, banging her cup gently against Henry's.
"Your parents must have set up this party while we were in town," Cole said to William.
William grinned as he looked around the deck. "It's pretty cool, actually."
"That's why Roger went to the general store earlier," Henry chimed in. "Anna's parents also do catering, remember? Roger must have been picking up the food."
Maggie laughed. "It's a good thing we solved all the mysteries," she said. "Otherwise—"
Just then Roger Redbeard popped up from behind Maggie. "I would have made you walk the plank!" he finished. " Aargh! "
"Whew! It sure is hot today," Henry's friend Cole said.
"That's why we're getting ice cream, remember?" Henry pointed to a shop just ahead. It was called the Sweet Shop. A board on the sidewalk outside listed the store's special flavors.

"Today's special flavors are raspberry mint chip and bubble gum banana swirl," Cole read aloud. "Maybe I'll try bubble gum banana swirl. No . . . Wait, I think I'll get marshmallow fudge. That's my favorite."
A bell over the door jingled when Henry and Cole entered the ice-cream shop. Several people were waiting in line. The woman behind the counter looked up when she heard the bell.
"Hello, boys," she said. "I'll be with you shortly."
"Thanks, Mrs. Sweet," Henry said.

Everyone in Belltown liked Mrs. Sweet and her homemade ice cream. She had owned the Sweet Shop since Henry's parents were babies. The shop never changed much, but the flavors did. Mrs. Sweet was always inventing new ones.
Henry and Cole waited until it was their turn to be served. "I'll try one scoop of raspberry mint chip in a cone, please," Henry said.
"Marshmallow fudge for me," Cole said.
"Coming right up, boys." Mrs. Sweet picked up two cones and leaned into the cooler to get the ice cream.
Henry looked around. "This place is busy today."
"It sure is. Hot weather always makes people want a nice cool treat!" Mrs. Sweet winked. "But you must know that already. How's business at your lemonade stand?"
"Great," Henry said. "That reminds me, we promised to bring back some ice cream for Maggie."
Cole nodded. "She wants a scoop of cherry vanilla in a cup."
Soon Henry and Cole were back outside with their ice cream. "We'd better hurry," Henry said. "We promised Maggie we'd be back soon to help with the customers."
"Yeah." Cole licked his ice cream, which was already starting to melt in the heat. "Besides," he added, "Maggie will be mad if her ice cream melts before we get back."
Half a dozen people were clustered around the lemonade stand when Henry and Cole reached it. Maggie saw the two boys coming.
"Hurry up, you two!" she called. "I can't do everything by myself!"
"Sorry. We tried to hurry." Henry ate the last bite of his ice-cream cone.
Then he handed Maggie her ice cream and grabbed a pitcher of lemonade. "Who's next?" he called to the customers.
"I am," a familiar voice said.
"Dad!" Henry looked up and saw his father grinning at him. "What are you doing here?"
"Are you writing a story about our lemonade stand, Uncle Kevin?" Maggie joked.
Henry's father chuckled. He was a reporter for the local newspaper.
"Nope," he said. "I'm just here for lemonade."
As Henry handed his father a cup, an older man arrived. "Well, hello, Kevin," he greeted Henry's father.
"Mr. Moss!" Henry's dad smiled. "I've been meaning to call you. You did a great job fixing our garage door last weekend."

"One lemonade, please," Mr. Moss said to Henry, handing him a quarter. Then he turned back to Henry's father. "I'm glad you're pleased with the repair job," he said. "Speaking of garages, did you hear about Mr. O'Malley's new car?"
The two men wandered away with their lemonade, still chatting.
"Mr. Moss fixed your garage door?" Cole asked Henry. "I thought he was an art teacher."

"He retired last year," Maggie told him. "Now he does odd jobs around town. My parents hired him to paint our garden shed, and they said he did a great job." She grinned. "Except he likes to chatter while he works about things going on around town."
"Mr. Moss loves to gossip," Henry agreed.
Cole looked around. "Whew!" he said. "That's the last of our customers for right now."
"Yeah," Maggie said. "The lemonade stand has been really busy all day." She glared at the boys. " Especially while you two were gone."
Henry grinned. "Having more customers means we make more money."
"That's true." Maggie looked happier. "I need all the money I can get. I'm still saving up to enter the horse show at my barn. And we're not making much from our detective business these days."
"True." Henry nodded. "We haven't had a new case in a few days."
Cole helped himself to some lemonade. "You're right. Maybe we've solved all the mysteries in Belltown!"
"Maybe," Henry said.
Maggie looked worried. "I hope not. Entering that horse show is expensive."
"Here comes another customer." Cole pointed down the street.
"Who is it?" When Henry turned to look, he saw a young man he didn't recognize. A moment later the man reached them. But he didn't even glance at the lemonade.
"Are you the kid detectives I've heard about?" he demanded. "Because I need someone to help me prove something—my ice-cream flavor was stolen!"
Henry stared at the stranger in surprise. "Yes, we're The Lemonade Detectives," he told him. "What do you mean, your ice-cream flavor was stolen?"
"I mean someone stole it!" the man exclaimed with a scowl. Then he sighed. "Sorry, I didn't mean to snap at you," he said in a calmer voice. "I'm just upset."
"Maybe we can help," Maggie said. "Tell us more about the case."
"My name is Mr. Tate. I'm getting ready to open a new business called the Dessert Den."
"The Dessert Den?" Cole licked his lips. "Sounds delicious!"
Henry thought the name of Mr. Tate's business sounded familiar. Then he remembered why. "The Dessert Den is in West Belltown, right?" he asked.
Mr. Tate nodded. "That's right."
"How did you know that?" Maggie asked Henry.

"My dad has been writing a series of stories about that part of town," Henry said. "There was a bad fire there a long time ago, and the neighborhood got run down. Now the town council wants to fix up the area and help new businesses open up."
"I know where you mean," Cole said. "A lot of West Belltown is just empty lots now. Some guys from my soccer team live there."

Henry nodded. "Dad says the people who live in West Belltown have been using the empty lots for all sorts of things. They hold neighborhood barbecues there and play soccer and kickball, stuff like that."
Mr. Tate cleared his throat loudly, looking impatient. "You kids are younger than I expected. Are you really detectives?"
"Yes," Maggie said. "We've solved lots of mysteries. If anyone in Belltown can solve your case, it's The Lemonade Detectives!"
"Okay." Mr. Tate still looked uncertain. "But I need this problem solved quickly. The Dessert Den's grand opening is this Friday."
"Friday?" Cole cried. "That's tomorrow!"
"But don't worry, we can do it," Maggie said quickly. "We've never failed to solve a case."
There was a sudden shout from nearby. Henry saw a group of kids rushing toward them. Several of the kids were carrying baseball gloves or bats. All of them looked sweaty and tired.
"Here come some customers," he told his friends. "They look thirsty."
"Excuse us," Maggie told Mr. Tate. "As soon as we take care of these lemonade customers, we can talk more about your case."

Mr. Tate checked his watch. "I'm meeting a plumber at the Dessert Den in a little while. There's a lot of last-minute work to do before the grand opening. Why don't you come over to the shop when you're finished here?"
He hurried away before The Lemonade Detectives could answer. By then the baseball players had reached the lemonade stand. One of them was Henry's friend Nathan.
"One lemonade, please," Nathan said.
Henry and his friends poured lemonade for all the kids. Most of them left after they got their lemonade, but Nathan sat down on the grass to drink his.
"We'd better get over to the Dessert Den," Cole told Henry and Maggie. "Mr. Tate needs us to solve this case fast."
"We can't all go," Maggie said. "Somebody has to stay here to sell lemonade."
"Okay," Cole said. "You stay here, and Henry and I will go talk to Mr. Tate."
"No way!" Maggie complained. "I stayed while you two went to get ice cream, remember? It's somebody else's turn."
She looked stubborn. So did Cole. Henry thought fast.
"Hey, Nathan," he said. "Want to sell lemonade for us? You can keep half of our profits."
"Sure!" Nathan said.
"What?" Maggie squawked.
Henry shrugged. "If you don't like my idea, you can stay instead," he told his cousin.
Maggie scowled. But finally she agreed to the plan.
"Let's take our bikes," Cole suggested. "West Belltown is pretty far away. It's too hot to walk there today."
Once they reached West Belltown, they spotted the Dessert Den right away. It was the only finished building on the main avenue. The area around the Dessert Den was mostly covered in grass and weeds.
Some kids were playing kickball in one of the grassy lots. "Look, there's my friend Emma," Maggie said. She waved and stopped her bike.
Emma and the other kids hurried over. Henry knew all of them from school.
"What are you guys doing in West Belltown?" asked a kid named Robby. He was a year older than Henry and Cole.

"The guy who owns the Dessert Den wants to hire us to solve a mystery," Maggie blurted out. Henry shot his cousin a warning look. Detectives had to be careful when they were talking about their cases.
Robby's smile instantly turned into an angry scowl. "Why would you want to help him ? Nobody wants him here! He should go back to wherever he came from and leave West Belltown alone!"
The Lemonade Detectives watched as Robby stomped away without another word.
"What's wrong with him?" Cole asked, still staring after Robby.
Henry was wondering the same thing. Robby's behavior seemed suspicious. "Why is Robby so mad at Mr. Tate?" he asked one of the other kids.
"I don't know," the kid said. "Anyway, I think I hear my mom calling me." He ran off.
Henry looked at another kid. "Why's everybody acting so weird?" he asked him. "Is it because of what Robby said?"
"No. Maybe. I mean, I have to go too." The second kid scooped up the ball and hurried away. Two others left after him, leaving only Emma.
"What's going on?" Maggie asked Emma. "Why did Robby get so angry just now? Does he really want Mr. Tate to leave West Belltown?"
"I guess," Emma said in a soft voice.
"But why?" Cole asked. "I think it would be cool to have a new ice-cream place in my neighborhood!"
Emma shrugged. "I'm not sure. But I should go home too," she said. "I told my dad I'd help him give our dog a bath."
She said good-bye and hurried away.
"That was weird," Cole said when she was gone. "Robby seemed really angry when we mentioned Mr. Tate."
"Yeah. He always seems pretty happy at school," Henry said. "Maybe he should be our first suspect."
"Do you think Robby stole Mr. Tate's ice cream?" Maggie asked. "Why would he do that?"
" All those kids were acting weird just now, not just Robby," Henry said. "Any of them could have done it."
Maggie looked doubtful. "You think one of those kids broke into the Dessert Den and carried off all Mr. Tate's ice cream?"
"Maybe they didn't carry it off." Cole grinned. "Maybe they ate it!"
"Mr. Tate didn't say his ice cream was stolen," Henry reminded them. "He said his ice-cream flavor was stolen."
"What does that mean?" Maggie looked confused. "How can someone steal a flavor?"
"I don't know," Henry said. "Let's ask Mr. Tate when we see him. We need to find out exactly what happened."
They walked their bikes the rest of the way to the Dessert Den. As they got closer, Henry saw a plumber leaving the shop.
"Wow," Cole said, peering inside the front door. "This place looks cool!"
Henry nodded. The Dessert Den had big glass windows and a fancy sign out front. Inside, tables and chairs were painted in bright colors, and there were bins filled with candy and other treats.
The front door was locked, but Henry could see Mr. Tate inside. He was sweeping the floor in the dining area. Maggie knocked on the door. Mr. Tate looked up and then came over to unlock the door.
"Hello," he greeted them. He sounded a lot more cheerful than he had earlier. "You're just in time."
"Just in time for what?" Cole asked as he walked inside with the others. "Did you solve the mystery?"

"No, nothing like that." Mr. Tate hurried over to the shiny, tiled counter. Several white boxes were sitting there. "I just got a very special delivery—some of the caramel-swirl brownies I'll be selling. Want a taste?"
"Sure!" Cole said eagerly. "I love brownies!"
"You love every kind of dessert," Maggie reminded him.
Mr. Tate chuckled. "Great! You're my perfect customer."
He opened one of the boxes and handed each of the kids a brownie.
Henry tasted his. "Yum! This is delicious!" he said. Cole and Maggie agreed.
"I'm glad you like it," Mr. Tate said, smiling. "Tell all your friends to come to my grand opening tomorrow, okay?"
"Sure." Cole licked his fingers. "But first, maybe you should tell us more about your mystery."
Mr. Tate's smile faded. He glanced at a menu that was hanging above the counter. Henry could only see part of the menu. The rest was covered with a sheet.
"You said someone stole your new ice-cream flavor," Henry reminded him. "What does that mean?"

"The Dessert Den is going to serve all kinds of desserts," Mr. Tate said. "But one of our specialties is ice cream. So I invented a brand-new, exclusive flavor for my grand opening. It's supposed to be top secret. But somehow, someone found out about it—and stole it!"
"How does someone steal a flavor?" Maggie wondered.
"And who would do something like that, anyway?" Cole added.
"I know exactly who stole it!" Mr. Tate snapped. "I just need you kids to help me prove it!"
Henry felt more confused than ever. "You already know who stole your flavor?" he said. "Who?"
Mr. Tate scowled. "It was Mrs. Sweet, who owns the Sweet Shop!"
"Mrs. Sweet?" Maggie exclaimed. "She'd never steal anything from anybody!"
"Yeah," Cole said. "Mrs. Sweet is great."
Henry nodded. "I know you're new in town," he told Mr. Tate. "But everyone in Belltown knows how nice Mrs. Sweet is. The Sweet Shop has been around since our parents were little."
"Exactly," Mr. Tate said with a frown. "Mrs. Sweet doesn't want any competition from the Dessert Den!"
"What makes you think Mrs. Sweet stole your flavor?" Cole asked.
"That's a good question." Henry turned to Mr. Tate. "You haven't told us exactly what happened."
"Oh right," Mr. Tate said. "Like I said, I invented a unique flavor of ice cream for the grand opening. I haven't told a soul in Belltown about it. It was top secret!"
"Then what happened?" Maggie asked. "Did someone break in here and steal the ice cream out of your freezer?"

"No, nothing like that," Mr. Tate said. "In fact, my ice-cream order isn't scheduled to arrive until this afternoon. But just this morning, I saw my flavor listed on the chalkboard outside the Sweet Shop!"
The Lemonade Detectives exchanged looks. "Really? That's weird," Cole said.
"It doesn't prove anything, though," Maggie said.
"Mrs. Sweet makes up new flavors all the time. Maybe she came up with the same idea on her own."
Mr. Tate shook his head. "I doubt it. How likely is it that she just happened to make up a flavor like bubble gum banana swirl?"
"Bubble gum banana swirl?" Henry echoed. He and Cole had seen that flavor on the Sweet Shop sign themselves. It was one of today's special flavors!
"Right. That's my flavor. See?" Mr. Tate strode over to the menu sign and pulled back the sheet. The sign said Dessert Den Grand Opening Exclusive: Bubble gum Banana Swirl Ice Cream!
"How do you think Mrs. Sweet heard about your flavor?" Henry asked.
Mr. Tate shrugged. "I assume someone at the factory told her."
"What factory?" Cole asked.
"The place where I'm having all my ice cream made," Mr. Tate explained. "I tell the owners what flavors I want, and they make it for me."
"Mrs. Sweet doesn't use a factory," Maggie said. "She makes all her own flavors in the back of her shop."
"She does?" Mr. Tate looked surprised.
"Yes," Henry said. "So she couldn't have heard about it from the factory."
Mr. Tate tugged on the sheet to cover his sign again. "Okay, I just thought of another way it could have happened," he said.
"I've been keeping my menu covered up. But a few days ago the painter forgot to cover it before leaving for the night. Somebody could have looked in the window and seen it then."
"You mean you think Mrs. Sweet sneaked over here at night and peeked in at your flavors?" Cole said. "That doesn't sound like something she would do."

Henry agreed with that. But as he looked around the Dessert Den, he had a moment of doubt. Mr. Tate's new shop really looked great. It had a brand-new ice-cream counter, the cool hand-painted sign, and a shiny silver soda fountain. It was a lot fancier than the old-fashioned Sweet Shop. Could Mrs. Sweet really be worried about the competition? Maybe even worried enough to sabotage the Dessert Den?
"No," Henry said out loud. "I can't believe Mrs. Sweet would steal your flavor idea. There must be another explanation."
"Oh yeah?" Mr. Tate frowned. "I thought you kids were supposed to be detectives. The evidence is right there on my menu—and on her flavor board!"
"Mrs. Sweet has the same flavor as you," Maggie said. "But that doesn't mean she's a thief."
Henry nodded. "Maggie is right," he said. "It's just circumstantial evidence."
"What kind of evidence?" Cole looked confused.
"Circumstantial," Henry said. "It's evidence that implies something, but doesn't actually prove it."
"Okay," Mr. Tate said. "So how do you explain what happened then?"
"I'm not sure yet," Henry said. "We need to investigate and figure it out. We'll get back to you later."
When the Lemonade Detectives got outside, they stopped by their bikes to talk. "You don't really think Mrs. Sweet is a thief, do you?" Maggie asked Henry.
"Of course not," Henry said. "But it's really odd that they both ended up with that same flavor."
Cole nodded. "Yeah. And it's not a common flavor like mint chocolate chip or fudge ripple," he said. "There's no way Mrs. Sweet and Mr. Tate both invented bubble gum banana swirl in the same week!"
"I agree," said Henry. "We need to start our investigation."
"How do we do that?" Maggie asked.
Henry bit his lip, thinking. "I guess we need to go question Mrs. Sweet. Even if it's just to rule her out as a suspect."
The Lemonade Detectives rode their bikes to the Sweet Shop as fast as they could.
"I still don't believe Mrs. Sweet would do anything wrong," Maggie said as she leaned her bike against a lamppost in front of the shop.
"I don't either," Henry said. "But a good detective has to investigate every lead and suspect."
The bell jingled as they walked in. There were a few customers sitting at the tables inside, but there was no one in line.
A young woman stood behind the counter, wiping it with a rag. Her name was Patty. Henry knew that she worked at the ice-cream parlor part-time to help pay for her college tuition.
"Hi, Patty," he greeted her. "Is Mrs. Sweet here?"
"Hi, Henry," Patty said. "Sorry, she's not here right now. She just stepped out to go to the bank."
"Oh." Cole sounded disappointed. "We need to talk to her about something."
"She'll be back in a few minutes," Patty said. "Want some ice cream while you wait?"
That gave Henry an idea. Maybe he could start investigating even before Mrs. Sweet returned.
"I tried one of the new flavors earlier—raspberry mint chip," he said. "It was really good. Do you know how Mrs. Sweet came up with the idea for that one?"
Maggie shot him a strange look. Henry could almost read her mind. She was thinking, "Why do you care about that flavor?"

Patty chuckled. "You know Mrs. Sweet; she always has a story about how she invents her flavors. She told me she was picking raspberries in her garden when she brushed against a pot of mint plants. The mint and the berries smelled delicious together. So she decided to experiment."
"Cool," Henry said. "What about the other new flavor? Do you know how she got the idea for that one?"

"You mean the bubble gum banana swirl?" Patty asked. When Henry nodded, she shrugged. "I'm not sure. When I asked Mrs. Sweet about that one, she just said that 'a little bird' had given her the idea."
Henry traded a worried look with his friends. That sounded kind of suspicious!
"It doesn't matter where she got the idea, though, because it turned out great," Patty went on. "Would you like a sample?"
"Sure!" Cole said eagerly. "Thanks."
Patty grabbed three small plastic spoons. Then she scooped out a mouthful of the bubble gum-banana-swirl ice cream for each of the kids.
"Yum!" Cole said when he tasted it. "This is awesome!"
"It sure is," Henry agreed. Now he could understand why Mr. Tate was so upset—the flavor tasted great!
Just then some teenage girls came in. Patty went to wait on them, and Henry and his friends wandered away to talk.
"What do you think?" Cole asked quietly.
"I don't know," Henry said. "It's weird that Mrs. Sweet told Patty that a little bird gave her the idea for bubble gum banana swirl."
Maggie frowned. "I still can't believe Mrs. Sweet would steal anything. We need to talk to her and find out her side of the story!"
Henry nodded. "I hope she gets back soon."

A few minutes later Mrs. Sweet finally returned. "Well, hello again, boys!" she greeted them. "Hi, Maggie! But what are you all doing here? Shouldn't someone be working at the lemonade stand? I hear your business is booming!"
"It is," Maggie told her. "Our friend Nathan is watching the stand right now."
"Yes," Henry said. "We were just over in West Belltown. There's a new business opening there this weekend. It's called the Dessert Den."
Mrs. Sweet was still smiling. "Oh my, yes, I've heard about the Dessert Den," she said. "I suppose that means I'll have some competition now for Belltown's dessert eaters!" She chuckled.
The kids exchanged looks.
"Don't worry, I'll always like the Sweet Shop best," Maggie said quickly.
"Um, actually there's a reason we were at the Dessert Den," Henry spoke up. "We're investigating a mystery."
"Oh? What sort of mystery?" Mrs. Sweet was bustling around, straightening the napkin dispensers on the tables.
"Well," said Cole. "The owner of the Dessert Den thinks someone stole the idea for his new ice-cream flavor. It was supposed to be a big secret. It's called bubble gum banana swirl."
"What?" Mrs. Sweet stopped what she was doing and spun to stare at Cole. "Bubble gum banana swirl? Are you sure?"
"Yes. Mr. Tate thinks you, um, stole his flavor," Henry blurted out. "We told him there had to be some kind of mistake, but—"
"Excuse me, kids." Mrs. Sweet wasn't smiling anymore. "I have something important to do."
"But Mrs. Sweet . . ." Maggie began.
It was too late. Mrs. Sweet was already rushing away. A second later she disappeared into the back room of the shop.
Henry and his friends waited for a while. But Mrs. Sweet didn't come out from the back room of the Sweet Shop. Finally they gave up and left.
"We should go see how Nathan is doing at the lemonade stand," Henry said. "We've been gone for a long time."
The others agreed. Back at the stand, Nathan was serving lemonade to some construction workers.
"Hi, guys," Nathan greeted his friends as the men left. "Business has been great today! How's the mystery going?"
"Not so great," Henry admitted. He and his friends told Nathan about the case.
"Wow," Nathan said. "That's weird that Mrs. Sweet rushed off like that."
"Yeah," Cole agreed. "She acted like she was guilty."
"But she's not guilty," Maggie insisted. "She's way too nice to be a flavor thief! We have to prove she didn't do it!"
"That means we have to prove that someone else did do it," Cole said. "Like Robby, for instance. He seemed really mad at Mr. Tate."
"Yeah!" Maggie said. "Maybe he hates Mr. Tate so much that he tricked Mrs. Sweet into inventing that flavor!"
"How would he do that?" Nathan asked.
"I don't know." Maggie shrugged. "But I know Mrs. Sweet didn't do anything wrong."

Henry sighed. "I like Mrs. Sweet too, Maggie. But we have to be logical. Mrs. Sweet has a good motive to cause trouble for the Dessert Den. And don't forget, she has the exact same flavor right there on her sign. Plus, she acted weird when we asked her about it just now."
"All that stuff is true," Cole said. "If Mrs. Sweet was mean, I'd definitely think she was the thief. But how could someone who seems so nice do something so rotten?"
Henry shrugged. He didn't have an answer for Cole's question.
"Maybe you guys should go talk to Mr. Tate again," Nathan suggested. "That might give you some new ideas about the case. I'll keep watching the lemonade stand if you want. I can use the extra money."
Maggie groaned. "It's so hot out. Do we really have to ride all the way back to West Belltown?"
"If you want to clear Mrs. Sweet's name, we do," Cole said. "Come on, let's go."
When The Lemonade Detectives reached the Dessert Den, Mr. Tate saw them coming and hurried to unlock the door.
"Did you solve the case?" he asked. "Did Mrs. Sweet admit that she stole my flavor?"
"Not exactly," Henry said. "We didn't get to talk to her for very long."
Mr. Tate frowned. "Well, once you kids finally get her to admit she's guilty, I'll pay your five-dollar detective fee."
"We still don't believe she did it!" Maggie blurted out. She glanced at Henry and Cole with a frown. "At least I don't."
"Huh?" Mr. Tate looked confused.
"We have a few theories," Henry explained calmly. "We need to rule out other suspects before we can be sure Mrs. Sweet is the culprit."
"Other suspects?" Mr. Tate folded his arms across his chest. "Like who?"
"Um, there's this kid, Robby," Cole said. "He seems to hate the Dessert Den. We're not sure why."
"Yeah," Maggie put in. "Or it could all be a coincidence. The flavor bubble gum banana swirl isn't that unique, you know."

Mr. Tate rolled his eyes. "Look, my grand opening is tomorrow. I don't have time to fool around. Do you want to solve this case or not?" he asked. "If you don't, I can find someone else to help me. Like the police, for instance. Or maybe I'll go to the press. I heard there's an award-winning investigative reporter in this town. Maybe he can figure out what's going on."

Henry realized Mr. Tate was talking about his father. "The Lemonade Detectives will solve your case," he said. "No matter what." He gave Cole and Maggie a shove toward the door. "Come on, guys. Let's get back to work."
Soon they were outside again. "What was that all about, Henry?" Maggie asked. "Why'd you rush us out of there? I thought we were going to ask Mr. Tate more questions about the case."
"We can't let him go to the police," Henry said. "Or ask my dad to investigate either."
"Why not?" Cole asked. "Maybe your dad can help us prove that Mrs. Sweet is innocent."
"Maybe," Henry said. "But if people hear he's investigating her, they might assume she's guilty. And that would probably be bad for her business."
Suddenly Maggie gasped. "That's it!" she cried. "I have a new theory about what's going on! If we can prove it, it'll clear Mrs. Sweet's name!"
"Really? What's your theory?" Cole asked.
"We've been taking Mr. Tate's word about what happened," Maggie said. "But what if he's lying? What if he's the one who stole that flavor?"
"What are you talking about, Maggie?" Cole asked. "Why would Mr. Tate steal his own flavor?"
"I see what Maggie's saying," Henry said. "What if bubble gum banana swirl isn't really Mr. Tate's invention? What if Mrs. Sweet came up with it first?"

"Mr. Tate could be trying to frame Mrs. Sweet by saying she stole it from him," Maggie said. "He claims she doesn't want competition from the Dessert Den. But maybe he's the one who's trying to steal customers!"
Cole shrugged. "I guess that's a pretty good motive. But we just talked to Mrs. Sweet. Wouldn't she have told us that bubble gum banana swirl is her flavor?"
"She's really nice," Maggie reminded them. "Maybe she didn't want to get Mr. Tate in trouble. Even if he is a dirty flavor thief!"

"I guess we should check out your idea, Maggie," Henry said. "Like I said, good detectives follow up on every lead and theory." Then he thought of another question. "But if Mrs. Sweet invented bubble gum banana swirl, why didn't she tell Patty how she came up with the flavor?"
"Good question," Cole said. "Usually she has a story to go along with all her flavors. Like raspberry mint chip, for instance."
Maggie grabbed her bike. "Just because Patty didn't know the story doesn't mean there isn't one," she said. "Let's go back to the Sweet Shop and ask Mrs. Sweet!" She raced off down the sidewalk.
Henry and Cole followed. As they rounded the corner, Henry saw Robby and some other kids sitting on the grass, drinking sodas.
"Wait!" he called to his friends. He wanted to stop and ask Robby why he was so mad at Mr. Tate. Plus, maybe one of the West Belltown kids had seen Mr. Tate do something suspicious.
But Maggie and Cole were too far ahead to hear him. Henry shrugged and kept going. He waved at Robby as he passed him. But Robby just stared back at him.
When they neared the Sweet Shop, Henry saw Mr. Moss standing outside. He was painting the shop's window frame.
"Hello, kids," Mr. Moss said cheerfully. "Are you here to get some ice cream?"
"Actually, we came to talk to Mrs. Sweet," Maggie said.

"I haven't seen her yet. I just got here a few minutes ago myself," Mr. Moss said. "I wanted to surprise her by getting started on this painting she asked me to do." He held up his paintbrush and smiled. "She might be inside."
The kids left their bikes leaning against the lamppost and entered the Sweet Shop. Patty was still behind the counter.
"Hi. Is Mrs. Sweet around?" Henry asked her.
"Sorry, no. She left half an hour ago to run an errand."
Henry was disappointed. They really needed to talk to Mrs. Sweet!
"We were wondering about something," he said to Patty. "How long has bubble gum banana swirl been on the menu?"
"Hmm, let me think." Patty tapped her chin. "I remember serving it on Monday afternoon. Mrs. Sweet must have added it that morning."
"Monday?" Henry traded a look with his friends.
"Do you kids want to order anything?" Patty glanced outside. "If so, you should probably do it now. It looks like a whole crowd of customers just arrived."
Henry looked out the front window. A van had just stopped by the curb outside. A bunch of little kids were jumping out of it.
"No, thanks," he told Patty.
The little kids rushed in, along with a couple of adults. As they clustered around the counter, Henry and his friends moved over to a private corner.
"Now we know how long Mrs. Sweet has had that flavor," Cole said.

"But we don't know when Mr. Tate invented it," Henry said. "We need to find out when he painted his sign. If it was after Monday morning, he's probably guilty. But if it was before Monday, then he's innocent."
"He's guilty." Maggie sounded confident. "Let's go ask him."
"Do you think he'll tell us the truth?" Cole wondered as they headed toward the door. They had to stop a few times to dodge excited little kids.
Maggie shrugged. "Why wouldn't he tell us the truth? He thinks we're on his side, remember?"
Outside the Sweet Shop, nobody was around. Even Mr. Moss had disappeared.
Cole looked around in confusion. "Hey," he said. "Where are our bikes?"
Just then Mr. Moss hurried into view from the alley between the Sweet Shop and the building next door. He was holding a new can of paint.
"Hello again, kids," he said. "Did you find Mrs. Sweet?"
"No," said Maggie. "And now someone stole our bikes!"
"Wait!" Cole called. "I see them! Look—over there!"
Henry looked where Cole was pointing and gasped. Their bikes were lying in a jumbled pile behind the van!
"Oh no!" Maggie cried. "Did that van run over our bikes?"
"I don't think so." Cole hurried over to the bikes. "Here's yours, Maggie," he said, picking it up. "It looks okay."
Henry picked up another bike. "I think they're okay. It looks like someone just threw them into the street behind the van."
"Oh my!" Mr. Moss looked alarmed. "Are you sure it wasn't an accident? I can't imagine anyone in Belltown wanting to harm your bikes."
Before becoming a detective, Henry couldn't have imagined it either. Now he wasn't so sure.
"Did you see anything suspicious while we were inside?" he asked Mr. Moss.
"I'm afraid not," Mr. Moss replied. "Shortly after you went in, I ran out of paint. I walked over to Belltown Hardware to buy more."
"Maybe those little kids knocked the bikes over on their way into the Sweet Shop," Cole suggested. "They seemed awfully excited."
"They might have knocked them down by accident, I guess," Maggie said. "But how did our bikes end up in the street behind the van?" she asked.
"Never mind." Henry got on his bike and rode in a circle, testing the steering and brakes. Everything seemed to be working. "We should get going," he told Cole and Maggie.
They said good-bye to Mr. Moss and rode toward West Belltown. "Do you think someone messed with our bikes on purpose?" Cole asked.
"Maybe," Henry said. "Someone might be trying to send us a message to stop our investigation."
Cole looked skeptical. "That doesn't make sense. Who would want to stop us? Besides, nobody even knew we were at the Sweet Shop just now!"

"Mr. Tate did," Maggie pointed out. "Maybe he figured out we were getting suspicious of him and he's trying to frame Mrs. Sweet again! He could have followed us to town and messed with our bikes while we were in the Sweet Shop. Patty was too busy with those kids to look outside and notice anything. We were in the back of the shop, so we wouldn't have seen Mr. Tate."
"And Mr. Moss was getting paint, so he wouldn't have seen Mr. Tate either." Cole looked skeptical. "Do you really think Mr. Tate did it?"
"I guess it's possible— if he's the one who stole the flavor," Henry said. "We need to find out."
When they reached the Dessert Den, an electrician's truck was parked outside. The electrician was inside with Mr. Tate.

"Hi, kids," Mr. Tate said when Cole knocked on the door. He glanced at the electrician who was working on an overhead light. "I can't talk right now," he told the kids. "I have to make sure the lights are ready in time for my grand opening. Can you come back later?"
"Sure, I guess," Cole said.
"Now what?" Maggie said as the door shut behind them.
They could see some neighborhood kids running around in a lot a short distance away. "Let's go see if Robby is over there," Cole suggested. "He's one of our suspects, remember?"
"Where's Robby?" Henry asked the other kids.
Emma shrugged. "He took off on his bike a while ago. I don't know where he went."
"Have you guys seen the menu inside the Dessert Den?" Maggie blurted out. "When did Mr. Tate get it?"
A kid shrugged. "I peeked in there once, but I didn't notice a sign."
"When did you peek in?" Maggie asked. "Was it before or after Monday morning?"
The kid looked surprised. "I don't remember. Why?"
"No reason," Cole said. "But have any of you noticed Mr. Tate doing anything weird during the past few days?"
"Wait," someone said. "I thought you guys were working for Mr. Tate. Now it sounds like you're investigating him!"
Emma's face lit up. "If you're trying to prove Mr. Tate did something wrong, I bet my parents would help you! Robby's too."
"They would? Why?" Henry asked.
"Our parents were upset when they found out about the Dessert Den," Emma said. "They were getting ready to ask the town council if they could start a community garden in some of the empty lots."
"Really?" Cole said, shooting a look at Henry.
Henry's head was already spinning with thoughts. Could Emma's news be a clue? It sounded as if some people in the neighborhood had a motive for harming Mr. Tate's business.
Still, Henry couldn't imagine a bunch of adults stealing an ice-cream flavor. Especially if they knew it would get nice Mrs. Sweet in trouble.
"Have any of you seen Mrs. Sweet hanging around here lately?" he asked.
Most of the kids shook their heads. But a girl named Hannah smirked.
"Are you kidding?" she said. "Mrs. Sweet doesn't have time to hang around West Belltown these days. She's too busy going out on dates with Mr. Moss!"
The Lemonade Detectives looked at Hannah in surprise. "Mrs. Sweet is dating Mr. Moss?" Maggie said.
Hannah giggled. "My mom works at a fancy restaurant on Baker Street. She says Mr. Moss and Mrs. Sweet have been there a lot recently."
Henry was surprised by Hannah's news. Was it a clue?
By now it was late afternoon. He looked over at the Dessert Den, and saw that the electrician's truck was still there. So they still couldn't talk to Mr. Tate.
"Did you know that Mrs. Sweet and Mr. Moss were dating?" Henry asked his friends as they wandered toward their bikes.
"Nope. Mr. Moss usually spreads around all the town gossip," Cole said with a smile. "I guess he doesn't like to gossip about himself though!"
"Maybe Mr. Moss pushed over our bikes because he knew we were investigating his girlfriend," said Maggie.
"Maybe," Henry said. "But Mr. Moss is just as nice as Mrs. Sweet. I can't believe he'd do something like that and then lie about it to us."
"Me neither." Cole gulped. "Not unless he knows Mrs. Sweet is guilty, that is."
"I have an idea," Henry said. "Let's go talk to my dad."
Maggie groaned. "You want to ride back to town again ?" she said. "Anyway, I thought you didn't want your dad to investigate Mrs. Sweet."
"He's written a few stories about West Belltown," Henry reminded her. "He might know something useful."
They rode to the newspaper office. Henry's dad was in the reception area shuffling through some papers.
"Hello, kids!" he greeted them with a smile. "What brings you here?"
"We're working on a tough case," Henry said. "We were hoping we could talk to you about it."
"Sure." Henry's dad checked his watch. "I have to go to a meeting in a few minutes. But we can talk until then."
He led the way to his office. After he closed the door, Henry and his friends told him all about the mystery.
"Wow," Henry's dad said when they finished. "That's quite a story."
"You can't tell anyone, Uncle Kevin," Maggie said. "We don't want to ruin Mrs. Sweet's reputation."
Henry's dad smiled. "I can keep a secret. But I'm sure the flavor theft is just some kind of misunderstanding."
"I hope so," Henry said. "But how can we prove it? Do you have any information that could help us crack the case?"
"I'm afraid not," his father said. "But it sounds like you still have a few clues to investigate. Like the timing of the two signs, for instance."
"Yeah." Cole bit his lip. "But what if we find out Mr. Tate had the flavor on his sign first? That means Mrs. Sweet is the culprit."
Henry's dad shrugged.
"Being a good detective, or a good reporter, means looking for the truth. You have to dig up all the facts, even if they lead to an answer you don't like."
There was a knock on the door. "Time for the meeting, Kevin," a woman called.
"Thanks." Henry's dad stood. "Sorry, kids. I have to go. We can talk more later if you like."
"Okay. Thanks, Dad."
As Henry and his friends left the building, someone stepped toward them. It was Robby.
"Hi," Cole greeted him. "What are you doing here?"
"Looking for you guys." Robby looked miserable. "I need to apologize."
"What for?" asked Maggie.
"For knocking over your bikes earlier," Robby said.
"That was you?" Cole exclaimed. "Why'd you do it?"

"I knew you were working for Mr. Tate," Robby said. "I'm mad at him because he ruined my parents' plans for a community garden. That's why I followed you to the Sweet Shop and knocked over your bikes." He sighed. "But when I told my dad what I did, he made me promise to find you and apologize. So I'm sorry."
"It's okay," Henry said. "Are your parents mad at Mr. Tate too?"
"I thought they were, but Dad says he's glad our neighborhood is getting some new businesses." Robby shrugged. "Maybe I am too. It might be cool to have a dessert place a few blocks from home."
Robby said good-bye and moved on.
"I guess that solves one mystery," Cole said.
"Yeah. But it doesn't help with identifying the flavor thief," Henry said. "Or with clearing Mrs. Sweet's name."
"I know how to do that," Maggie said. "We need to talk to Mr. Tate about that sign!"
This time it was Cole who groaned. "It's getting late," he said. "Plus, Nathan's still selling lemonade for us. Do we really have to ride to West Belltown again?"
"Yes!" Maggie insisted. "Come on!"
She hopped on her bike and rode down the street. But suddenly she stopped short.
"What is it?" Henry asked as he caught up.
"Look!" Maggie pointed to Mrs. Sweet's flavor board. "Bubble gum banana swirl is gone!"
Henry stared at the flavor board outside the Sweet Shop. "Mrs. Sweet erased bubble gum banana swirl!"
"She probably decided that if Mr. Tate was going to copy her flavor, she didn't want it anymore," said Maggie.
"Or she's trying to hide all traces of her crime!" chimed in Cole.
"Let's go find Mr. Tate," Henry said.
When they reached the Dessert Den, the electrician's truck was gone. The front door was standing open as Mr. Tate hurried back and forth carrying boxes inside.
"Good, you're back," he said to the kids. "Grab a box and come on in. Did you get Mrs. Sweet to confess?"
"We're still working on the case," Henry said. "We have a question. When did you hang up the menu with your secret flavor on it?"
"Right after Mr. Moss finished painting it on Saturday. Why?"
"Mr. Moss painted your sign?" Cole said, surprised.
Mr. Tate nodded. "At first I thought I'd made a mistake hiring him. The old guy never stops talking! But he did a fantastic job on the sign."
"Aha!" Henry smiled. "I think I know what happened."
Maggie didn't seem to hear Henry. "But Mr. Moss is dating Mrs. Sweet!" she blurted out.
"He is?" Mr. Tate frowned. "That proves it! Mrs. Sweet must have heard about my flavor from him. I knew she was guilty!"
"Mrs. Sweet isn't guilty," Henry said.
"I knew it!" Maggie pointed at Mr. Tate. "You found out about Mrs. Sweet's new flavor from Mr. Moss! Then you decided to frame her to drive her out of business!"
"What are you talking about?" Mr. Tate said.
"Wait," Henry said. "Maggie, Mr. Tate isn't guilty either."
"He's not?" Cole said. "Then who is guilty?"
"The guilty person is . . . nobody!" Henry shrugged. "At least, nobody doing anything wrong on purpose."
"I don't get it." Maggie was still glaring at Mr. Tate. But she looked a little less certain.
"Everybody in Belltown knows Mr. Moss likes to gossip," Henry began.
"I only moved here a month ago, and I already know that," Mr. Tate agreed.
"Usually Mr. Moss' gossip is harmless," Henry said. "He just likes to share interesting news. I bet he thought your special flavor was interesting, so he mentioned it to Mrs. Sweet."
"Right," Mr. Tate said. "And she decided to steal it to ruin my grand opening!"
"Not exactly," Henry said. "My guess is that he didn't tell her where he'd seen it."
"I get it now!" Maggie said. "Mrs. Sweet thought the flavor sounded interesting, so she added it to her menu."

Cole nodded. "Without realizing that she was stealing Mr. Tate's flavor!" He frowned. "But wait. If this is just a misunderstanding, why did Mrs. Sweet behave so suspiciously when we talked to her earlier?"
"Because she didn't want to get her boyfriend in trouble," Henry said.
"That's right," a voice said from the door.
"Mrs. Sweet!" Maggie cried. "What are you doing here?"

"I came to apologize to Mr. Tate." Mrs. Sweet stepped toward Mr. Tate. "I'm sorry for accidentally stealing your flavor. It took me a little while to find Mr. Moss and confirm what happened. He's sorry too, of course. He didn't realize that flavor was supposed to be a secret until I told him a few minutes ago. I took the flavor off our menu right away."
"Oh, I see." Mr. Tate looked sheepish. "Thank you for the explanation, Mrs. Sweet. Maybe I owe you an apology too. I was ready to believe the worst about you."
"It's all right." Mrs. Sweet smiled. "By the way, welcome to Belltown. I hope we can be friends."
"How can you say that?" Maggie blurted out in surprise. "The Dessert Den is your competition!"
Mrs. Sweet chuckled. "Perhaps. But everyone loves ice cream. I'm sure there's room for both businesses."
"Of course, we'll be friends," Mr. Tate said. "And I hope you'll stop by my grand opening tomorrow. All of you," he added, looking at the Lemonade Detectives.
"That reminds me—I owe you kids your five-dollar detective fee." He reached into his pocket for the money.
"Here's another five dollars from me." Mrs. Sweet took a bill out of her purse and handed it to Henry. "For clearing my name and for believing in me despite the evidence."
"It was only circumstantial evidence," Maggie said.
Mrs. Sweet laughed. "In any case, you three are welcome to all the free ice cream you can eat for the rest of the summer."
"Good idea," Mr. Tate chimed in. "You kids are welcome to free dessert here for the rest of the summer as well."
"Wow, thanks! That's what I call a sweet reward!" Cole licked his lips.
"Wow!" said Maggie. "Look at how many people are at the horse show. We're going to make tons of money!"
Henry laughed. "Stop counting your future profits and help me hang up our sign."
"Sorry." Maggie held the sign while Henry tacked it to a tree near where they'd set up their lemonade stand.
Once the sign was hung, Henry wiped his brow. "Wow, it's pretty hot today."
"I know." Maggie smiled. "That should make people buy even more lemonade. Riding horses in the heat makes you really thirsty. Trust me, I know!"

Henry nodded. They were at the stable where Maggie took riding lessons. Today the stable was putting on a horse show for its students to show off what they'd been learning all summer. The stable's owner, Ms. Wood, had told Maggie that she and her friends could sell lemonade during the show.
A rider hurried over. "Is the stand open yet?" she asked. "I'll take a lemonade, please."
"Coming right up." Henry poured the girl a cup of lemonade. As he handed it to her, several more riders came over.
For the next few minutes Henry and Maggie stayed busy serving lemonade to customers. "Where's Cole?" Maggie asked as she dropped a quarter into the cashbox. "We could use his help."
"I think he went to look for more napkins," Henry said. "I'm not sure why, though. We already have plenty of them."
A few girls hurried over. One of them was Daisy, who also rode at Maggie's stable.
"One lemonade, please," a girl said. "I hope it's nice and cold!"
"It is," Maggie said as she poured the girl a cup.
The girl drank her lemonade quickly and left.
"Some of these riders would be cooler if they took off their long-sleeved jackets," Henry said.
"Those are show coats," Daisy said. "That's what you're supposed to wear for horse shows."
"Oh. How come you and Maggie aren't wearing them?" Henry asked.

Maggie frowned. "I wish I had a show coat to wear," she said. "But my mom and dad wouldn't buy me one. And I definitely can't afford to buy one myself. I barely had enough money to enter two classes in the show!"
"Don't worry, Maggie," Daisy said. "Ms. Wood said you don't need fancy show clothes, remember? This show is supposed to be for learning and having fun."
Henry looked at Daisy's T-shirt. "Are you wearing that bright pink T-shirt in the show?" he asked.
Daisy shook her head. "I'm just wearing it in case I get dirty while I get my pony ready. My new show clothes are hanging by her stall."
"Oh." Henry shrugged. He didn't know much about horseback riding. "Well, enjoy your lemonade." He handed Daisy a cup.
"Thanks." Daisy took a sip, and then walked off.
A moment later Cole rushed over. His face was sweaty and he was breathing hard.
"Where are the napkins?" Henry asked him.
"Huh?" Cole looked down at his empty hands. "Oh. I couldn't find any." He shrugged and glanced at the table. "Anyway, it looks like we have enough of them."
Maggie frowned. "We've been busy, and you missed all the work," she complained.
"Not all of it." Cole pointed toward some people. "Here come more customers."
Henry and his friends served several thirsty riders and a few parents. Then Maggie checked her watch.
"I need to get ready for my first class in the show," she said. "You guys will be okay without me for a while, right?"
"Sure. Good luck," Henry said.
After she left, a few more customers wandered over. Then several minutes passed without any customers at all.
"Are you sure you don't want to go to your swim practice?" Henry asked Cole. "Maggie and I can probably handle the lemonade stand by ourselves."
"No, that's okay," Cole said. "The coach said today's practice is mainly for the divers on the team." He pulled two bright green lollipops out of his pocket. "Want one?"
"Sure, thanks!" Henry took one of the lollipops. "Aren't these the homemade ones from the Dessert Den?"
"Yeah. I bought them when we went there yesterday," Cole said. "They're kiwi-flavored—my favorite!"
Henry unwrapped his lollipop. It was sticky and partly melted because of the heat. But it still tasted good.
After a moment he noticed that Cole's tongue was turning bright green. "Is my tongue green too?" Henry asked, sticking out his tongue.
Cole grinned. "Yeah. You look like a zombie."
"Too bad you don't have any cherry-flavored lollipops," Henry joked. "Then we could dye our tongues back to red."
Before Cole could answer, Daisy raced up to the lemonade stand. Maggie was right behind her.
"I need The Lemonade Detectives!" Daisy blurted out. "Someone stole my brand-new show shirt!"
"What's a show shirt?" Cole asked.

"It's a special kind of shirt that you wear under your show coat," Daisy said with a frown. "Mine was hanging by my pony's stall earlier. But when I went back there just now to get changed, it was gone!"
"Is your show coat missing too?" Henry asked.
"No, it's just her shirt," Maggie said. "Don't worry, Daisy," she went on. "The Lemonade Detectives are on the case!"
"Thanks." Daisy still looked worried. "I really hope you can solve the mystery before my first class. I'll never win a blue ribbon if I'm wearing this!" She pointed to her T-shirt.
"Ms. Wood said fancy clothes aren't mandatory," Maggie reminded her. "You just told me that."
"I know," Daisy said. But she still looked worried.
"What does your shirt look like?" Henry asked.
"It's mostly white, with long sleeves and a high collar," Daisy said. "There's a pocket in the front with a strip of pink and yellow polka-dotted ribbon across the top."
Henry looked around. A lot of the other riders were wearing long-sleeved white shirts with high collars. But none of them had pockets like that.
"It sounds like your shirt will be easy to spot," he told Daisy. "We'll see what we can do."
"Thanks." Daisy sounded distracted. "I'd better go see if anyone has an extra shirt I can borrow, just in case."
"Are you guys crazy?" Cole said after Daisy left. "We don't have time to solve a mystery today. We're supposed to be selling lemonade!"
"We can do both." Maggie sounded excited. "If we solve the case quickly, maybe I can use the detective fee to enter more classes!"

Cole frowned but didn't say anything else. Henry wondered if he was thinking about swim team practice. Cole loved being on the swim team, and he hated to miss a practice. If they finished early at the show, Cole might have time to get to the pool for part of today's practice. But that probably wouldn't happen if they were busy trying to solve a mystery.
"I agree with Maggie," Henry told Cole. "I think we should try to solve the case. Daisy seems really upset."
"Good, then let's get started," Maggie said. "Why don't we—" She stopped talking when Ms. Wood hurried up to the lemonade stand.
"There you are, Maggie," the stable owner said. "It's time to get Big Spot ready for your first class."

"Oh, right." Maggie slapped her forehead. "Sorry, Ms. Wood. I got distracted." She started to follow Ms. Wood toward the barn. Then she rushed back to the lemonade stand and whispered, "You guys should start investigating!"
Henry nodded as Maggie hurried off again. "Okay," he said to Cole. "We should start by checking out the scene of the crime. Maybe the thief left some clues."
Cole glanced past him. "Here come some more customers," he said. "Why don't you serve them while I go look for clues in the barn?"
Henry was surprised that Cole was volunteering to look for clues. Cole hadn't seemed very interested in the case. But Cole rushed off before Henry could say anything about that.
"One lemonade, please!" a little boy cried, tossing a quarter on the table.
"You got it," Henry said, reaching for the nearest pitcher.
For the next few minutes, he was too busy to think about the case. Finally the latest group of lemonade customers had all been served.
Henry looked over toward the barn. Henry guessed that Cole was still inside looking for clues. He thought about going to help him. But he wasn't sure he should leave the lemonade stand.

Then he spotted Daisy walking past, leading a pony. The pony was a little taller than Maggie's favorite pony, Big Spot. It had a glossy brown coat and a black mane and tail. Daisy led the pony into the shade of some tall trees nearby. She leaned against one of the trees, and the pony began to graze.
Henry looked around to make sure no more lemonade customers were coming. Then he left the lemonade stand and hurried over to Daisy.
"Hi," he said. "What are you doing?"
"Coco likes to roll in her stall," Daisy said, gesturing toward the grazing pony. "I'm trying to keep her moving so she doesn't get dirty before our classes. Did you find my show shirt yet?"

"We're working on it," Henry said. He opened his mouth to ask her more questions about her show shirt. But then he noticed someone rushing toward them. It was a girl around Daisy's age with a long blond braid. She looked angry.
"Hey!" the girl yelled, ignoring Henry and pointing a finger at Daisy. "You stole my pony!"
"What?" Daisy was insulted. "I didn't steal your pony!"
"Yes, you did!" The girl with the braid jutted out her chin.
Henry recognized the girl. She lived in West Belltown, and her name was Rebecca. But he didn't know her very well, since she was a grade ahead of him in school.
Rebecca stomped over to the pony. "Everyone knows I wanted to ride Coco in the show today," she said, giving the pony a hug.
Daisy pulled on the lead rope to move the pony away from Rebecca. "I wanted to ride her today too," she said. "I've been riding her in my lessons for the past month."
"Me too," Rebecca said.
"Wait a minute." Henry was confused. "How can both of you ride the same pony at the same time?"
Daisy looked surprised, as if she'd forgotten Henry was listening. "We don't ride her at the same time," she said. "Rebecca and I take lessons on different days."
"Oh," Henry said. Then he remembered something Maggie had told him. "But wait, why can't you both ride Coco in the show? Maggie said a boy is riding Big Spot today too."

"Maggie is riding in the beginner classes for people under age eleven," Daisy explained. "The boy is riding later, in the advanced classes for older riders. Big Spot will have plenty of time to rest in between classes."
Rebecca nodded, still looking angry. "My class is right before Daisy's class, so Coco can only do one or the other. And I was supposed to ride Coco until she stole her!"

Daisy rolled her eyes. "I didn't steal Coco from you," she said. "We chose straws to decide who'd get to ride her in the show. You lost when you got the short straw. It was a fair way to decide, so you should just forget about it!"
"Don't tell me what to do!" Rebecca yelled, clenching her fists. "Anyway, you'll be sorry!"
She stomped away. Daisy stared after the other girl.
"Wow," she said. "Rebecca seems really mad at me."
Henry nodded. "Do you think she's mad enough to steal your shirt?"
Daisy's eyes widened. "Definitely!" she exclaimed. "Maybe she thought that would make me drop out of the show. Then she'd be able to ride Coco after all."
"That seems like a pretty good motive," Henry agreed.
Just then he noticed some people standing by the lemonade stand. He said good-bye to Daisy and hurried back to work.

Henry thought about the case as he poured lemonade and collected quarters. Could Rebecca be the shirt thief? She had a good motive. And it was very busy and crowded at the stable today. She probably could have grabbed the shirt without anyone seeing her. Maybe Cole would come back from the barn with some good clues.
"Hello, Henry," a familiar voice said. "How's business?"
