Henry looked up. Maggie's father was smiling at him. "Hi, Uncle Bruce," Henry said. "Would you like some lemonade?"
"Sure." Uncle Bruce reached into his pocket for a quarter. "I'm getting thirsty standing around waiting to watch Maggie ride."
Henry glanced over at the barn. "Hey, Uncle Bruce, can you do me a favor?"
"Sure, Henry. What is it?" his uncle said.
"Will you watch the lemonade stand for a few minutes?" Henry said. "I need to go find Cole."
"No problem." Uncle Bruce stepped behind the table. "Step right up for Belltown's best lemonade!" he called to a passing woman.
"Thanks," Henry told him. "I'll be back in a few minutes."
When Henry entered the barn, it was very busy. Ponies were standing in stalls and tied in the aisles. Lots of kids were running around with grooming tools or saddles and bridles.
Henry dodged around a fat brown pony, looking for Cole. He didn't see Cole, but he spotted Maggie near Big Spot's stall.
"Have you seen Cole?" Henry asked, hurrying over.
"Nope." Maggie fiddled with her pony's halter. "Haven't seen him since I left the lemonade stand."
"That's weird," Henry muttered. Then he noticed Daisy leading her pony into the barn. She stopped in front of a stall a few doors down from Big Spot's. "Is that Coco's stall?" Henry asked Maggie.
"Yeah," Maggie said. "You should go look for clues there."
"That's what Cole is supposed to be doing." Henry started walking toward Coco's stall. But he had to stop when a dark-haired girl led a dapple-gray pony out of the stall next to Big Spot's.
"Excuse me," the girl said with a smile.
Henry smiled back. The girl was about Daisy's age, but he didn't recognize her.
Suddenly Henry's smile faded. The girl's shirt had long sleeves, a high collar, and a strip of polka-dotted ribbon on the front pocket.
"You!" he blurted out. "You took Daisy's show shirt!"
The dark-haired girl froze in place, her eyes wide with surprise.
Just then Daisy hurried over with a smile. "That's not my shirt, Henry," she said. "That's Kira's. We went shopping together last week and bought matching show shirts."
Maggie had followed Henry down the aisle. "Yeah, Kira's nice," she told Henry. "She and Daisy ride together a lot."
"Oh." Henry felt sheepish. "Sorry," he told Kira. "I didn't know that you and Daisy had matching shirts."
"It's okay," Kira said softly.
Daisy grinned. "We almost didn't have the same shirts," she told Henry. "Kira didn't have enough cash with her. So I lent her a few dollars to pay for her shirt."
Kira nodded and looked down at her shirt. "My parents were pretty mad about that," she admitted. "They didn't think I should spend so much without asking them first."
"Sounds like my parents," Maggie said with a snort. "Except they don't even care if I do ask them. They still say no!"

Henry laughed, but Daisy was starting to look a little upset again as she stared at Kira's shirt. "Our shirts were expensive," Daisy said. "I spent three whole weeks' allowance on mine. And now it's gone!"
"Come on, Daisy," Kira said in her soft voice. "Let's take the ponies for a walk."
"Okay." Daisy led Coco out of her stall again. After Daisy and Kira left, Henry followed Maggie back toward Big Spot's stall. He looked around to make sure nobody else was close enough to hear him.
"We have our first suspect," he said. Then he told Maggie about what Rebecca had said about Coco.
When he finished, Maggie nodded. "Rebecca is pretty spoiled," she said. "She's always whining about something. She's definitely a good suspect."
"Now we need to look for proof she did it." Henry glanced around the barn again. "Are you sure Cole didn't come in here to look for clues by Coco's stall?"
"I'm positive," Maggie said. "I definitely would have seen him."
"So where did he go?" Henry mumbled.
Maggie giggled. "Maybe Cole should be a suspect too," she joked. "His motive could be that he wants to wear Daisy's show shirt to his next swim meet."
"Very funny." Henry grinned. "Anyway, I guess the mystery of the missing friend can wait. If Cole hasn't looked for clues yet, I'd better do it."
"I'll help you," Maggie said. "Big Spot is almost ready for the show. All I have to do is put his bridle on when it's time for our class."
Henry and Maggie walked over to Coco's empty stall.
"Look." Henry pointed to an empty clothes hanger hanging on the stall door next to a coat. "This must be where Daisy's shirt was hanging."
"Yeah," Maggie agreed. "It's weird that Daisy's show coat is still here." She touched the wool coat. "A show coat costs a lot more than a show shirt. Why wouldn't someone steal that instead?"
"I don't know." Henry saw a boy walking by. "Excuse me," he said to him. "Did you notice anyone near this stall earlier?"
The boy blinked at him. "No," he said. "I just got back from giving my horse a bath."
The next rider Henry asked, a teenager named Jill, shook her head. "I didn't notice anyone," she said. "Why? Are you guys investigating another mystery?"
"Yes," Henry admitted. "Daisy's show shirt is missing."
"Oh, is that all?" Jill glanced over at Big Spot and grinned. "Big Spot probably ate it. That pony is always hungry!" She hurried away.
"Do ponies really eat shirts?" Henry asked Maggie.

"Big Spot tries to eat everything, remember? Or at least he likes to grab things and taste them." Maggie hurried back to Big Spot's stall. She stepped inside and looked around. "I don't see the shirt in here, though."
Henry glanced from Big Spot's stall to the spot where Daisy's things were hanging. "There's no way Big Spot could reach the shirt from here. I don't think your pony is our culprit."
Henry questioned a few more riders who passed by. But none of them seemed to know anything about the crime. Everyone was distracted by the show preparations.
Then Ms. Wood stepped into the barn. "Riders in the beginners class, please bring your ponies out!" she called in a loud voice. "It's time to start warming up in the ring."
"Warming up?" Henry said. "I thought everybody would be warm enough already."
"Very funny." Maggie grabbed Big Spot's bridle. "Hold still, Big Spot," she said. "I just need to . . . Ugh!" She jumped back quickly.
"What happened?" Henry asked. "Did Big Spot bite you?"
"No! He slimed me!" Maggie turned around, revealing a huge, bright blue stain on the front of her white shirt.
"Oh no!" Maggie exclaimed. "My shirt is ruined!"
Ms. Wood came over. "Oh dear," she said when she saw Maggie's shirt. "What happened?"
"Big Spot slobbered on me!" Maggie said.
"Is pony slobber always blue?" Henry asked. He didn't know much about ponies and horses. But the blue stain seemed kind of strange.
Maggie scowled at him. "Of course not!" she said. "Big Spot must have eaten something blue."
"None of our usual horse treats are that color." Ms. Wood opened Big Spot's mouth to look inside. She sounded a little worried. "I wonder what he ate."
"I can't wear this shirt in the show," Maggie wailed. "I look ridiculous!"
"Now, Maggie," Ms. Wood said. "The judge won't be looking at what you're wearing. She'll be looking at how you're riding."
"Maybe." Maggie didn't sound convinced. "But I'll still look like a slob in front of everyone!"
"I have an idea, Maggie," Henry said. "Try turning your shirt inside out. Maybe the stain won't show that way."
Maggie's face brightened instantly. "Henry, you're a genius!" she cried. "I'll be right back." She ducked behind the stall door.
"Thanks, Henry." Ms. Wood smiled with relief. "I think you just saved the day."
Seconds later Maggie emerged with her shirt turned inside out. "Much better," she said. "Try not to slime this side too, okay, Spot?"
She put on the pony's bridle. Then she hurried out of the barn leading Big Spot behind her. Ms. Wood left too.
Henry headed back to the lemonade stand. "Oh good," Uncle Bruce said when Henry arrived. "I just saw Maggie getting on her pony."
"Yeah, her class will be starting soon," Henry said. "Have you seen Cole since I left?"
"No." Uncle Bruce shook his head. "But I could have used his help. The lemonade stand was pretty busy."
"The next class will begin in three minutes!" Ms. Wood said over the loudspeaker.
"I want to find a good spot to watch the show," Uncle Bruce told Henry. "Want to come along?"
"I have to stay with the lemonade stand," Henry said. "I can watch Maggie from here."

Uncle Bruce nodded and hurried off. There were no customers at the moment, so Henry sat down to think. He needed to figure out whether Rebecca was the shirt thief. He wished Cole was there to help him come up with a plan.
"Where is Cole, anyway?" Henry muttered.
He looked around. He didn't see Cole, but he saw Kira walking by. She was still wearing her show coat, and her face was red and sweaty.
"Hi," Henry said to her. "You look hot. Why don't you take off your coat for a while?"
Kira paused. "It's okay," she said. "I'm not that hot."
Henry wondered if she was afraid someone might steal her coat, just like someone had stolen Daisy's shirt. "Have you seen my friend Cole anywhere?" he asked. He described what Cole looked like.

"I know who you mean," Kira said. "I saw him earlier. He was behind the barn helping Daisy wash some mud off her pony's legs with the hose. That was over an hour ago, though. Maybe longer. I haven't seen him since then." She glanced at the ring, where Maggie and the other riders were trotting in a circle. "Excuse me, I'd better go check on my pony."
She hurried off.

"Well, at least that's one mystery solved." Henry said with a sigh. Now he knew where Cole had been earlier when Cole was supposed to be looking for napkins. Too bad that wasn't the mystery Henry was trying to solve!
"Riders, please ask your horses to walk," Ms. Wood said over the loudspeaker. "The judge is watching you now."
As Henry turned to watch the show class, he saw Cole hurrying toward him. "Finally!" Henry exclaimed. "Where have you been?"
"Sorry," Cole said breathlessly. "I started to look for clues in the barn. But then a little kid asked me to help her carry a saddle."
"Well, it took you an awfully long time," Henry said.
"Maggie's class is starting," Cole said. "We'd better watch."
Henry noticed that Rebecca was riding in the class too. She wasn't riding Coco though. She was riding a different pony.
"Look, there's Rebecca," Henry said. "We should watch her to see if she does anything suspicious."
"Why?" Cole asked.
Henry realized Cole didn't know that Rebecca was a suspect yet. Henry told him what had happened between Rebecca and Daisy.
"That's weird," Cole said. "Look! I think the class is finished."
The riders were lining up in front of the judge. A few moments later, Ms. Wood began announcing the winners. Soon she got to the final ribbon.
"The first-place ribbon goes to . . . Maggie riding Big Spot!"
"Way to go, Maggie!" Henry yelled. Cole let out a cheer too.
Maggie grinned proudly as Ms. Wood attached the blue ribbon to her pony's bridle. Most of the other riders looked happy too.
Only one rider looked unhappy. That was Rebecca. She'd come in fourth.
"I knew it!" she yelled, riding out of the ring and jumping down from her pony. "I would have won if I'd been riding Coco!"
She flung her pony's reins away and kicked at the ground. Then she grabbed the white ribbon from the pony's bridle and stomped on it.
"Rebecca!" Ms. Wood exclaimed. "You should be ashamed of yourself! That's very poor sportsmanship."
"I don't care!" Rebecca yelled. "It's not fair! I wanted to ride Coco today. This stupid pony made me lose!"
"Don't say that!" another girl spoke up. "Red is a great pony too."
"Yeah," Maggie agreed. "I rode him once. He was awesome! Almost as good as Big Spot."
"They're right, Rebecca." Ms. Wood sounded stern. "Now stop complaining and go take care of your pony. He did his best, and he deserves a nice grooming and some treats."
A woman pushed through the crowd. "I think that's Rebecca's mother," Henry whispered to Cole.
"Stop this tantrum right now and do as Ms. Wood says!" Rebecca's mother said. "Or you won't get to take riding lessons anymore."
"Fine!" Rebecca cried. "But it's not fair!" She stomped off toward the barn, dragging her pony behind her.
"Wow. Did you see that?" Henry said to Cole. "Rebecca is obviously still mad about not getting to ride Coco."
Cole just shrugged. "Yeah. She's probably the shirt thief, like you said."
Henry rubbed his chin thoughtfully. "She has a good motive. And she definitely could have done it. Now all we have to do is prove it."

"That's not going to be easy," Cole said. "If there were any witnesses, somebody would have said something by now. Plus, if Rebecca hid that shirt somewhere, it will be tough to prove that she was the one who stole it. Maybe we should just forget about this case and focus on selling lemonade."

Henry frowned at his friend. Cole wasn't acting like himself today. "The Lemonade Detectives agreed to accept this case. That means we need to try to solve it! If you don't want to help, Maggie and I can do it without you."

Cole frowned too. "I'm not saying I don't want to help," he said. "I'm just saying it's not going to be easy to prove anything. Besides, Daisy's family lives in that big, fancy house over on Elm Street. They have plenty of money to buy her another shirt. So what's the big deal?"

Henry was surprised to hear Cole say something like that. "Stealing is wrong!" he reminded Cole. "If Rebecca stole Daisy's shirt, she should give it back to Daisy and apologize. And if she didn't do it, we should figure out who did."
Just then he saw Rebecca come stomping out of the barn.
"There's our suspect now," Henry told Cole. "Stay with the lemonade stand. I'll be right back."
Henry hurried off without waiting for an answer. He caught up to Rebecca near the parking lot.
"Hi, Rebecca," he said. "Can I talk to you?"
"Sure, what do you want to talk about?" Rebecca asked.
Henry shrugged. "I just wanted to congratulate you," he said. "I saw you win fourth place just now. That's pretty good, especially since you didn't get to ride your favorite pony."
"Tell me about it!" Rebecca scowled. "I still can't believe Daisy stole Coco from me! It's totally unfair!"
"Yeah," Henry said, pretending to go along with her. "So did you go visit Coco in her stall earlier? You know, before the show started?"
"Huh?" Rebecca blinked at him. "Yeah, I stopped by and gave her a carrot when I first got here. Why?"
"Just curious." Henry cleared his throat. "Was that before or after Daisy arrived at the show?"
"How should I know?" Rebecca said. "Why are you asking all these questions, anyway?"

"I, uh . . ." Henry tried to think of something to say. Lots of people in Belltown knew about The Lemonade Detectives. If Rebecca had stolen that shirt, Henry didn't want her to guess that he knew she'd done it. Otherwise it might be even harder to prove.
Just then Henry heard a clatter of hooves behind him. Turning, he saw Maggie rushing over, still leading Big Spot.
"I need to talk to you, Henry," Maggie said breathlessly. "In private."
She yanked him away from Rebecca.
"What is it?" Henry asked.
Maggie spun to face him. "I just found Daisy's missing shirt!"
"You found the shirt?" Henry exclaimed. "Where is it?"
Maggie grinned. "On TV, detectives always want to examine the crime scene exactly as they found it. So I left it where I found it."
"Let's go look," Henry said. "We should tell Daisy too."
"I just saw her in the barn." Maggie headed back to the barn with Big Spot. So did Henry.
Daisy and Kira were brushing Coco's mane.
"Maggie found your show shirt," Henry told Daisy.
"Really? Where?" Daisy cried.

"Follow me." Maggie put Big Spot into his stall. Then she headed out the barn's back door. She stopped beside the water trough just outside. "Look!" Maggie said, pointing. A blob of white fabric was floating in the water.
"My shirt!" Daisy shrieked. She reached in and grabbed the wet shirt. "Yuck! It's a mess! There's no way I can wear it for my class!"
"Attention, please!" Ms. Wood said over the loudspeaker. "Riders in the next class, please come to the ring."
"That's us." Kira buttoned her show coat. "We'd better get our ponies."
"Okay." Daisy shoved the wet shirt at Henry. "You have to find out who did this. Whoever it is should pay!"
The two older girls rushed back into the barn.
Henry was examining the shirt. It looked just like Daisy had described, white with a ribbon on the pocket.
"Wow, this shirt is really a mess," he said. "It's not just wet. It's stained too. There's a spot just below the ribbon."
"Maybe the colors in the ribbon ran when they got wet," Maggie suggested. "That happened once when I did the laundry. All Dad's underwear turned pink."
"It can't be that," Henry said. "The ribbon is pink and yellow. This stain is blue."
"Blue?" Maggie looked interested. "Like the blue stuff Big Spot slobbered on me?"
"Maybe. It's hard to tell, since the shirt has been in the water and the spot is pretty faded."

"Let me see." Maggie took the shirt. "The stain is right on the pocket. Maybe something in the pocket is staining it from the inside." She stuck her fingers into the small pocket. "Nope, nothing in here. But it feels sticky."
"Maybe Daisy left gum or candy or something in the pocket earlier," Henry said.
"That makes sense," Maggie said. "Those lollipops at the Dessert Den come in all kinds of colors. And Daisy was looking at them yesterday when we saw her there, remember?"
"Daisy was at the Dessert Den yesterday?" Henry said. "I didn't see her."
"She left a few minutes after we got there." Maggie laughed. "Besides, you were busy drooling over the new chocolate cake. But Cole and I talked to her."
"So did Daisy buy any blue lollipops?" Henry asked. "If she didn't, this stain could be a clue."
Maggie shrugged. "Let's go ask her. If she fed one to Big Spot, that would solve the mystery of the blue drool."
"Yeah. But it wouldn't explain who took Daisy's shirt," Henry said. "Big Spot couldn't have put it in the water trough."
They walked to the ring. "Daisy's class already started," Maggie said.
Henry nodded. He watched as Daisy, Kira, and several other students rode around the ring. In the end Daisy won the blue ribbon, and Kira came in second.
"That was great!" Daisy exclaimed as she and Kira rode out of the ring. "Hey, Kira, let's enter another class in the show. How about the obstacle course class?"
"I can't," Kira said. "I don't have enough money."
"I know how that feels," Maggie told her. Then she turned to Daisy. "Can we talk to you?"
"Sure. I'll catch up to you in the barn," Daisy told Kira. She followed Henry and Maggie to a more private spot. "What's up? Did you guys figure out who wrecked my shirt?"
She didn't sound as angry as she had earlier. Henry guessed that she was in a good mood after winning her class.
"Not exactly," he said. "But we noticed a blue stain on the pocket. Did you put anything blue in there?"
"Like one of those blue lollipops from the Dessert Den, for instance?" Maggie said. "Did you bring one to feed to Coco?"

Daisy looked surprised. "I love those lollipops, especially the blueberry ones. But they're much too expensive to feed to ponies! I didn't even buy any yesterday. I wanted to save my money for today's show."
"Oh," Maggie said. "Hey, I think Kira is calling you. You'd better see what she wants."
"She is? Okay, see you guys later!" Daisy hurried off with her pony.
"Why'd you say that?" Henry said. "I wanted to ask her more questions."
"Because I just thought of a new theory," Maggie blurted out. "Maybe the person who wrecked Daisy's shirt is . . . Daisy!"
"Huh?" Henry said. "Why would Daisy want to ruin her own shirt?"
"To get sympathy!" Maggie said. "Maybe Daisy thought the judge would hear that Daisy's shirt was missing and feel sorry for Daisy. Then the judge would be more likely to give Daisy a blue ribbon!"
Henry shook his head. Maggie's theory was a little crazy. "I don't think that's very likely, Maggie. For one thing, it doesn't explain the blue stain."

"Yes, it does," Maggie argued. "Daisy probably tried to stain the shirt with one of those lollipops first. Then she decided that wasn't bad enough. So she pretended someone stole the shirt, and then put it in the water trough herself."
"But she just told us the blue lollipops are her favorite," Henry said. "She probably wouldn't admit that if she had made that stain herself."
Maggie frowned, looking stubborn. "How do you know?"
"Because Daisy's not stupid," Henry said. "Besides, if she is the culprit, there's no way we'll get that detective fee. So you'd better hope it was somebody else."
"Oh. I guess you're right." Maggie thought for a second. "Okay, then maybe we should go investigate Rebecca again. She seems like a better suspect anyway."
"Let's go talk to Cole first," Henry suggested. "Maybe he'll have some ideas."
Soon Henry and Maggie were telling Cole the latest news. Cole listened quietly, sucking on another green lollipop. Two more green lollipops were sitting on the table beside him.
"So now we think it's Rebecca again," Maggie finished. "What do you think?"
Cole glanced at the lollipops on the table. "Are you sure the shirt didn't get ruined by accident?"
"By accident?" Maggie made a face. "How would Daisy's shirt accidentally get from her pony's stall to the water trough? Or accidentally get that weird blue stain on it?"
"I don't know." Cole shrugged again. "But your dad is always joking about how messy horses are. And you already said your pony drooled on your shirt, right?"
"Hey, guys," Henry put in before Maggie could respond. "Look, Rebecca's heading this way. This could be our chance to question her."
"What should we ask her?" Maggie wondered.
Henry bit his lip. How could they ask Rebecca any more questions about the case without letting her know she was a suspect?
"I'm not sure," he said.
"Wait!" Maggie whispered. "I think I have an idea."
"Uh-oh," Henry thought. Some of Maggie's ideas were good, but others weren't so good.
"Hi, Rebecca," Maggie said with a big smile. "Welcome to our lemonade stand!"
"Um, thanks." Rebecca still looked grumpy.
"Guess what?" Maggie went on. "We're having a special right now. If you buy a cup of our delicious lemonade, you get a free lollipop!"
"Hey," Cole protested as Maggie grabbed one of the lollipops off the table.
Maggie ignored him, waving the lollipop in Rebecca's face. "This one's kiwi. Do you like that kind? What's your favorite flavor?" she asked.
Henry guessed what Maggie was trying to do. She was hoping that Rebecca would admit to liking blueberry lollipops best. That would be a clue that she might have stolen Daisy's shirt.
But Rebecca just frowned and pushed the lollipop away. "I can't have candy," she said. "Or lemonade, either. I have diabetes, so I'm not allowed to eat sugar."
Henry blinked in surprise.
Maggie was surprised too. "Really?" she said.
"Yeah." Rebecca shrugged. "Anyway, I came to tell you, Maggie, that Ms. Wood is looking for you. She wants us to start getting ready for our second class."
"Oh, right." Maggie looked at her watch, and then at Henry and Cole. "I've got to go."
"Good luck in your class," Henry said. "We'll be cheering for you."
"Thanks." Maggie hurried off toward the barn with Rebecca.
"Wow," Henry said to Cole when the girls were gone. "I didn't know that Rebecca has diabetes. I guess that means she didn't cause that stain on Daisy's shirt. Not if it was made by candy, anyway."
"Yeah," Cole said.
"Of course, that doesn't prove that she's not the shirt thief," Henry realized. "The stain could be a coincidence."
"I guess," Cole said.
Henry glanced over at him. Cole was still sucking on his green lollipop. That made Henry think of something else.
"Wait," he said. "What if Rebecca already guessed that we're suspicious of her? Do you think she's telling the truth about not being able to eat sugar?"
"She's telling the truth," Cole blurted out with a frown. "At least about the candy stain."
"Huh?" Henry was surprised by how certain Cole sounded. "How do you know?"
Cole took a deep breath and looked Henry in the eye. "I know for a fact that Rebecca didn't put a blue lollipop in Daisy's shirt pocket," he said. "Because I did it."
"What?" Henry exclaimed, staring at Cole. "What do you mean, you put the lollipop in Daisy's pocket? Why?"

Cole shrugged, looking sheepish. "I knew that Daisy loves those blueberry lollipops from the Dessert Den. She couldn't stop talking about them when I saw her there yesterday. So I decided to surprise her with one as a . . . um . . . good luck gift. I waited until she left to get some lemonade," he continued. "Then I sneaked into the barn and stuck a lollipop in the pocket of her show shirt."
"You did?" Henry said. "Why? You didn't get Maggie anything. She likes candy too."
"That's different." Cole looked embarrassed. "Maggie's just . . . Maggie. Daisy is, you know, really nice and pretty and smart."
"Oh!" Henry thought. "Cole has a crush on Daisy!"
"Is that why you skipped swim team practice today?" he asked. "Because of Daisy? You wanted to watch her compete?"
"Maybe." Cole shrugged. "I mean, I wanted to help you guys too."
"Okay," Henry said. "So what happened with the shirt? Did you leave it in the water trough?"
"No!" Cole said. "I just put the lollipop in Daisy's shirt pocket. Then I left it hanging in the barn by Coco's stall."
"When you said you were looking for more napkins, you were really hanging out with Daisy," Henry guessed. "That's when you put the lollipop in her pocket."

Cole nodded. "I was going to tell Daisy later that the lollipop was from me. But then her shirt disappeared!" He sighed. "I was afraid someone saw me near her shirt. That person could tell Daisy—and make her think that I stole it!"
Henry sighed. "Why didn't you just say so in the first place?"
"I don't know." Cole looked sheepish again. "I thought I could find the shirt myself. That way nobody would ever know about the candy and stuff."
Henry nodded. Now he understood why Cole had been acting so strange all day.
The trouble was, Cole's explanation didn't explain what had happened to Daisy's shirt.
"So you have no idea how the shirt got into the water trough?" he asked.
"Nope." Cole shook his head.
Normally Henry wouldn't doubt his best friend. But Cole had told a lot of lies today. Still, he wanted to trust his best friend. "Maybe it's a red herring," he muttered.
"A what?" Cole said.

"A red herring," Henry said. "That's something that seems like a clue, but isn't. Like that blue stain. Maybe it's just a coincidence. Maybe Rebecca—or someone else—grabbed the shirt without even noticing the lollipop in the pocket."
"That makes sense," Cole agreed.
Henry frowned as he kept thinking. "But in that case, what happened to the lollipop? It wasn't in the pocket when we found the shirt. And I didn't see it in the water trough."
"Maybe a horse ate it," Cole suggested.

Henry thought about Big Spot's blue slobber. "Maybe. But why would someone steal the shirt and then leave it in such an obvious place?" he asked. "If Rebecca was trying to ruin things for Daisy, Rebecca would have found a better hiding spot for the shirt. This just doesn't make sense."
Henry had the feeling he was missing some important clue. But he couldn't figure out what it was.
He glanced around. Everyone was gathering near the ring to watch the next class. There were no lemonade customers in sight.
"Let's go check the scene of the crime again," he suggested.
"Okay," Cole said. "Listen, I'm sorry I didn't tell you earlier. About the lollipop, I mean."
"That's okay." Henry led the way toward the barn.

When Henry and Cole entered, Cole went over to Maggie, who was near Big Spot's stall. Henry saw Coco in her stall, though Daisy was nowhere in sight. Instead Rebecca was standing there patting the pony.
"Hi," said Henry. "Did you notice the clothes that were hanging on this stall earlier?"
"Clothes?" Rebecca rubbed Coco's nose. "No. Why?"
"There was a show shirt—" Henry began.
Before he could finish, Cole hurried over to Henry. "Excuse us," Cole said to Rebecca. Then he pulled Henry away. "That's not where Daisy's shirt was hanging!" he whispered.
"Yes, it was," Henry said. "That's Daisy's pony right there. Her show coat was hanging there too, until she put it on for her last class."
Cole looked confused. "It was? But I saw Daisy's shirt hanging on that stall over there."
Cole pointed to the stall next to Big Spot's. Kira's pony was standing there, looking out.
Henry looked at Kira's pony, and then slowly he smiled. "Let's go find Daisy," he told Cole. "I think I know exactly what happened to her shirt."
Maggie heard Henry and came running over.
"I knew it!" she cried. "It was Rebecca, wasn't it?"
"Hold on," Henry said. "I need to find one last bit of evidence."
Henry ducked into Big Spot's stall and felt around in the bedding until he found something. Then he hurried out of the stall and down the aisle—right past Rebecca.
Maggie and Cole rushed after him.
"What's going on?" Maggie demanded.
Henry stopped and quickly told her about how Cole had put the lollipop in Daisy's shirt.
Maggie looked confused. "So Cole is the shirt thief?"
"Not exactly," Henry said. "But he's the one who caused the shirt to get stolen."
"I did?" Cole sounded just as confused as Maggie. "How?"
Henry smiled. "By putting that lollipop in the wrong shirt pocket!"
"Huh?" Cole said.
Henry spotted Daisy and Kira near the lemonade stand.
"Where have you guys been?" Daisy complained. "We're thirsty. Plus it's getting late. Have you solved the case yet?"
"The case?" Kira said. "What case?"
Daisy shrugged. "Haven't you ever heard of The Lemonade Detectives? I asked them to find my missing shirt."
"You guys are detectives?" Kira stared at Henry. "Is that why you were asking me questions earlier?"
"Yes." Henry noticed that Kira looked pale. "Is there anything you want to tell Daisy?"
Kira took a deep breath. "I do have something to say, Daisy. It wasn't your shirt that got ruined. It was mine!"
"What?" Daisy exclaimed.
"What?" Maggie shrieked.
"Huh?" Cole said.
"Just let Kira explain," Henry told them. "It all started when Cole put a lollipop in the pocket of the wrong shirt."
Daisy shot a look at Cole.
"I was trying to surprise Daisy," Cole mumbled. "I didn't know you two had matching shirts."
Daisy smiled. "Aw, that's sweet. It almost makes me wish I had a little brother like you!"
Cole looked away. Henry guessed that Cole didn't like having Daisy treat him like a little brother.
"Kira's stall is right next to Big Spot's," Henry said. "Close enough for Big Spot to grab Kira's shirt when he smelled that candy."

Kira nodded. "When I came into the barn earlier, Spot was chewing on my shirt." She looked away. "My parents are already mad at me for spending so much money on it. I knew they'd be even angrier if the shirt got ruined. I rinsed out most of the horse slobber in the water trough. But I couldn't get the blue stain out." She ducked her head, looking ashamed. "I left my shirt in the water trough and ran inside. Daisy wasn't around, so I grabbed her shirt and put it on so everyone would think it was mine."
"That explains why you've been wearing your show coat all day despite the heat," Henry guessed.
Kira pulled off her coat.
"I didn't want anyone to notice and figure out the truth," she admitted.
"This stick explains how Big Spot got blue slobber on Maggie's shirt." Henry held up the empty lollipop stick he'd found in the pony's stall. "This was all that was left of that lollipop."
Kira's eyes filled with tears as she turned to Daisy. "I'm sorry. Can you ever forgive me?"
Daisy didn't say anything for a second. Then she sighed.
"I guess it's partly my fault too," she said. "I practically forced you to buy that expensive shirt. I'm sorry. Friends?"
"Friends." Kira smiled with relief. She and Daisy hugged. Then they linked arms and started walking away.
Suddenly Daisy turned back. "I almost forgot," she said, digging into her pocket. "Here's your detective fee. Thanks for solving the case."
"You're welcome." Maggie took the money and put it in the cashbox.
"You don't look very excited, Maggie," said Henry. "What's wrong?"
"I wanted to enter more classes in the show," Maggie said. "But I still don't have enough money." She sighed. "That's okay, though. I'll just keep saving money until the next show."
Henry was surprised that Maggie was acting so mature. He traded a look with Cole. Then he grabbed the cashbox.
"Here," he said, handing it to Maggie. "This should be enough to enter more classes."
"Huh?" Maggie said. "But only a third of that money is mine."
"Not today," Henry said.
Cole nodded. "Take it, Maggie."
"Wow, thanks!" Maggie grabbed the cash and took off toward the barn.
"Just don't get used to it!" Cole called after her. "Next time it's back to splitting the cash three ways."
Henry laughed. "I guess that's another case closed." He pointed to a bunch of thirsty-looking riders heading their way. "Time to go back to selling lemonade."
"That will be 25 cents, please," Henry said.

He handed a cup of lemonade to Tiny. Tiny was Henry's neighbor and the tallest kid in the tenth grade. Tiny was also one of the lemonade stand's best customers. He stopped by the stand to buy lemonade almost every day, sometimes more than once.
"Here you go." Tiny handed over a few coins. "Thanks for the lemonade!"
"You're welcome."
After Tiny left, Henry looked at Cole. "I hope Maggie comes back soon," he said. "We're almost out of lemonade."
Just then Nathan hurried over. "Hi, guys," said their friend. "How are the lemonade and detective businesses?"
"Hi, Nathan," Henry said. "The lemonade business is great."
"Yeah," Cole agreed. "But the detective business is a little slow."
"It's a good thing we haven't been busy solving any mysteries this week, though," Henry reminded Cole. "Otherwise we wouldn't have had enough time to work on our float."
Nathan looked interested. "A float? You mean for the parade?"
Henry nodded. Belltown's annual Summer Parade was coming up that Saturday afternoon. Anyone in town could sign up to enter a float.
"It's going to be awesome!" Cole told Nathan. "This is the first time The Lemonade Detectives are entering."
Henry laughed. "It would have been hard for The Lemonade Detectives to enter a float last year. Our business didn't exist then!"
"Good point." Cole grinned. "Anyway, we're sure to win the grand prize for Best Float."
"That's what Maggie is hoping," Henry said. "She really wants that cash prize, especially since she spent all her money on that horse show last week."
Cole pointed. "Speaking of Maggie, here she comes."
Maggie was rushing toward them. She was clutching a pitcher of lemonade and a laptop computer.
"You guys will never believe what I just found out!" she exclaimed. "There are going to be two prizes awarded at the parade this year!"
"Two prizes?" Henry said. "Do you mean there's a first prize and a second prize?"
"No, there will be two first prizes," Maggie said.
"Huh?" Cole looked confused. "How can there be two first prizes?"

Maggie looked impatient. "I'm trying to tell you," she said. "The mayor will award a cash prize for the best float, just like he does every year. But there's also going to be a poll on the town website. Anyone in town can vote for his or her favorite float."
"Wow, cool!" Nathan said. "Does the winner of the popular vote get a cash prize too?"
"No," Maggie said. "But the popular vote winner gets to be interviewed on TV."
"That could be fun," Cole said.
"Not just fun," Maggie said. "It would be great publicity for both of my—I mean our —businesses." She waved a hand at the signs advertising the lemonade stand and the detective business.
Henry grabbed the laptop and opened it. The screen showed Belltown's website. "It looks like the popular poll isn't open yet," he said.
"Of course it's not, silly." Maggie shrugged. "Nobody has seen any of the floats yet. They're all top secret."
Henry scanned the website. "It says voting will start as soon as the parade is over on Saturday."
Cole looked over Henry's shoulder. "What's that?" he asked, pointing to something at the bottom of the computer screen.
Henry scrolled down for a better look. "It's a place where people can write comments about the parade. See? Here's a note from Mrs. Sweet."
"It says, 'My float will be the sweetest treat in town,'" Maggie read.
"Here's one from Miss Bishop, the lady who owns the jewelry store right across from the Sweet Shop." Cole leaned closer to read the comment. "She says, 'My float will win the gold medal for sure.'"
Maggie snorted. "Those ladies can keep dreaming," she said. "The Lemonade Detectives are definitely going to win both of those prizes!"
"I'll vote for you guys," Nathan promised. "What does your float look like?"
Henry opened his mouth to answer, but Maggie spoke first. "We can't tell you," she said to Nathan. "It's top secret."
"Don't be silly, Maggie!" Cole laughed. "We can trust Nathan."
Maggie looked uncertain. "Do you promise not to tell anyone? Especially your little sister, Nora. She has a big mouth."
"I promise," Nathan said. "My sister is staying with my grandparents this week, so I couldn't tell her even if I wanted to."
"Our float is really cool," Cole told him. "We made a huge lemon out of papier-mâché, and we're dressing it up to look like Sherlock Holmes."
"Get it?" Henry said. "Sherlock Holmes is a famous detective. And we're The Lemonade Detectives."
Nathan was laughing. "A lemon dressed like Sherlock Holmes? That's funny!"
Suddenly Maggie spun around. "Hey!" she cried, pointing at a figure. "Who are you? Are you spying on us?"
Henry looked where Maggie was pointing. A teenage boy had just walked up behind the lemonade stand. He was wearing jeans and a black T-shirt, and he had a tattoo of a snake on his arm.
"It's okay, Maggie," Henry said quickly. The teenager looked pretty tough, and Henry didn't want to cause trouble. "I'm sure he wasn't spying on us."
Maggie frowned. "How do you know? Maybe he's building a float for the parade, and he was eavesdropping so he can steal our ideas."

The teenager laughed. "Actually, my rock band is entering a float. But we're not doing any silly lemon stuff. We're going to make our float look like a concert stage. Then we're going to play our music during the parade. It will be awesome!"
"Do you live in Belltown?" Henry asked.
"I moved here at the beginning of the summer," the teenager said. "My name is Stan, but everyone calls me Snake."
"Welcome to Belltown, Snake." Cole poured a cup of lemonade. "Here's some lemonade—on the house."
"Thanks." Snake drank the lemonade. "Maybe my band will stop by later to buy more. We'll probably be thirsty after we practice. That reminds me—I have to go."
Soon there were no customers in sight.
"Hey, Nathan, can you watch the lemonade stand for a while?" Henry asked. "We should go work on our float. We only have two more days to finish it."
"Yeah." Maggie picked up the laptop. "Plus, my mom doesn't know I have her computer."
"Sure," Nathan said. "Have fun."
The papier-mâché lemon was in Maggie's house. When it was finished, the kids were planning to attach it to a garden cart. Maggie's father would pull the cart behind his lawn tractor.
"It looks awesome," Cole said. "But we still need to attach Sherlock Holmes' hat."
Maggie dug into their craft supply box. "I think we're out of glue."
"I'll go buy some," Henry offered. "You guys can keep working."
Henry's house was right next door. He grabbed his bike and rode toward Main Street.
On the way there, he heard loud rock music. It was coming from the garage of a nearby house.
The garage door was open, so Henry stopped and looked in. Four teenagers were inside playing instruments. One of the musicians was Snake. There were two other boys and a girl.

Snake saw Henry looking in. He held up a hand, and the band stopped playing. The other three teens stared at Henry. Henry knew the drummer's name was Eddie and that this was his house. He also recognized the other two teens as students from the high school. But he didn't know any of them well.
"Hey, it's the lemonade kid," Snake called with a smile. "Did you bring us a drink?"
"No," Henry said. "I like your music, though."
"Cool," one of the other boys said with a grin. "You have good taste."
Henry glanced at the girl. He was pretty sure her name was Jade. She was ignoring everyone else as she tuned her guitar.
"Are you here to spy on us, Lemonade Kid?" Snake laughed and glanced at the others with a grin. "He and his friends are making a float too."
"Uh-oh," Eddie said. "So he's our competition for the prizes, huh?"
"No way," the other boy said. "Our float is going to be awesome! We'll win for sure."
Jade looked up from her guitar with a frown. "Can we get back to practicing?" she said. "I have to go to work soon."
"Okay, okay." Snake strummed his bass guitar. "See you at the parade, Lemonade Kid."
"See you." Henry hurried on as the music started again.
"May I be excused, Mom?" Henry asked.
It was the next day, and he'd just finished eating lunch.
"Of course," his mother said. "Put your dishes in the sink. Are you going back to Maggie's house to work on your float?"
Henry carried his plate and glass to the sink. "No, we worked on it all morning. I'm supposed to meet Maggie and Cole at the lemonade stand."
When Henry reached the lemonade stand, his friends were already there. Maggie had her mother's laptop again.
"What are you doing?" Henry asked her.
"I want to leave a comment on the town website about our float," Maggie said. "Then people will look for us during the parade."
"Are a lot of people leaving comments?" Cole asked.
He and Henry watched as Maggie scrolled down to the comment section. Henry's eyes widened when he saw the latest comment. "Look at that!" he exclaimed.
The comment was typed in capital letters.
THE SUMMER PARADE IS FOR LOSERS. THE MAYOR SHOULD CANCEL IT—OR ELSE!
"Wow," Henry said. "Who would leave a message like that?"
"I don't know," Maggie said. "I thought everyone in town loved the summer parade."
Cole shrugged. "Maybe someone is joking around."
"If it's a joke, it's not very funny." Henry stared at the message. "It sounds more like a threat."
Cole grinned. "Are you trying to turn it into a mystery, Henry?"
Just then two teenage girls, Jill and Ashley, raced up to the lemonade stand.
"Oh my gosh! Did you guys hear what happened?" Jill asked.
Ashley continued before The Lemonade Detectives could respond. "Someone broke into the shed where Mrs. Sweet is keeping her float!" she cried.
"Huh?" Cole said. "Why would someone do that?"
"Was the float damaged?" Henry asked.
Jill shook her head. "We're not sure. Mrs. Sweet is keeping her float top secret until the parade, so she didn't tell us exactly what happened. But she's afraid that someone wants to sabotage it."
Just then Ashley's cell phone rang. "Oops, we have to go," she said. "Come on, Jill."
The girls raced off. Maggie looked worried. "This is bad. What if someone is trying to sabotage all the floats?"
"Why would anyone do that?" Cole sounded skeptical.
Maggie shrugged. "Maybe to win those great prizes. We should probably investigate before someone tries to destroy our float!"

"How could anybody do that?" Cole said. "It's inside your house, Maggie. Besides, we don't have time to mess around with a mystery right now." He laughed. "I don't think this is a mystery anyway. Right, Henry?"
Henry didn't answer for a second. He was thinking about that threatening message on the town website. "Maybe we should go talk to my dad," he said. "Just in case something really is going on."
"Good idea," Maggie said. "Uncle Kevin is a newspaper reporter. It's his job to know about weird stuff happening around town."
"Fine." Cole shrugged. "You two go talk to him. I'll stay here and watch the lemonade stand."
Henry and Maggie walked toward the main part of town, where the newspaper office was located. On the way they passed Eddie's house. The garage door was shut; no music was coming from behind it.
"I guess Snake's band isn't practicing today," Henry said. He told Maggie about seeing the band the day before.
Maggie stared at the garage. "I wonder if Snake and his band members should be suspects," she said. "He seemed really excited about winning the contest."
"Lots of people want to win," Henry said. "That doesn't mean all of them want to sabotage the other floats."
"Maybe not." Maggie shrugged. "But Snake seemed kind of sneaky."
Henry didn't answer. He thought Snake seemed okay. But when Maggie got an idea in her head, it could be hard to change her mind.
A few minutes later, they reached the newspaper office. "Hi, Henry," the receptionist said. "Your dad just left."
"Really?" Henry was disappointed. "Do you know when he'll be back? We wanted to ask him some questions about the summer parade."
The receptionist pointed to a young man who had just come into the lobby. "If it's about the parade, maybe Jackson can help," she said. "He's assigned to cover that story."
Henry had met Jackson several times. He walked over to the reporter with Maggie right behind him.
Jackson smiled when he saw them coming. "Hi, Henry," he said. "Hi, Maggie. What's up? Did The Lemonade Detectives uncover an exciting crime for me to write about?"
"Maybe," Henry said. "Is it true that you're covering the parade this year?"

"That's right." Jackson didn't sound very excited. Henry wasn't surprised. His father said Jackson was always looking for important and dramatic stories. Unfortunately for him, there weren't very many of those in Belltown.
"We heard someone might have tampered with Mrs. Sweet's float," Maggie spoke up.
Jackson nodded. "I heard it too. Actually, I was just on my way over to the Sweet Shop to talk to her. You two can come along, if you like."
The three of them headed outside. "Do you think someone is trying to sabotage Mrs. Sweet's float?" Henry asked as they walked toward the Sweet Shop.
Jackson shook his head. "I doubt it. Her float was probably damaged by animals or something. Or maybe she just got confused and forgot to lock the shed."

Henry thought about that. Mrs. Sweet was always joking about her bad memory. She often said she'd forget her head if it wasn't attached to her neck! Could Mrs. Sweet's forgetfulness explain what Jill and Ashley had said?
Henry was still wondering about it when they reached the Sweet Shop. Just then there was a blood-curdling scream from the alley beside the shop!
"Was that Mrs. Sweet?" Jackson raced down the alley.
Henry and Maggie followed. The alley was between the Sweet Shop and another store. At the back was a small shed.
Mrs. Sweet stood there facing Miss Bishop, who owned the jewelry store across the street.
"Oh my, Laura!" Miss Bishop fanned her face with one hand. "You nearly gave me a heart attack sneaking up on me like that!"
"I wasn't sneaking, Jane," Mrs. Sweet retorted. "I was just walking to my shed. What were you doing back here anyway? Trying to get a peek at my float, hmm?"
"Of course not!" Just then Miss Bishop noticed Henry and the others. "Oh, hello."
"Is everything all right, ladies?" Jackson asked. "We heard a scream."
"That was me." Miss Bishop smiled. "Mrs. Sweet startled me."
Henry traded an amused look with Maggie. They both knew that Miss Bishop was a very dramatic person.
"I see," Jackson said. "Mrs. Sweet, can I talk to you?"
"Of course." Mrs. Sweet shot Miss Bishop a suspicious look. "Just let me lock my shed first. I wouldn't want anyone wandering in and getting a look at my float."
Miss Bishop rolled her eyes. "Why would anyone want to do that?"
Soon Miss Bishop returned to her shop. Henry, Maggie, Jackson, and Mrs. Sweet headed into the Sweet Shop.
"I heard you had some trouble last night," Jackson said to Mrs. Sweet. He pulled out a notebook and pen. "Someone broke into your shed?"
"Yes." Mrs. Sweet shook her head. "It was a terrible shock."
"What happened?" Maggie blurted out. "Did someone sabotage your float?"
"I'm not sure." Mrs. Sweet looked troubled. "I left the shed unlocked last night so Mr. Newman could stop by on his way home from work. I needed him to fix the taillight on my tractor."
"Mr. Newman from the auto repair shop?" Henry asked.
"Yes, that's right," Mrs. Sweet said. "He's a good mechanic, isn't he? In any case, I went to check the float this morning. The taillight was fixed, but a whole case of candy was missing!"
"Candy?" Jackson looked confused.
"Yes." Mrs. Sweet leaned forward. "I was going to use it to decorate my float," she whispered.
Henry covered his mouth to hide his smile. Mrs. Sweet was whispering, acting as if everything was top secret. But she decorated her float with candy every single year!
"There have been some problems with raccoons around town lately," Jackson said. "Or perhaps a stray dog."
"I don't think it was an animal." Mrs. Sweet said, frowning. "The shed door wasn't locked, but it was shut tightly. The latch can only be opened by a person."
"I see." Jackson jotted a few notes, and then tucked his notebook away. "Well, give me a call if you think of anything else."
Henry and Maggie followed the reporter outside.
"Is that it?" Maggie asked. "Aren't you going to examine the crime scene?"
Jackson looked surprised. "That's a job for the police, not for me."
"But we thought you'd want to get to the bottom of the story," Henry said. "Why don't you go interview Mr. Newman?"
Jackson shrugged. "I suppose I could. The auto repair shop is on my way back to the office."

Soon the three of them were at Newman's Auto Shop. Henry had known Mr. Newman all his life. Henry's parents said the people of Belltown were lucky to have such an honest and hardworking mechanic in town.
Mr. Newman listened to why Jackson was there. "What do you want to know?" he asked in his usual gruff way.
"Did you stop by to fix Mrs. Sweet's taillight last night?" Jackson asked.
Mr. Newman nodded. "Fixed the light and then went home."
"Did you see a case of candy near the float?" Maggie asked.
"Didn't notice. I was there to fix the light, not to sightsee." Mr. Newman checked his watch. "Is there anything else? I have work to do."
"No, there's nothing else. Thanks for your time," Jackson said.
"Wait," Maggie said as Jackson turned to leave. "Mr. Newman, are you making a float for the parade?"
Mr. Newman looked surprised. "Of course not. I don't have time for that sort of silliness." He hurried off.
"Sorry, kids," Jackson said. "It looks like there's no mystery here."
"What about the missing candy?" Maggie asked.
"And that threat?" Henry added.
"Threat? What threat?" Jackson asked.
Henry realized they'd never told the reporter about the comment on the website. He quickly filled Jackson in.
Jackson pulled out his smartphone and opened the website. "I don't see any threatening comments."
"I'll show you." Henry took the phone and scrolled through the comments. The ones from Mrs. Sweet and Miss Bishop were there, along with several others.
But the threatening comment was gone!
"Are you sure the threatening comment is gone?" Maggie asked.

"It's no big deal, kids." Jackson sounded distracted. "Maybe the mayor deleted it." He pulled out his notebook. "I think I'll talk to the police and see if they found anything suspicious in Mrs. Sweet's shed. You kids should go home and work on your float."
"Are you sure you don't want any help?" Henry asked. "The Lemonade Detectives have solved lots of mysteries."
Jackson smiled. "I know, Henry. But don't worry. If there's really a mystery here, I'll get to the bottom of it."
He rushed off, whistling cheerfully. Henry glanced at Maggie. "Should we follow him and try to talk him into letting us hear what the police say?"
"No, Jackson is right," Maggie said. "We need to finish our float, or we'll never win those prizes."
"I guess you're right." Henry smiled. "Maybe I just miss solving mysteries so much that I was hoping we'd found another one!"
Maggie shrugged. "Not me. Nobody is offering to pay our detective fee. That means we don't have time to investigate."
The two of them headed out of the auto shop. Right outside Henry spotted Snake leaning against a lamppost.
"Hi, Snake," Henry said. "Is your band's float ready for the parade tomorrow?"
"Hi, Lemonade Kids." Snake sighed. "We're not doing a float after all."
"Really? What happened?" Maggie asked.
"Our practice was going great yesterday," Snake said. "We were all having so much fun that we forgot about the time. One member of the band got grounded for coming home late."
"Wow, that's too bad," Henry said. "So the whole band is dropping out of the parade?"
"We don't have much choice." Snake shrugged. "Our music wouldn't sound right without all of us playing."
"Oh. Well . . . sorry," Henry said. "See you around."
He and Maggie wandered off. Maggie glanced back to make sure Snake was out of earshot.
"Snake looked pretty upset," she said. "But this is good news for us. It means we'll have less competition for those prizes!"

Henry nodded, but he wasn't really listening. He'd just noticed the town hall building up ahead. "Jackson said Mayor Porter might have deleted that threatening comment from the website," he said. "Maybe we should stop in and ask the mayor if that's true."
Maggie looked uncertain. "Do you still think there's a mystery going on?"
"I don't know," Henry said. "It's possible that the threatening comment was a joke, and Mrs. Sweet just misplaced her candy. But it's also possible that someone is trying to ruin the parade."
"Okay," Maggie said. "But let's hurry. I want to get back to our float soon."
They went into the town hall building. The mayor's secretary was a cheerful young man named Mr. Beck.
"I'm sorry, kids," he said after Henry and Maggie asked to see the mayor. "Mayor Porter has meetings all afternoon. I can make an appointment for you on Monday, if you like."
"Monday's too late," Maggie said. "It's about the parade tomorrow."
Henry nodded. "It might be important."
"Might be?" Mr. Beck echoed. "What do you mean?"

"We're afraid someone might be trying to sabotage the parade," Henry said. "Mrs. Sweet thinks someone broke into her shed last night. And there was a threatening message in the comments on the town website."
"Oh dear. Really?" Mr. Beck quickly opened the town website on his computer. "I didn't notice anything like that when I was updating the site a few minutes ago."
"You mean you didn't delete the comment?" Maggie asked.
"Only the person who leaves the comment can delete it." Mr. Beck sounded skeptical now. "What did you kids see?"
"There was a message right after the one by Miss Bishop," Henry explained. "It said the parade was for losers, and the mayor should cancel it, or else."
"Hmm." A second later Mr. Beck closed the town website page. "Well, I'll mention the comment to the mayor when I see him."
Henry could tell the secretary wasn't taking this seriously. "But what if—," he began.
"This is an outrage!" an angry shout interrupted him. An older, white-haired man had just stomped into the office. He looked familiar, but Henry didn't know his name.
"Good afternoon, Mr. Fleming," Mr. Beck greeted the older man. "Is something wrong?"

"You bet your life something's wrong!" Mr. Fleming pushed past Henry and Maggie and glared at the secretary. "The window of my art studio overlooks an empty lot. I like it that way—very quiet. But this week the high school soccer team has been building a float there. So there's been hammering, sawing, shouting, and laughing all day long. I can't take it anymore! If someone doesn't do something, I'll sue the town to call off the parade!"
"Calm down, please, Mr. Fleming. Come with me." Mr. Beck stood up. "You kids should run along."
The secretary led the older man away. Henry and Maggie wandered outside.
"That was weird," Maggie said. "Mr. Fleming seemed really mad. Maybe he's the one who made the threatening comment on the website!"
"That's exactly what I was thinking." Henry frowned. "But why would he steal Mrs. Sweet's candy? And if he left that comment, why would he delete it if he's still mad?"
"I don't know," Maggie said. "We should tell Jackson about this, though. Maybe he can figure it out." She looked at the town clock. "It's getting late. We need to finish our float."
"Okay, let's go," Henry said. "We'll tell Jackson about Mr. Fleming the next time we see him."
They walked back to the lemonade stand. Nathan was there with Cole. Henry and Maggie quickly told them what they'd found out during their trip into town.
"I know Mr. Fleming," Cole said when they finished. "He lives on my block."
"Is he always that cranky?" Maggie asked.
Cole shrugged. "Yeah, he's pretty cranky. But my mom says he's like a yappy dog. His bark is worse than his bite."
"Do you think he could have left that nasty website comment?" Henry asked. "Or stolen Mrs. Sweet's candy?"
"I doubt he'd steal anything," Cole said. "I don't know about the comment."
Maggie looked restless. "If you guys want to keep talking about this, let's do it while we work on our float," she said. "Nathan, can you watch the lemonade stand?"
Nathan agreed, and The Lemonade Detectives headed into Maggie's house. Her father was in the backyard putting gasoline into the lawn tractor.
"Are you ready for tomorrow, Dad?" Maggie asked.
"Almost." Her father scratched his head. "There's just one problem. I've looked everywhere, but I can't find the hitch pin."
"What's a hitch pin?" Cole asked.
"It's the part that attaches our float to the tractor," Henry explained. "We'll definitely need it for the parade tomorrow. Maybe I should go over to Newman's Auto Shop and get another one."
"Good idea, Henry." Maggie's dad pulled some bills out of his pocket. "This should be enough money to buy a new one."
Soon Henry was biking to the auto shop. When he arrived, a fancy black convertible was parked out front. Its hood was up, and Mr. Newman was looking at the engine.
"Hi, Mr. Newman," Henry said. "Isn't that the mayor's car?"
Mr. Newman nodded. "He dropped it off for a tune-up so it will be ready for tomorrow's parade."
Henry told Mr. Newman what he needed. Mr. Newman pointed inside.
"My daughter is in the office," he said. "She'll help you."
"Thanks." Henry went inside. He immediately recognized the girl in the office. "Oh, hi, Jade," he said. "I forgot that Mr. Newman is your dad."
"Yeah, lucky me," Jade muttered. She sounded grouchy. "What do you want?"
Henry told her. Jade grabbed a hitch pin out of a bin behind the counter.
"Thanks," Henry said, handing her the money. "By the way, Snake told me your band had to drop out of the parade. Sorry about that."
"I'm not sorry," Jade snapped. "Snake's the one who wanted to sign up for the parade. He thought being on TV would help our band get famous."

Just then Mr. Newman entered. "What's taking so long?" he asked Jade with a frown. "You're supposed to be helping me with the mayor's car. I need to drop it off at the high school parking lot by the end of the day."
"The high school parking lot?" Henry said. "Why are you taking it there?"
Mr. Newman shrugged. "That's where the parade starts. I suppose the mayor wants it waiting there for him when everyone gathers for the parade tomorrow afternoon."
"I'll be out to help you in a minute. I'm waiting on a customer," Jade told her father, waving toward Henry.
"Well, stop gossiping about your silly band and finish up," Mr. Newman said. "Maybe you'll be a rock star someday, but for right now you have a job to do."
"Whatever," Jade muttered. "Here's your change, Henry." She shoved some coins at Henry and then stomped out of the office with a scowl.
Soon Henry was back on his bike, heading for home. As he passed the newspaper office, he saw Jackson near the entrance.
"Hi there!" Henry called, stopping his bike. "I'm glad I ran into you. Something weird happened a little while ago."
He told Jackson about Mr. Fleming's visit to the mayor's office.
Jackson nodded. "Yes, I already heard about that," he said. "I also just heard that the mayor is seriously thinking about canceling the parade!"
"The mayor might cancel the parade?" Henry exclaimed. "Why? Does he think that threat on the website was serious? Or did Mr. Fleming talk him into canceling the parade?"
Jackson shrugged. "I don't know. I didn't hear it from the mayor. I was talking to Miss Bishop. She's the one who told me."
"How did she hear about it?" Henry asked.

"I'm not sure. I couldn't talk to her for very long because I had to leave for a meeting." Jackson checked his watch. "Speaking of which, I've got to get inside or I'll be late." He hurried into the newspaper office.

Henry thought about what Jackson had just said. Should Miss Bishop be a suspect? She seemed determined to win the contest for best float. She seemed especially interested in beating Mrs. Sweet. Could Miss Bishop be the one who'd tampered with Mrs. Sweet's float?
Then Henry remembered the threatening website message. Why would Miss Bishop do something like that? If she wanted to win, it didn't make sense for her to try to shut down the whole parade.
Henry started walking his bike down the sidewalk. The jewelry store was up ahead. He decided to stop in and talk to Miss Bishop.
A little bell over the door jingled when Henry entered the jewelry store. Nobody was inside except Miss Bishop. She was wiping a display case with a rag.
"Oh, hello, Henry," she said. "Did you come to buy your mother a diamond necklace?"
Henry smiled politely as Miss Bishop laughed at her own joke. "No, sorry," he said. "Our lemonade business doesn't make quite enough money for that."
"Too bad." Miss Bishop smiled, and then sighed. "I could really use some new customers. Business has been slow this summer."
"Oh," Henry said. "That's a shame."

"Yes, that's why I decided to enter a float in the parade this year," Miss Bishop said. "I thought it would be good publicity. And if I win the popular vote contest, I'll get to be on TV. That's like winning a free ad for my store."
"You must be worried about the mayor canceling the parade then," Henry said.
"What?" Miss Bishop looked alarmed. "The mayor is canceling the parade? Who told you that?"
"Jackson, the reporter from the newspaper," Henry said. "He said you told him that."
"I told him no such thing!" Miss Bishop exclaimed. "He must be thinking of someone else. Do you think it's true? Why would the mayor cancel the parade?"
Henry wasn't sure what to say for a moment. He was confused by Miss Bishop's reaction. She seemed very surprised and upset.
"Was Jackson here talking to you earlier?" Henry asked.
Miss Bishop nodded. "Yes, he stopped by a few minutes ago, and we had a nice chat. I was telling him about my business problems."
"And you didn't say anything about the parade?" Henry asked.

"I did mention the parade, but I didn't say anything about the mayor canceling it," Miss Bishop said. "I told Jackson that I was hoping my float would bring me more customers. And that if it didn't, I might have to shut down my store."

"Oh." Suddenly Henry had a brainstorm. "I bet I know what happened. You told Jackson you might have to shut down your store. But Jackson thought you were talking about the mayor shutting down the parade."
"Hmm." Miss Bishop looked unsure. "That seems odd. But Jackson did seem to be in a hurry. Maybe he wasn't listening closely."

As Henry left the store, he wondered if Jackson had really misunderstood Miss Bishop's comment. The young reporter was always looking for exciting news stories. What if he was the one trying to get the parade shut down? That would definitely give Jackson an interesting story to write about.

Henry thought some more about his theory as he biked toward Maggie's house. Jackson could have posted that threatening message on the website just as easily as anyone else. He could have broken into Mrs. Sweet's shed. And he was definitely the one spreading the rumor about the parade being canceled—either by accident or on purpose.
When Henry reached Maggie's house, Maggie and Cole were putting away their craft supplies.
"What took you so long?" Maggie asked Henry. "It's dinnertime. We'll have to finish the float in the morning."
"Sorry," Henry said. "I ended up doing a little extra investigating on my way home from the auto shop."
He told his friends about his trip to town. When he explained his theory about Jackson being the culprit, Cole looked worried.
"If Jackson is a suspect now, we can't count on him to solve the mystery," he said.
Henry nodded. "You know what that means," he said. "We'll have to solve it ourselves!"
The next morning the Lemonade Detectives discussed the mystery as they put the finishing touches on their float.
"Let's list everything suspicious that's happened," Henry suggested.
"Okay," Cole said. "The first thing we found out about was that threat on the website."
"True," Henry said. "But that wasn't the first thing that happened. The threat appeared sometime yesterday. Mrs. Sweet's candy disappeared before that, on Thursday night."
"Don't forget Mr. Fleming's threat," Maggie said. "That happened yesterday too."
"So did Jackson's comment about the parade being cancelled," Henry finished. "So who are our suspects?"
"Jackson," Cole said. "If your theory is right, he could be trying to create an interesting story to write about."
"Yeah," Maggie said. "I think Snake is a better suspect, though."
"Snake?" Henry had forgotten about the teenager. "Why?" Henry asked Maggie. "His band isn't even making a float anymore."
"Exactly," Maggie said. "This stuff started happening after the band dropped out of the parade. Maybe Snake is mad about dropping out. And now he doesn't want anyone else to win those prizes either."
"Maybe," Henry said. "I guess we should keep him on the list. Who else?"
"Mr. Newman," Cole said.
"What about him?" Maggie asked.
Cole shrugged. "He was in Mrs. Sweet's shed the night her candy disappeared."
"True," Henry said. "The rumor Jackson started and the threat from Mr. Fleming could be red herrings—false clues that are confusing us. Why do you think Mr. Newman should be a suspect?"
"You said his daughter is in Snake's band," Cole said. "Maybe Mr. Newman wanted to sabotage other floats because of that."
"Maybe," Henry said. "But he didn't seem very excited about the band when I heard him talking to Jade."
"Yeah," Maggie agreed. "But what about Miss Bishop? She was sneaking around Mrs. Sweet's shed yesterday."
"True," Cole said. "But she has no reason to want the parade cancelled. So she probably didn't post that threat on the website."
"I guess you're right," Henry agreed. "That leaves one more suspect: Mr. Fleming."
Maggie nodded. "He definitely wants the parade shut down."
"But why would he steal Mrs. Sweet's candy?" Henry asked.
"Who knows?" Cole grabbed a bottle of glue. "Let's finish our float and then go try to find out. We still have a few hours to investigate before the parade starts."

An hour later The Lemonade Detectives waved to Maggie's dad as he drove away down the street on his tractor. The float was on the cart behind him. It was covered in a sheet so nobody would see it until the parade started.
"I'll meet you kids at the high school at three o'clock," Maggie's dad said.
"See you then," Henry called back. "Thanks, Uncle Bruce!"
Henry and his friends walked to Mr. Fleming's house. A plump older woman was out in the yard watering some flowers.
"That's his wife," Cole whispered to the others. Then he waved to the woman. "Hi, Mrs. Fleming!"
"Oh, hello, Cole!" Mrs. Fleming put down her watering can and hurried over. "It's so nice to see you! Are you excited for the parade this afternoon?"
"Definitely," Cole said.
"We heard your husband isn't very happy about the parade," Henry put in. "He thinks everyone is being too noisy building their floats."

Mrs. Fleming sighed. "Yes, I know. He's been complaining all week. He hates noise. He's always yelling at the neighbors about their barking dogs or their loud lawn mowers." She smiled at the kids. "He's really a nice man, though. Too much noise just makes him cranky."
Maggie stepped forward. "Do you think he was crabby enough to post a threatening message on the town website?" she asked.
Mrs. Fleming chuckled. "Oh my, no," she said. "My husband hates computers. He won't touch one unless he has to. He even asks me to send emails to his clients for him."
"Yes, that's true," Henry said. "Sorry to bother you, Mrs. Fleming."
"It's no bother at all." Mrs. Fleming waved as they walked away. "Enjoy the parade, kids!"
"She's a lot nicer than her husband," Maggie said as The Lemonade Detectives headed down the sidewalk.
"Yeah," Henry said. "It sounds like Mr. Fleming isn't the culprit. He hates computers, so he probably wouldn't have posted that threat."
Cole nodded. "Plus, it's hard to imagine him breaking into Mrs. Sweet's shed. So who should we investigate next?"
"How about Jackson?" Henry suggested. "Let's go to the newspaper office and see if he's there."
Soon they reached the office.
"I'm sorry, kids," the receptionist told them. "Jackson isn't here. He just rushed out. He said there's some urgent breaking news that will make the newspaper's front page!"
"Urgent breaking news?" Henry said. "What is it?"
"I don't know," the receptionist said. "Jackson didn't give me many details. He just said he was heading to the corner of Pine and Church Streets."
"That's in our neighborhood," Henry said. "Let's go!"
The Lemonade Detectives rushed out of the newspaper office.
"What if Jackson is sabotaging our float?" Maggie exclaimed. "He might have crashed a car into it while Dad was driving it to the high school. And now he's pretending to cover the story!"
"I doubt it," Henry said. But he felt a flutter of nervousness too. Maggie could be right.
They rushed to the corner of Pine and Church Streets. As they got closer, they saw a fire truck parked there.
"Oh no!" Maggie cried. "What if Jackson set our float on fire?"
"I don't smell smoke," said Cole.
A ladder was leaning against a tree. A fire fighter was near the top of the ladder. Jackson was watching from below, along with a small crowd.
"What's happening?" Henry asked Jackson.
Jackson grinned. "It's big news. Tiny's cat got stuck in that tree. When Tiny climbed up to rescue her, he got stuck too."
Henry looked up. Tiny was handing a cute calico cat to the fire fighter. After the cat was safely on the ground, the fire fighter helped Tiny down the ladder.
"Thanks, guys." Tiny looked sheepish. "Sorry for the trouble."
The fire fighters laughed. "No problem," one said. "This is our favorite kind of emergency—one that isn't serious!"
Tiny laughed too. Then he noticed that Jackson had a camera. "Uh-oh, am I going to be in tomorrow's newspaper?"
"Definitely." Jackson replied. "I'm sure this will be the story of the weekend! Can I take some photos of you?"
Tiny grinned. "Sure. If you wait a second, I'll get my cat to pose for a photo too."
Everyone laughed. Then Tiny wandered off to look for his cat, while the fire fighters put their ladder away. The Lemonade Detectives stayed with Jackson.
"So this was your urgent breaking news?" Cole said. "We thought it was something important about the parade."
"Yeah," Maggie agreed. "Aren't you hoping something else happens? Like more sabotage, or the parade gets canceled?"
"Of course not." Jackson looked confused. "Why would I want that?"
"Never mind," Henry said quickly. "Come on, guys. Let's go." He led his friends away from Tiny's house.
"I guess Jackson isn't the culprit," Maggie said. "Neither is Mr. Fleming."
Cole nodded. "Who should we investigate next?"
"Nobody," Maggie said. "It's almost two-thirty. Time to go to the parade."
Henry felt uneasy about leaving the mystery unsolved. But they didn't have much choice. Maggie was right—they were out of time.
"Wow," Cole said as The Lemonade Detectives rode their bikes into the high school parking lot. "There are lots of people here!"
"And lots of floats," Henry added. "I guess everyone wants to win those prizes."
"But we're going to win them," Maggie said confidently.

As he looked around for their float, Henry saw many people he knew. Jill and Ashley were there with their soccer team. They were climbing onto their float while some other teenagers watched. Henry spotted Tiny and his friends and Snake and his band.
"Look." Cole pointed to a float decorated with candy in bright colors. "There's Mrs. Sweet."
"Hi, Mrs. Sweet," Henry called. "Your float looks great."
She beamed. "Thank you, Henry. Oh, and guess what—I found that missing candy."
"You found the candy?" Maggie exclaimed. "But I thought someone stole it out of your shed."
Mrs. Sweet looked sheepish. "I thought so too. But it was in the trunk of my car all along. Silly me!"
Henry smiled weakly. "See you later," he said, dragging his friends away.
"Wow," Cole said. "I guess Mr. Fleming's threat wasn't the only red herring in this mystery! Nobody was trying to ruin Mrs. Sweet's float."
"Yeah," Henry said. "The only problem left is the threat on the website."
"I wonder if that threat was even real," Cole said. "Whoever wrote it deleted it pretty quickly."
"Look, there's Dad," Maggie cried. "Come on, let's go!"
Soon the parade began. The Lemonade Detectives' float was right behind the mayor's car. It seemed as if everyone in Belltown was gathered along Main Street to watch and cheer.
"This is fun," Cole said, waving to the crowd.
"Yeah." Henry smiled as he saw Mr. and Mrs. Fleming watching the parade. By now he'd decided that this case was no mystery at all.
Everyone seemed to like The Lemonade Detectives' float. "Mom!" Henry heard a boy cry. "Look at that giant lemon!"
Suddenly the mayor's car sputtered to an abrupt stop.
"Oh no!" the mayor cried. "Something is wrong with my car!"
"What's going on?" someone shouted.
"My car just stopped!" the mayor exclaimed.
Several people rushed toward the mayor's car, including Mr. Newman. After a moment Mr. Newman let out a shout.
"The car is out of gas," he announced.
The mayor frowned. "You said you filled it before you dropped it off at the parking lot last night."
"I did." Mr. Newman looked perplexed.
"Maybe there's a hole in the gas tank," someone called out.
More people gathered around the car. Henry and his friends watched from their float.
"Uh-oh," Maggie blurted out. "It looks like that threat is coming true!"
"The car was parked at the high school all night," Cole said. "Someone could have sneaked in and drained most of the gas. That way the car would stall after a few minutes."
"And mess up the parade," Henry finished. "That's exactly what I was thinking. But who could have done that?"
"What about Jackson?" Cole suggested. "He knew all about the parade plans because of his newspaper story. So he probably knew the mayor's car was parked at the high school."
"Mr. Newman knew too." Maggie shot a look at the auto shop owner, who was under the car, checking the gas tank. "Maybe he didn't really fill the mayor's gas tank."
"But Mr. Newman doesn't have a motive for ruining the parade," Henry reminded her.
"I know someone who has a motive." Maggie pointed toward the shops. "We're stopped right in front of Miss Bishop's store. Maybe that was her plan all along—to get people to notice her store!"
"Maybe," Cole said. Then he grinned. "But I can't imagine Miss Bishop getting her hands dirty by draining gas from a tank!"
"Why not?" Maggie challenged him. "Because she's a woman? Lots of girls and women know how to drain gas."
Cole shrugged. "That's true. I'm just not sure Miss Bishop is one of them. She wouldn't want to mess up her manicure."
Henry gasped. "That's it!"
"What?" Cole asked. "Is Miss Bishop the culprit?"
"No, but I'm pretty sure I know who is." Henry peered into the watching crowd, and then smiled. "Come with me!"
He jumped down from the float and led his friends toward Snake and his band. The band was watching from the sidewalk as Mr. Newman and others checked the mayor's car.
Maggie gasped when she saw them. "It was Snake, wasn't it?" she whispered. "I knew it!"
"No, it wasn't Snake." Henry stopped in front of the band. "Hi, guys. Jade, can I talk to you?"
"What is it?" Jade sounded sullen.
Henry took a deep breath. "You did it, didn't you?" he said. "You left that threat on the website, and you emptied the gas tank."
Jade gasped. "How did you know?" she blurted out. Then she covered her mouth. "Um, I mean, I don't know what you're talking about!"
Snake and the other band members looked confused.
"What's going on?" Snake asked. "Jade, what's the Lemonade Kid talking about?"
"Nothing," Jade muttered, glaring at Henry.
"So Jade is our culprit?" Cole said. "How'd you know that, Henry?"

"It was what Maggie said about girls being able to drain gas," Henry said. "That's when I remembered that Jade works at her father's garage. So she probably knows all about stuff like that. I also remembered that Mr. Newman is pretty strict. So I figured Jade was the band member who got grounded for being late."
"Yeah, so what?" Eddie said. "That doesn't prove anything."
Snake nodded. "It wasn't Jade's fault she got grounded. We talked her into staying late."

"Okay," Henry said. "But I think she still felt guilty about making the band drop out of the parade. So she left that threat on the website. Then she messed with the mayor's car to try to ruin the parade."
"I'm sorry!" Jade burst into tears. "I was just mad, that's all. I was only ten minutes late to work! Why does my dad have to be so strict?"
Snake stared at her. "So you did this?" He waved a hand toward the mayor's car. "Not cool, Jade."
"I know." Jade sniffled.
"You've got to tell the mayor you did it," Henry said. "Otherwise he might blame your dad."
Jade sniffled again. "Okay," she mumbled. "I'll go confess right now."

Soon someone brought more gas for the mayor's car, and the parade continued. In the end Mrs. Sweet won the mayor's prize, and Miss Bishop won the popular vote. Henry thought Maggie might be mad that The Lemonade Detectives hadn't won either prize.
But Maggie didn't mind a bit. Because The Lemonade Detectives still got interviewed on TV. They were the kid detectives who'd solved the parade mystery!
"Wow, there are a lot of people here," Cole said.
"I know." Maggie sounded happy. "We might need to make more lemonade."

Henry smiled. It had been Maggie's idea to set up their lemonade stand at the park for Belltown Arts Day. She'd thought they would make lots of money. And it looked like she was right. The stand had been busy all morning long.

Belltown Arts Day was a popular tradition in Belltown. It was a whole day of art, music, and crafts for all ages. There was a crafts fair at one end of the park. People had set up booths there to display crafts like glassblowing and basket weaving.

At the other end of the park, right in front of the Belltown Museum of Art, was an art show. Anyone could enter a painting, sculpture, or other piece of art in the show. That afternoon a committee of experts was going to judge all the pieces. The pieces that won first place would be displayed in the museum for the rest of the year.

The bandstand in the middle of the park featured a full schedule of musical acts and dance groups. Right now a fiddler was playing a lively tune. Henry, Maggie, and Cole had set up the lemonade stand near the bandstand.
Cole tapped his foot along with the music. "Here come some more customers," he said.
For the next few minutes, The Lemonade Detectives stayed busy pouring lemonade and collecting money. When the last customer wandered off, Henry turned to his friends.
"We should look for Nathan," he said. "I want to see his painting before the judging starts."
"Me too," Cole agreed. "I heard it's really good."
Their friend Nathan was a talented artist. This was his first year entering the art show. He was competing in the Age 12 and Under category. The other two categories were for teenagers and adults.
