Maggie looked around. "I guess we can take a short break," she said. "I want to see Nathan's painting too. His little sister, Nora, can't stop talking about it."
Cole laughed. "Nora can never stop talking!" he joked. "She talks more than any other little kid I know."
The Lemonade Detectives set out a Closed sign. Then they headed across the crowded park to the art show.
They found Nathan standing in front of his painting. Nora was sitting on the ground, playing with a doll. Nathan's mom was chatting with a friend nearby.
Nathan was talking to a red-haired boy named Patrick and his parents. Patrick was in the grade below Henry, Cole, and Nathan.
"Hi, Patrick," Henry greeted him. "Did you enter the art show too?"
"Of course," Patrick said. "I enter the show every year. My painting came in third place last year."
"Wow." Nathan sounded impressed. "I'd be thrilled to come in third place."
Patrick looked at Nathan's painting. Henry looked closely too. Nathan had painted a very good watercolor of a calico cat.
"I'm sorry to say this, Nathan, but you probably won't win," Patrick declared. "Art judges don't usually like pictures of animals."
Maggie frowned. "I think Nathan's cat painting is amazing!"
Nora looked up. "Are you talking about my kitty?"
"Your kitty?" Henry looked at the painting again. "Oh, I get it. It's a painting of Patches." That was the name of Nora's pet cat.
"You should try painting a landscape next year, Nathan," Patrick went on. "That's what I did. My art teacher thinks I'll win first place this year."
"We'll see about that," Maggie told Patrick. "If Patches winds up in the museum and your painting doesn't, you'll regret bragging!"
Nora's eyes widened. "No!" she blurted out. "Patches can't live in the museum. She lives in my room with me!"
"Don't worry," Henry told her. "We're not talking about sending Patches away to live in the museum. Just the painting of her."
Nora still looked upset. "Nathan said I could hang the painting in my room after the show. She's my kitty, so I should have the painting!"
"It's okay, Nora," Nathan said. "I'm sure my painting won't win anyway."
Just then another kid ran up to them. His name was Owen, and he was one of Patrick's friends.
"Guess what, you guys?" Owen said. He stopped to take a big breath. "I just heard the judges talking about the paintings they liked!"
"Really?" Nathan sounded surprised. "I thought judging didn't start until two o'clock."

"It doesn't. But I guess they walked through the show and saw some of the artwork already," Owen said. "All three judges were talking about how good Nathan's cat painting is. It sounds like he might win!"
"Wow!" Cole exclaimed. "That's awesome, Nathan. The judges really like your painting!"
But Patrick was frowning at Owen. "Are you sure you heard the judges right?" he demanded. "Did they mention my painting?"
Owen shrugged. "Not while I was listening."
Maggie smirked. "Too bad, Patrick," she said. "Come on, guys. We'd better get back to the lemonade stand."
Henry and Cole followed her.
"Do you think Nathan might actually win?" Cole asked.
Henry shrugged. "He might. His painting is really good."
Near the lemonade stand the fiddler had finished his performance. Now several bongo drummers were setting up their equipment on the bandstand.
"It looks like we don't have any customers," Cole said. "Want to check out the crafts fair?"
"Sure," Henry said.
"Okay," Maggie agreed. "But we shouldn't stay away for long. We'll probably have more customers when the music starts up again."
The crafts fair was crowded and colorful. There were lots of interesting handmade items for sale everywhere Henry looked. Some of the booths featured demonstrations or classes too.
Henry stopped to watch a woman churning butter by hand. Meanwhile Maggie waved at someone in the basket-weaving booth across the way.
"Look," Maggie said. "There's Hannah."
A dark-haired girl was sitting on a stool, weaving grasses into the shape of a large, flat basket. She looked up when The Lemonade Detectives approached.
"Oh hi," Hannah said, pushing her hair out of her eyes. "It's the lemonade gang."
"Hi." Maggie smiled at Hannah, looking at the basket in Hannah's lap. "Your parents have a booth every year, don't they?"

Hannah nodded. "They look forward to Belltown Arts Day all year. They love showing off their baskets and teaching people about weaving." She pointed into the booth. Her parents were helping a young boy weave a small, round basket.
Henry stepped inside. The booth was filled with baskets of every size, shape, and color.
"Wow," Henry said. "These baskets are really cool."
Cole grinned. "Look, this one has a picture of a cat woven into it," he said. "Just like Nathan's painting! Did you make it, Hannah?"
She nodded. "I love cats."
"You should enter it in the art show," said Maggie.

Hannah frowned. "No way. Those snobby art people don't want anything from the crafts booths in their contest. That's why the organizers made sure the crafts show was stuck way over here at the opposite end of the park."
Henry was surprised. Hannah sounded really annoyed.
"Not all artists are snobby," Maggie reminded Hannah. "Our friend Nathan is really nice. He's a painter who might win the Under Twelve category this year."
Hannah shrugged. "Whatever," she muttered, staring at the basket in her lap.

Cole was digging through a bin full of small, colorful baskets. "Hey, how much is this one?" he asked, holding up one of the baskets. "I just remembered my mom's birthday is next week. She loves handmade stuff like this."
Hannah told him the price, and Cole dug some money out of his pocket. Meanwhile Maggie grabbed Henry's phone to check the time.
"Come on, you guys," she said as Hannah slipped Cole's basket into a small shopping bag. "We should get back to the lemonade stand."
"Okay," Henry said. "See you, Hannah."
"Bye," Hannah said. "Maybe I'll come by for some lemonade later if I have time."

Back at the lemonade stand, Henry and the others were busy for a while serving thirsty customers. They knew all the customers. But then a stranger appeared. She was a very tall, very thin woman dressed in a shiny green dress. Her bright red hair was piled high atop her head and held in place with sparkly barrettes. Enormous white-framed sunglasses covered half her face.
"One lemonade, please," she said, setting a quarter on the table.
"Coming right up." Henry picked up a pitcher. "And welcome to Belltown."
The woman peered at him over the top of her sunglasses. Her eyes were suspicious. "What do you mean by that?" she demanded. "How do you know I don't live here?"
Henry traded a surprised look with Maggie and Cole.
"It was a guess," Henry replied. "Because we know almost everybody in town."
"Yeah," Cole added. "Belltown is not very big."
"How did you hear about Belltown Arts Day?" Maggie asked the woman. "I didn't think it was very famous."
"Famous? What would someone like you know about being famous?" the woman snapped. Suddenly she spun around and rushed away.
Cole stared after her. "What a weirdo!"
"Yeah." Maggie picked up the quarter the woman had left. "She didn't even wait for her lemonade."
Henry didn't answer. He'd just noticed Nathan rushing toward them, looking very upset.
Nathan skidded to a stop in front of the stand. "My painting," he cried. "It's gone!"
"What do you mean, your painting is gone?" Henry asked Nathan. "Where did it go?"
"I don't know." Nathan sounded upset. "That's what I need The Lemonade Detectives to figure out!"
Cole handed him some lemonade. "Here, drink this," he said. "Then tell us what happened."
Nathan gulped down the lemonade. "I wanted to get a snack before the judging started," he said. "I left the art show for a few minutes to go to the taco stand. When I got back, my painting was gone!"
"How could it just disappear?" Maggie asked. "There were all kinds of people around. Somebody must have seen what happened."
Nathan shook his head. "Nora wandered off a little while ago. My mom went to look for her. So they weren't there when it disappeared." He looked upset. "Will you guys take the case?"
"Of course," Henry said. "Let's go take a look at the scene of the crime."
They closed the lemonade stand and walked over to the art show. The spot where Nathan's painting had hung was empty.
Nathan bit his lip. "What do you think happened to my painting?"
"That's what we need to find out." Henry looked around. There were other paintings hanging nearby. "Did you ask any of the other artists if they saw anything?"
Nathan nodded. "There weren't many people nearby. Nobody saw a thing."
"Why would someone steal a painting?" Maggie wondered. "Wait, I know! What about Patrick?"
Henry nodded. "I was about to ask the same thing. Patrick seems suspicious to me."
Cole nodded. "Patrick seemed mad when Owen told us what the judges said about Nathan's painting. Patrick might be trying to knock out the competition."
Maggie clenched her fists. "Let's go talk to him!"
"Wait." Henry turned to Nathan. "Has anyone else said anything about your painting?"
Nathan shrugged. "Just Mr. Collins."
"Mr. Collins?" Henry was surprised. Mr. Collins was a barber who entered the art show every year. "What do you mean?"
"He noticed my painting earlier today and seemed kind of upset," Nathan said. "He says it's really similar to his painting."
"Is it similar?" Henry asked.
Nathan shrugged. "I don't know. I haven't seen his painting."
"What are we waiting for?" Maggie said. "Let's go check it out."
It didn't take long to find Mr. Collins' painting.
Cole wrinkled his nose when he saw it. "That doesn't look like your painting at all," he told Nathan.
"Yeah," Maggie agreed. "It looks like a bunch of crazy cubes."

A woman standing nearby heard them and looked over. "Are you talking about Mr. Collins' piece?" she asked. "It's wonderful, isn't it? He calls it Calico at Rest . He has such a way with the Cubist style!"
"It's very nice," Henry said politely. Then he led his friends away. "I guess both paintings have calico cats. But they don't look alike."
"That's for sure!" blurted out Maggie.
"Mr. Collins is pretty sensitive," said Cole. "Maybe he thinks Nathan copied his idea."
"But I didn't!" Nathan protested.
"We know you didn't copy him," Henry assured Nathan. "But Mr. Collins might not. He should probably be on our suspect list."
"And Patrick too, right?" Cole asked.
"Definitely," Henry said. "Nathan and Patrick are in the same age category. That means Patrick has a better motive than Mr. Collins."
Maggie was biting her lip, looking worried. "What about Hannah?" she said.
"What about her?" Cole asked.
"She got upset when we mentioned Nathan's painting earlier, remember?" Maggie said. "And she loves cats."
Henry realized Maggie was right. "Hannah didn't seem to like the painting part of the show," he said. "But I'm not sure that would make her steal Nathan's painting."
Cole shrugged. "We should probably talk to Hannah, just in case."
"I thought of another suspect," Maggie said. "That woman with the big sunglasses. She seemed pretty weird."
"True," Henry said. "But why would she steal Nathan's painting? We don't even know who she is."
"Maybe she's an international art thief." Maggie sounded excited. "She could be lurking around the show, looking for valuable paintings to steal!"
Henry traded a look with Cole and Nathan. Maggie liked to exaggerate things sometimes.
"I doubt the woman is a thief," Henry told Maggie. "But she was acting pretty weird. I guess we can put her on the list of suspects."
Nathan looked impatient. "So what do we do now?"
"We should find our suspects quickly and question them," Henry said.

Before his friends could answer, the PA system came on. "I hope you're all enjoying Belltown Arts Day," the mayor's voice said. "Everyone is very excited to find out the winners of our yearly art show. The official judging will begin in an hour and a half."
"The judging starts in an hour and a half?" Nathan cried. "Oh no! What if we don't find my painting in time?"
"Don't worry. The Lemonade Detectives are on the case," Maggie assured him. "Come on, guys. Let's get started!"
Henry nodded. "First we should look for Patrick near his painting. Then we can look for Mr. Collins."
"Hannah is probably still at her family's booth," Cole added. "And what about that weird woman? We don't know where to find her."
"Maybe she'll go back to the stand for her lemonade," Maggie said. "She already paid for it, remember?"
Henry nodded. "Why don't you go back to the lemonade stand?" he told Maggie. "You can keep selling lemonade while you watch for all our suspects."
"Especially the sunglasses woman," Cole said.
"Good idea." Maggie hurried off.
"I know where Patrick's painting is hanging," Nathan told Henry and Cole. "Come on, I'll show you."
Nathan led the way to another section of the art show. Patrick's painting was an oil painting of a pretty pond at sunset.
"Wow, he really is good," Cole said, studying the painting. "Do you think this painting will end up in the museum?"
"Never mind that," Henry said. "I don't see Patrick around here. Let's look for Hannah."
At the crafts show, Hannah was still at the basket-weaving booth. She smiled when she saw the boys coming.
"Hi, lemonade gang," she said. "Where's Maggie?"
"Selling lemonade," Henry said. "What have you been doing since we saw you last?"
Hannah looked confused. "The same thing I've been doing all day." She held up the basket she was weaving. "Making baskets, selling baskets, and talking about baskets."
"Did you leave this booth to go anywhere?" Cole asked.
"Like over to the art show, for instance?" Nathan added hopefully.
"I went to the bathroom once." Hannah frowned. "Why are you guys so interested in what I've been doing?" Suddenly she gasped. "Wait! Are you investigating a mystery? Am I a suspect?"
Henry sighed. That was the only problem with The Lemonade Detectives' success in solving mysteries. Everyone in town had heard about them by now. It made it hard to interview people.
"Actually, we are investigating a mystery," he admitted. "Nathan's painting disappeared."
"Oh." Hannah stared at Nathan with a slight frown. "You entered the art show?"
"Yes," Nathan said.
"And we heard the judges love his painting," Cole added. "He might end up winning a spot in the museum. It's a huge honor, you know!"
Hannah was still frowning. "Excuse me," she said, tossing her half-woven basket aside. "I have to go."
"Wait!" Henry exclaimed.
But it was too late. Hannah rushed off and disappeared around the corner of the next booth.
"That was weird," Cole said, staring after her. "Do you think she ran off because she feels guilty?"
"Maybe," Henry said. "Or maybe she was insulted that we were accusing her of stealing Nathan's painting."
Nathan bit his lip. "What do we do now? The judging starts in an hour and ten minutes."
"Let's look for our other suspects," Henry said. "We can question Hannah again later if necessary."
They hurried back to the art show. But there was still no sign of Patrick or Mr. Collins.
The park was more crowded than ever as people arrived for the art judging. Every year people in town loved to join the march over to the museum to display the winning artwork.
"Now what?" Cole said.
Henry looked at Nathan. "Why don't you go see if anyone returned your painting?" he said. "Cole and I will check in with Maggie."
"Okay." Nathan didn't look very hopeful as he hurried off.
Maggie was pouring lemonade for a middle-aged couple when Henry and Cole arrived. "Any news?" she asked as soon as the couple left.
Henry shook his head. "We still haven't found Patrick or Mr. Collins. We did find Hannah, but we only talked to her for a minute." He quickly described the encounter with Hannah.
"Have you seen any of our suspects?" Cole asked Maggie.
"Nope." Maggie patted the cashbox. "I've sold a lot of lemonade. But I haven't seen anything suspicious at all."
"The woman with the sunglasses didn't come back for her lemonade?" Henry asked.
"Nope," Maggie said again.
Just then Nora hurried over to the lemonade stand. "It's not right!" she announced loudly. "About the painting of Patches, I mean."
Henry was too distracted to pay much attention to Nora. "We know," he told her. "We're trying to find Nathan's painting. Don't worry."
"No!" Nora's voice was louder than ever. "It's not right! Patches is my kitty. She shouldn't be in a museum. She's mine—all mine! And the picture of her is mine too!"
Spinning around, Nora raced away.
"Nora?" Henry called. "Wait! What are you talking about?"
"Who cares?" Maggie said.
"We care," Henry said. "What if Nora took that painting?"
Cole gasped. "That actually makes sense! Well, as much sense as anything Nora ever does, anyway. Nora seemed really upset when she heard Nathan's painting might end up in the museum."
"Exactly," Henry agreed. "And the stuff she was saying a minute ago made her sound guilty."
"So are we adding her to the suspect list?" asked Maggie.
"Definitely," Cole said. "She's sneaky enough to snatch that painting and hide it somewhere."

"Luckily, we already know she's not very good at covering her tracks," Henry said, smiling. He was talking about an earlier case involving Nora, which had led to her adopting Patches. "Let's go look for clues at the scene of the crime."
"Okay." Maggie put out the Closed sign again. "How much time do we have before judging starts?"
Henry glanced at his phone. "Almost an hour."
They hurried over to the art show. When they arrived at the empty spot where Nathan's painting had been, Nathan wasn't there. But someone else was.
"Hi, Mr. Collins," Henry said. "What are you doing?"
Mr. Collins spun around and laughed sheepishly. "Oh! You startled me."
"Were you looking for Nathan's painting?" Maggie asked.

"Yes, I admit it." Mr. Collins tugged on his flowered tie. "It's been on my mind ever since I saw it this morning. Can you believe two artists found such similar inspiration? Young Nathan's subject could be the twin of mine!"
"Um, okay." Cole sounded doubtful. Henry knew what his friend was thinking. Mr. Collins' crazy cat painting looked nothing like Nathan's!
"What if the judges think your paintings are too similar?" Maggie asked. "Are you worried they might not pick yours for the museum?"

"I suppose not." Mr. Collins winked and smiled. "Nathan and I are not even in the same age category, in case you couldn't tell. I'm just worrying over nothing, as usual! It's the curse of being a sensitive artist." He glanced at the empty spot. "So where is your friend's masterpiece?"
"We're not sure," Henry said. "It disappeared about forty minutes ago."
"Oh dear!" Mr. Collins looked alarmed. "Is there an art thief at the show?"
"Maybe," Cole said. "Have you seen anything suspicious?"
"Where have you been for the past hour?" Maggie demanded before Mr. Collins could respond.
Henry winced. Sometimes Maggie could sound rude when she questioned people!
Mr. Collins looked surprised. "Am I a suspect? Luckily I have an alibi."
"You do?" Henry was glad the man didn't seem insulted.
Mr. Collins nodded. "I've been at Mrs. Sweet's booth for the past hour or so, learning how to make candy. She could tell you that too."
"Okay," Henry said. "Well, we'd better get back to investigating."
The Lemonade Detectives hurried away. "Are we going to check his alibi?" Maggie asked.
Henry shrugged. "I suppose we should, just to be sure. But I bet he's telling the truth."
"Yeah," Cole agreed. "His alibi explains why we couldn't find him earlier."
They walked toward the crafts fair. As they passed the bandstand, Henry spotted Owen.
"Hi," Henry greeted him. "Have you seen Patrick?"

Owen frowned. "Not since I saw you guys earlier," he said. "We were supposed to meet at the crafts fair ten minutes ago. When he didn't show up, I came here to see if he was at the burger stand. But he wasn't."
Just then Henry noticed a tall, thin figure moving through the crowd. "Look," he said. "It's that strange woman!"
"Quick! We have to catch her!" Cole took off, with Henry and Maggie right behind him.
The woman was walking quickly toward the museum at the edge of the park.
"Excuse me!" Henry yelled. "Wait up!"
The woman glanced back. When she saw Henry and the others coming, she gasped and dashed toward the museum. She ran up the steps, disappearing inside.
"Stop!" Maggie yelled.
The Lemonade Detectives ran into the museum. It was cool and dim inside. The sound of footsteps echoed off the walls, but Henry couldn't tell which direction they were coming from.
"This way!" Cole cried, pointing.
Henry turned just in time to see the woman disappear around a corner. He ran after her and burst into a large room filled with sculptures.
"Where'd she go?" Maggie exclaimed.
"There!" Henry cried.
The Lemonade Detectives followed the woman through the next room, which was filled with paintings. Then she escaped into a hallway with lots of doors.
Cole glanced at all the doors. "Which way did she go?" he asked breathlessly.
A door leading outside was swinging shut. Henry hurried over and looked out into the Belltown Arts Day crowd.
He sighed. "I think we lost her."

The Lemonade Detectives hurried back outside. Henry scanned the crowd, looking for the mysterious woman. He spotted some shiny green fabric and stepped forward. Then he stopped. It was just a man wearing a green shirt.
"I don't see her," Cole said.
Henry sighed. "Me neither. It's hard to see anything in this crowd."
"We need to figure out where she went," Maggie declared. "Because she was definitely acting suspicious!"
"You're right," Cole said. "But why would a stranger steal Nathan's painting?"
Henry was wondering the same thing. "It doesn't make sense," he said.
Maggie frowned. "I told you, that woman is probably an international art thief. Anyway, why would she run unless she's guilty?"
"I don't know." Henry checked his phone. "We only have thirty minutes until the judging starts. We need to keep investigating all our suspects."
Cole nodded. "We can watch for that woman along the way."
"Let's ask Mrs. Sweet about Mr. Collins' alibi," Henry said. "After talking with her, we might be able to cross one suspect off the list."
They headed to the crafts fair. It was easy to spot Mrs. Sweet's booth by the long line near the free candy samples.
"Hi, kids. How's the lemonade business?" Mrs. Sweet asked.
"Great," Maggie said.
"Good!" Mrs. Sweet beamed at them. "Did you come to sign up for my candy class? The next one starts right after the art show judging."
"Maybe," Henry said. "Actually, we were wondering something. Was Mr. Collins here for your last class?"
"Oh yes." Mrs. Sweet chuckled. "I think that man ate more candy than he made! I had to chase him away after the class ended so I could clean up for the next class."
"Okay, that's one suspect off the list," Cole said as The Lemonade Detectives left the candy booth. "Who's left?"
Maggie ticked them off on her fingers. "Sunglasses woman, Nora, Hannah, and Patrick."
"Let's try to find Patrick first," Henry said. "It's kind of suspicious that he didn't meet Owen when he was supposed to."
"True," Cole agreed. "Maybe he was late because he was busy hiding Nathan's painting in the bushes somewhere."
They headed back toward the art show. Halfway there they spotted Patrick and Owen standing in line at the burger stand.
"We've been looking for you," Henry told Patrick.
"Join the club." Owen laughed. He didn't seem annoyed anymore.
"You found me," Patrick said. "What's up?"
"Did you hear about Nathan's painting?" Cole asked. "It's missing."
"Yeah, I heard." Patrick didn't look very upset. "So?"
"So where have you been for the past hour?" Maggie blurted out.
Owen laughed again. "Hey, dude," he told Patrick. "They're detectives. They must think you stole it!"
Patrick's eyes narrowed. "It wasn't me," he said. "Why would I want a dumb cat painting? Anyway, I was in the basket-weaving booth. You can ask Hannah if you don't believe me."
"Okay," Henry said. "Thanks for talking to us." He led Cole and Maggie away.
"Another alibi," Cole said. "I guess we can cross Patrick off the list too."
"I guess so." Henry shrugged. "We can double-check his alibi when we talk to Hannah."
Soon they reached the basket-weaving booth. Hannah was arranging baskets on a shelf.
"Hi," Henry said. "We were just talking to Patrick. He said he was over here earlier."
"Yeah." Hannah straightened a large blue basket. "He wanted me to teach him how to weave a basket."
"Really?" Cole asked. "You mean he actually wove one himself?"

Hannah nodded. "He did a pretty good job for a beginner. You can see for yourself if you want." She gestured toward a large shopping bag in the back of the booth. "His basket is in that bag. He wanted to leave it here so he wouldn't have to carry it around all day."
"That's okay. We don't need to see it." Henry led the way out of the booth.
"I just realized something," Maggie said. "Hannah is Patrick's alibi, right? That means Patrick is Hannah's alibi too. They were together when the painting disappeared."
"So that's two names off the suspect list," Henry said.
"Wait, I just thought of something else." Maggie frowned. "What if Hannah and Patrick are covering for each other? They could be in cahoots."
"I doubt it," Cole said. "They don't know each other that well. They're not even in the same grade."
"You're probably right," Maggie said. "I still think the weird woman with the sunglasses did it. Why else would she run away from us like that?"
Henry bit his lip. "I still don't know what her motive could be. But I guess she's our only suspect left." Suddenly he noticed Nora tiptoeing past them, looking rather guilty. "Well, except for one."
"Nora!" Maggie called. "Stop!"
Nora looked over at them. Then she ran away.
"Hey," Henry exclaimed in surprise.
"Catch her!" Cole took off after Nora.
Henry followed, with Maggie right beside him. Nora was surprisingly fast for a little kid. She turned into a booth filled with pottery.
"Careful," Maggie exclaimed as The Lemonade Detectives ran into the booth behind her. "This stuff looks breakable."
Just ahead Nora scooted under a low table full of vases.
"We can't fit under there," cried Henry. "We'll have to go around!"
Cole had already dashed out of the booth. Henry and Maggie followed as Cole sprinted after Nora.
"Nora, stop!" Maggie yelled. "We just want to talk to you!"
"There she goes." Cole pointed. Nora was ducking into another booth.
Maggie ran after her. Henry and Cole followed.
They found themselves in a quilting booth. "Hey, what are you kids doing?" a woman exclaimed. "This isn't a playground!"
"Sorry," Henry said breathlessly. Then he ran out of the booth after Nora.
She was heading out of the crafts fair and across the central part of the park. She ducked between two people waiting in line to buy hot dogs.
"Excuse me," Henry said, trying to push after her.
"Hey! Get in the back of the line!" one of the customers said.
"We're just passing through," Maggie said. Then she pointed at Nora. "We need to catch that little girl!"
"Oh, why didn't you say so?" the customer grumbled, finally moving aside.
For a second Henry thought they'd lost Nora. Then he spotted her running into the art show. She ducked behind the nearest display.
"Hurry!" Henry called to his friends, running after Nora. "We have to—oof!" He crashed into someone.
"Hey," a familiar voice said. "Watch where you're going!"
It was Hannah!
"What are you doing here?" Maggie sounded surprised.
"I decided to go for a walk," Hannah replied. "It's a free country."
"Okay," Henry said. "We're just surprised to see you here."
"Yeah. We thought you didn't like the art show," Cole added.
Hannah shrugged. "Does that mean I'm not allowed to walk past it?"
"No," Henry said. "But it makes you look a little suspicious."
Maggie nodded. "I bet she's trying to sabotage the whole art show by stealing the best painting!"
"What?" Hannah exclaimed. "No way, I wouldn't do that!"
"Are you sure?" Cole said. "You acted pretty weird when we mentioned Nathan's painting earlier. And a few minutes later, it disappeared!"
"I didn't take it." Hannah didn't sound annoyed anymore. "I'd never do that. Nathan's really talented. He deserves to win that spot in the museum!"
She sounded sincere. "Why would you care about his painting?" Henry asked. "I thought you didn't like art."
"That's not true," Hannah said quickly. "Actually, I love art."
"Huh?" Maggie looked confused. "But you said—"
"I know," Hannah interrupted. "I was just mad because I couldn't enter the art show myself."
"You were going to enter?" Cole asked.
Hannah nodded. "I like basket weaving. But I'm not crazy about it like my parents are. I'm a sculptor."
"Really?" Henry said.
"Yes. Want to see my latest sculpture?" Hannah asked shyly. "I have pictures of it on my phone."
"Sure," Henry said.
Hannah pulled out her phone and showed Henry and the others photos of her sculpture. It was of a girl holding a cat.
"Wow," Cole said. "You're really good!"

"Thanks." Hannah sounded sad. "I wanted to enter the art show this year. But my family was so busy getting ready for the crafts fair, I didn't have much time to sculpt. So my piece wasn't ready in time."
"That's why you sounded mad earlier," Henry guessed.
"I guess I was jealous." Hannah sighed. "But I wouldn't steal another artist's work—I promise."
Henry believed her. He could tell his friends did too.
"Thanks for showing us your sculpture," he said, handing back Hannah's phone. "Sorry we suspected you."
"It's okay," Hannah said. "I don't blame you. I was acting weird."
"You sure were," Maggie told her. "But I understand why now."
Hannah smiled. "Want to watch the judging with me?" she asked. "I figure that will help me get inspired to enter next year."
"Sorry, we can't," Cole said. "We still have to solve the mystery."
"Yeah," Henry said. "We need to track down . . . Nora!" he shouted.
The little girl was tiptoeing past them again. She heard Henry yell and started running.
Maggie leaped forward and grabbed Nora's arm before the little girl could duck under the next display.
"Got her!" Maggie exclaimed.
Nora burst into tears. "I'm sorry!" she wailed. "I only took it because of Patches!"
"It's all right, Nora," Henry said. He was relieved that they'd finally solved the mystery. "Just tell us where it is."
"Patches is mine!" Nora cried. "She's mine!"
"We know," Cole said. "But you can't just take other people's stuff, okay? You need to give it back now."
Nora stopped crying. Now she looked stubborn. "You're not the boss of me!" she said.
Maggie looked impatient. "Just hand it over. There's not much time left before the judging starts."
Cole looked at his phone. "Ten minutes," he said. "That's plenty of time to get the painting back in place."
Henry crouched down in front of Nora. "Please give it back, Nora," he said. "We won't yell at you, we promise."
"Okay." Nora sniffled. Then she reached into the pocket of her shorts.
"What are you doing?" Maggie demanded. "Show us where you hid the painting!"
Nora pulled something out of her pocket. "Here," she said, shoving it at Henry. "I didn't break it, even though Mommy thinks I break everything."
Henry stared at the item in surprise. It was a cell phone!
"What's this?" he blurted out.
"Mommy's phone," Nora said. "I used it to take pictures of Patches." She giggled. "I mean, the painting of Patches. That way I'll have it even if it goes to live in the museum."
"But where's the painting?" Maggie exclaimed. "We know you took it!"
"No, I didn't." Nora shook her head. "I took Mommy's phone though." She looked worried. "I think she's mad. She keeps chasing me."
"Wait. You mean you didn't take Nathan's painting?" Cole asked.
"No." Nora stared at him. "Why would I do that?"
Henry wasn't sure what to say for a moment. They hadn't solved the mystery after all!
"Nora!" a breathless voice called out. "There you are. Don't you dare run away from me again, young lady!"
Nora squeaked with surprise. "Mommy!" she exclaimed.
Nathan's mother reached them, looking out of breath and annoyed.
"I've been chasing her all over this park for the past hour!" she told The Lemonade Detectives.
"Here. She just gave this to us." Henry said.
"Thanks." Nora's mom took the phone and stuck it in her purse. Then she grabbed Nora by the arm. "Let's go have a serious talk, Nora."
She dragged the little girl away. The Lemonade Detectives wandered toward the lemonade stand.
"Nora was acting oddly because she took her mom's phone," Cole said. "She didn't steal the painting."
Henry nodded. "I'm not sure she could have reached the painting to steal it anyway."
"It would be hard for her to carry it too," Maggie added. "It's pretty big."
"You know what this means," Cole said. "The judging starts in ten minutes, and we're almost out of suspects."
Henry had been thinking the same thing. "It definitely wasn't Mr. Collins. He was at Mrs. Sweet's class the whole time," he said. "And Hannah and Patrick are each other's alibis."
Cole nodded. "Hannah doesn't have a motive and now we know it wasn't Nora, either."
"The only one left on the list is that sunglasses woman," Henry said. "But we don't know how to find her."
"She might not even be in the park anymore," Maggie added. "She's probably on her way to the big city to sell Nathan's painting!"
Henry didn't seem to hear Maggie. He was looking at the lemonade stand, which was just ahead.
"I think we have some customers," he said.
Cole gulped. "It's the judging committee!"
Henry, Cole, and Maggie all recognized the three art show judges. One was an art teacher from the high school. The second was the curator of the museum. And the third was a well-known local painter.
Maggie hurried forward. "We're here!" she called. "Would you like some lemonade?"
The museum curator, a slender woman with short gray hair, smiled at her. "Yes, please," she said. "We're about to start judging."
"And that makes us thirsty," the art teacher added with a chuckle.
The Lemonade Detectives poured each judge a cup of lemonade. As the committee wandered off, Henry looked at his friends.
"What should we do?" he wondered. "We're almost out of time."
Cole sighed. "I guess we should find Nathan and tell him we couldn't—"
"There she is!" Maggie shouted, pointing. "The woman with the sunglasses!"
Maggie was right. The woman was rushing away from the food stands. She had both hands up, covering her face.
"What's she doing?" Cole wondered.
Maggie looked grim. "I bet she recognized us," she said. "She must know we suspect her."
"Let's go!" Henry jumped out from behind the lemonade stand. "We can't let her get away again!"
Henry ran as fast as he could. The woman was walking quickly.
"There she goes—behind the restrooms!" Maggie said. "We might be able to trap her back there!"
The Lemonade Detectives sped after her. When they rounded the corner, the woman had stopped to look at some flowers.
"Don't take another step!" Maggie cried.
The woman looked startled. She backed away from them. "Who are you?"
Henry stepped forward. "We were about to ask you the same thing." His heart was pounding. They had to get the woman to confess!
"Very funny," the woman snapped. "Now what do you want?"
"We want you to give back our friend's painting," Cole said.
The woman blinked. "What?"
"Nathan's painting," Henry said. "We know you took it. Now tell us why you did it."
The woman shook her head, looking puzzled. "I didn't take anybody's painting."
"Then why did you run away from us earlier?" Maggie demanded.
The woman peered at her. "Oh, was that you? I didn't get a good look at you then." She frowned. "Wait! Were you kids chasing me earlier because you thought I stole some painting?"
"That's right," Henry said.
The woman touched her bright red hair. "So you weren't following me because you recognized me?"
"Yes, we were!" Maggie crossed her arms over her chest. "We recognized you as an international art thief!"
"Wait." Henry was listening carefully. "Why else would we recognize you? We already guessed you were from out of town, remember?"
This time the woman turned to peer at Henry. "You did?" Suddenly she nodded. "Oh right. You're the kids from the lemonade stand!"
"Yes," Cole said. "Who are you?"
"Daniella Diaz, of course!" The woman paused, looking at each of the kids. "The world-famous artist?"
Henry and the others looked at each other.
Cole shrugged. "Sorry," he said. "I guess we don't know much about art."

"Clearly." Daniella frowned. "Well, that's all right. I didn't want to be recognized today anyway. That's why I was trying to get out of sight when I saw the judges heading my way. I knew they'd spot me even in this wig." She patted her hair again.
"That's a wig?" Maggie stared at it. "Wow."
"So if you're really a world-famous artist, what are you doing in Belltown?" Cole asked.
"Yeah," Henry added. "And if you're a famous artist who doesn't want to be recognized, what are you doing at an art show?"

"I'm visiting relatives in the area," Daniella replied. "I didn't know this art show was going on until I got here." She shrugged. "But once I heard about it, I couldn't resist coming to take a look. I wanted to check for small-town talent."
"So you really didn't have anything to do with our friend's painting disappearing?" Henry asked.
"Of course not." Daniella looked insulted. "I create art—I don't steal it."
Henry nodded. "Okay. Sorry we suspected you."
"Yeah. And sorry we don't know who you are, even though you're famous," Cole added.
Daniella frowned. "Yes, well, I suppose that's for the best," she said. "You kids won't give away my secret, will you?"
"Of course not," Cole promised.
Maggie pulled a coin out of her pocket. "Here's your quarter back," she added. "You never got the lemonade you paid for."
Daniella looked surprised. "Thanks." She took the coin. "Now I'd better go. I don't want to miss the judging, and it's about to start."
As she hurried off, Henry glanced at the town clock. "She's right," he said with a sigh. "It's two o'clock."
"We'd better find Nathan and give him the bad news," Cole said.
"Yeah," Maggie looked hopeful. "Maybe he found his painting while we were running around chasing Nora and a world-famous artist we never heard of."
But when they found Nathan, he looked sad. He was staring at the empty spot where his painting had hung.
"Oh well," he said when The Lemonade Detectives told him what had happened. "I guess I can try again next year. My painting probably wouldn't have won a prize anyway."
Henry felt terrible. This was the first case that The Lemonade Detectives had failed to solve.
They all wandered over to the judges, to watch them make their rounds. The judges were examining Patrick's painting.
"Lovely use of light and shade," the art teacher was saying.
"Indeed," the curator agreed. "Quite accomplished for such a young artist."
Henry looked around to see what Patrick thought of their comments. To his surprise, Patrick was nowhere in sight.
However, he did notice Hannah watching nearby. Henry stared from Hannah to Patrick's painting and back again.
"I just remembered something that doesn't quite make sense," he told his friends. "Hurry—let's go check it out!"
"Huh?" Cole said to Henry. "Where are we going?"
Henry just started running. Cole, Maggie, and Nathan followed.
"Hey, where are you going?" Nora appeared behind them.
"Nowhere," Nathan called. "Go away."
Nora ignored her brother's orders and chased after them as Henry led the way to the basket-weaving booth. They arrived just in time to see someone scurrying out, holding a large shopping bag.
"Patrick!" Henry called. "Stop!"
Patrick scowled. "What? I need to get back to the art show for the judging."
"You're too late," Maggie informed him. "The judges already looked at your painting. Why weren't you there?"
She still looked confused. So did Cole and Nathan. Nora wasn't paying attention to any of them. She was looking at some pretty baskets nearby.
Henry stared at the shopping bag. "We heard you made a basket," he said. "It must be really large if you need that huge bag to carry it."
"Yeah, so what?" Patrick glared at Henry.
Henry smiled. "Can we see it?"
Just then Hannah appeared. "His basket isn't large," she said. "He made a little round basket, just like everyone else."
"What are you doing here?" Maggie asked her.
"I saw you guys run off." Hannah shrugged. "I was curious, so I followed you. What's going on?"
"If Patrick made a small basket, why'd you put it in such a big bag?" Henry asked Hannah.
"That's Patrick's bag," Hannah said. "He told me he'd put his basket in there. He said it had extra canvases in it."
"If that's true, maybe you should show us," Henry told Patrick.
Patrick looked stubborn. "Why should I? It's none of your business what I have in my bag."
Maggie stepped forward. "You'd better show us what's in your bag! And if there's a painting of a cat in there, you're going to be in big trouble!"
Nora rushed over. "A painting of a cat?" she cried. "No! That's mine!" She grabbed the shopping bag out of Patrick's hand.
"Hey!" Patrick cried.
But Nora was already dumping out the contents. A tiny basket tumbled onto the ground—followed by Nathan's painting!
"Aha!" Cole cried. "But wait. I thought Patrick had an alibi."

"Me too," said Henry. "Then I realized something: Hannah told us that Patrick was in her booth. But she didn't say exactly when he was there. And I remembered he had a big bag, but probably made a tiny basket." He shrugged. "Besides, Patrick was the one with the best motive all along."
Patrick's eyes looked watery. "I'm sorry, Nathan," he blurted out. "I really wanted my painting to be in the museum. When Owen told us how much the judges liked yours, I panicked."
Patrick's parents were standing nearby. "Patrick!" his mother cried. "I cannot believe what I am hearing!"
Patrick slunk over to his parents. While they scolded him harshly, Cole grabbed the painting. "We need to get this back before it's too late!"
But when the kids arrived back at the art show, the judges were finished.
"Wait!" Maggie cried. "We have one more painting."
"I'm sorry, young lady," the art teacher said. "I'm afraid it's too late. We've already chosen the winners."
"But it's not Nathan's fault his painting wasn't here!" Cole protested.
The curator shook her head. "I'm sorry. We can't—"
Suddenly Daniella stepped out of the crowd. "Perhaps I can change your minds?"
She whipped off her red wig, revealing dark hair beneath. The judges all gasped.
"Can it be?" the art teacher exclaimed.
"It's Daniella Diaz!" the local painter cried.
The curator looked awed. "I'd recognize her anywhere."
Henry glanced at his friends. They looked surprised.
"I guess she really is world famous," Cole whispered.
"Please, dear art lovers." Daniella took Nathan's painting out of Cole's hands. "Could you include my young friend's painting in your little contest? I'd consider it a personal favor."
"Of course!" the local painter exclaimed. "We'll take a look right now."
The curator peered at the painting. "Oh, I remember this one," she said. "It was one of my favorites."
Henry stepped over to Daniella. "Thanks for helping my friend," he told her. "Even though you didn't want to be recognized."
Daniella winked. "Anything for art, my boy."
"Wow," Henry said later as the curator hung up Nathan's painting. "It looks great!"
Nathan looked stunned. "I can't believe my painting is in the museum!"
Nora stared up at the painting. "Hi, Patches," she said sadly.
"Don't worry." Nathan put an arm around her. "The painting is yours, just like I promised. The museum is just borrowing it for a year, okay?"
"Mine! Hooray!" Nora cheered.
Nathan laughed. "And hooray for The Lemonade Detectives!" he added. "They always solve the case—eventually!"
